abstract: Single nerve cells with static properties have traditionally been viewed as the building blocks for networks that show emergent phenomena. In contrast to this approach, we study here how the overall network activity can control single cell parameters such as input resistance, as well as time and space constants, parameters that are crucial for excitability and spatio(cid:173) temporal integration. Using detailed computer simulations of neocortical pyramidal cells, we show that the spontaneous background firing of the network provides a means for setting these parameters. The mechanism for this control is through the large conductance change of the membrane that is induced by both non-NMDA and NMDA excitatory and inhibitory synapses activated by the spontaneous background activity.

paragraphs: This paper studies how activity across a neural network can alter the operating properties of an individual neuron. It focuses on input resistance and the time and space constants that influence excitability and the integration of signals. These properties determine how a cell combines inputs arriving at different locations and times.

The authors use detailed computer simulations of neocortical pyramidal cells. Their simulations show that spontaneous background firing can set these cellular parameters. The mechanism is a substantial change in membrane conductance caused by synaptic activity, involving excitatory and inhibitory inputs and the excitatory receptor types described in the abstract.

The result makes the surrounding network's activity part of the explanation for a single cell's behavior. A neuron's integration properties are not treated as fixed ingredients supplied to the network; they can depend on the network's ongoing activity. This matters for interpreting cellular responses because the background state helps determine how subsequent signals are combined and how readily the cell responds.
summary.tldr: Simulations show that spontaneous network activity changes membrane conductance and thereby controls how individual neurons integrate inputs.

title: Network activity determines spatio-temporal integration in single cells

abstract: A board is described that contains the ANN A neural-network chip, and a DSP32C digital signal processor. The ANNA (Analog Neural Network Arithmetic unit) chip performs mixed analog/digital processing. The combination of ANNA with the DSP allows high-speed, end-to-end ex(cid:173) ecution of numerous signal-processing applications, including the prepro(cid:173) cessing, the neural-net calculations, and the postprocessing steps. The ANNA board evaluates neural networks 10 to 100 times faster than the DSP alone. The board is suitable for implementing large (million con(cid:173) nections) networks with sparse weight matrices. Three applications have been implemented on the board: a convolver network for slant detection of text blocks, a handwritten digit recognizer, and a neural network for recognition-based segmentation.

paragraphs: The paper describes a computing board that pairs the ANNA neural-network chip with a DSP32C digital signal processor. ANNA combines analog and digital processing for neural-network arithmetic. Bringing these components together supports an entire signal-processing application, including preparation of inputs, neural-network calculations, and processing of the resulting outputs.

The reported speed advantage concerns network evaluation: the board evaluates neural networks 10 to 100 times faster than the digital signal processor alone. The architecture also supports large networks with around a million connections when their weight matrices are sparse. Sparsity is therefore a stated part of the intended large-network use case.

Three implemented applications illustrate the board's range: detecting the slant of text blocks with a convolver network, recognizing handwritten digits, and performing recognition-based segmentation. Together, they show how dedicated neural arithmetic can serve several stages and types of visual processing. The contribution is both a hardware combination and its use in working applications, with the digital processor helping turn the neural chip into an end-to-end computing system.
summary.tldr: The ANNA board combines neural hardware with a digital signal processor to evaluate networks 10 to 100 times faster than the processor alone.

title: A Neurocomputer Board Based on the ANNA Neural Network Chip

abstract: We present a framework for programming tbe bidden unit representations of simple recurrent networks based on the use of hint units (additional targets at the output layer). We present two ways of analysing a network trained within this framework: Input patterns act as operators on the information encoded by the context units; symmetrically, patterns of activation over tbe context units act as curried functions of the input sequences. Simulations demonstrate that a network can learn to represent three different functions simultaneously and canonical discriminant analysis is used to investigate bow operators and curried functions are represented in the space of bidden unit activations.

paragraphs: The paper presents a way to guide the internal representations of simple recurrent networks. It adds hint units, which are extra output targets used during training. These targets provide supervision that helps shape what the hidden units represent, making the network's internal organization an explicit part of the learning problem.

The authors offer two complementary interpretations of the trained network. An input pattern can be viewed as an operator that changes information stored in the context units. Conversely, a context activation pattern can be viewed as a curried function: it fixes part of a computation and determines how subsequent input sequences are processed.

Simulations show that a network can learn to represent three different functions simultaneously. The authors then use canonical discriminant analysis to examine how the operator and curried-function interpretations appear in hidden-unit activity. The contribution combines a method for shaping representations with ways to analyze them, linking recurrent computation to functional descriptions of both incoming inputs and stored context.
summary.tldr: Hint targets shape recurrent-network representations that can be analyzed as input-driven operators and context-dependent functions.

title: Operators and curried functions: Training and analysis of simple recurrent networks

abstract: Memory-based classification algorithms such as radial basis func(cid:173) tions or K-nearest neighbors typically rely on simple distances (Eu(cid:173) clidean, dot product ... ), which are not particularly meaningful on pattern vectors. More complex, better suited distance measures are often expensive and rather ad-hoc (elastic matching, deformable templates). We propose a new distance measure which (a) can be made locally invariant to any set of transformations of the input and (b) can be computed efficiently. We tested the method on large handwritten character databases provided by the Post Office and the NIST. Using invariances with respect to translation, rota(cid:173) tion, scaling, shearing and line thickness, the method consistently outperformed all other systems tested on the same databases.

paragraphs: Memory-based classifiers depend on a measure of similarity between an input and stored examples. The paper argues that simple distances between pattern vectors can poorly reflect meaningful visual resemblance. More elaborate matching methods can address this mismatch, but the authors identify computational expense and ad hoc design as concerns.

They propose an efficiently computable distance that can be made locally insensitive to a chosen set of input transformations. Local invariance means that small changes of the specified kinds need not make two patterns appear substantially different. This places knowledge about acceptable variation directly into the comparison used for recognition.

The method was tested on large handwritten-character databases from the Post Office and NIST. The selected invariances covered translation, rotation, scaling, shearing, and line thickness. The authors report that it consistently surpassed every other system tested on those same databases. The result supports the importance of a task-appropriate distance: accounting for transformations that preserve character identity can improve recognition while retaining efficient comparison.
summary.tldr: An efficient, locally transformation-invariant distance improves handwritten-character recognition by discounting selected identity-preserving changes.

title: Efficient Pattern Recognition Using a New Transformation Distance

abstract: One approach to invariant object recognition employs a recurrent neu(cid:173) ral network as an associative memory. In the standard depiction of the network's state space, memories of objects are stored as attractive fixed points of the dynamics. I argue for a modification of this picture: if an object has a continuous family of instantiations, it should be represented by a continuous attractor. This idea is illustrated with a network that learns to complete patterns. To perform the task of filling in missing in(cid:173) formation, the network develops a continuous attractor that models the manifold from which the patterns are drawn. From a statistical view(cid:173) point, the pattern completion task allows a formulation of unsupervised learning in terms of regression rather than density estimation. A classic approach to invariant object recognition is to use a recurrent neural net(cid:173) work as an associative memory[l]. In spite of the intuitive appeal and biological plausibility of this approach, it has largely been abandoned in practical applications. This paper introduces two new concepts that could help resurrect it: object repre(cid:173) sentation by continuous attractors, and learning attractors by pattern completion. In most models of associative memory, memories are stored as attractive fixed points at discrete locations in state space[l]. Discrete attractors may not be appropriate for patterns with continuous variability, like the images of a three-dimensional object from different viewpoints. When the instantiations of an object lie on a continuous pattern manifold, it is more appropriate to represent objects by attractive manifolds of fixed points, or continuous attractors. To make this idea practical, it is important to find methods for learning attractors from examples. A naive method is to train the network to retain examples in short(cid:173) term memory. This method is deficient because it does not prevent the network from storing spurious fixed points that are unrelated to the examples. A superior method is to train the network to restore examples that have been corrupted, so that it learns to complete patterns by filling in missing information. Learning Continuous Attractors in Recurrent Networks

paragraphs: This paper proposes representing continuously varying objects with continuous attractors in a recurrent neural network. In conventional associative memory, each stored pattern corresponds to an isolated stable state. An object seen from continuously changing viewpoints instead produces a family of related patterns. A continuous attractor represents that family as a connected set of stable states.

The network learns through pattern completion: it receives corrupted examples and is trained to restore missing information. This training develops an attractor that models the manifold from which the patterns were drawn. The paper contrasts this with simply teaching a network to retain examples, which can also leave it storing unrelated, spurious stable states.

The contribution links a representation choice to a learning task. Continuous attractors capture smooth variation, while restoration teaches the network how incomplete observations relate to that structure. Statistically, this casts unsupervised learning as regression through pattern completion instead of density estimation. The demonstrated network illustrates how learning to reconstruct examples can organize recurrent dynamics around their underlying continuous family.
summary.tldr: Training recurrent networks to complete corrupted patterns can produce continuous attractors that represent smoothly varying families of observations.

title: Learning Continuous Attractors in Recurrent Networks

paragraphs: A decision tree's number of leaves is a simple measure of complexity, but it may exaggerate how much of the tree the data actually use. This paper develops generalization bounds that capture that distinction. Its starting point is a set of techniques for thresholded real-valued classifiers whose guarantees can be smaller than conventional bounds based on VC theory.

The authors extend these techniques by expressing Boolean functions as two-layer neural networks built from thresholded convex combinations of Boolean functions. For a tree that correctly classifies its training examples and has bounded depth, the resulting bound uses an effective number of leaves. This quantity becomes smaller when training examples are distributed unevenly across the leaves.

The guarantee also reflects the training sample size, tree depth, and complexity of the functions used at decision nodes. Thus, nominal tree size alone does not determine the bound. The authors obtain related results for disjunctive normal form formulas. Their contribution is theoretical: data-dependent use of a classifier's structure can support sharper error guarantees.
summary.tldr: Generalization bounds for decision trees and DNF formulas can reflect effective structural complexity rather than nominal size alone.

title: Generalization in Decision Trees and DNF: Does Size Matter?

abstract: The S-Map is a network with a simple learning algorithm that com(cid:173) bines the self-organization capability of the Self-Organizing Map (SOM) and the probabilistic interpretability of the Generative To(cid:173) pographic Mapping (GTM). The simulations suggest that the S(cid:173) Map algorithm has a stronger tendency to self-organize from ran(cid:173) dom initial configuration than the GTM. The S-Map algorithm can be further simplified to employ pure Hebbian learning, with(cid:173) out changing the qualitative behaviour of the network.

The simulations suggest that the S(cid:173) Map algorithm has a stronger tendency to self-organize from ran(cid:173) dom initial configuration than the GTM. The S-Map algorithm can be further simplified to employ pure Hebbian learning, with(cid:173) out changing the qualitative behaviour of the network.

paragraphs: The S-Map is designed to combine two desirable properties of topographic mapping networks: the capacity to organize itself during learning and a probabilistic interpretation of the resulting model. The paper draws these properties from the Self-Organizing Map and Generative Topographic Mapping, respectively, and brings them together through a simple learning algorithm.

The simulations focus on whether useful organization emerges from a random initial configuration. They suggest that S-Map has a stronger tendency to self-organize than Generative Topographic Mapping. This matters because the starting arrangement is part of the learning problem: an algorithm must develop structure from an initially unorganized configuration.

The authors also simplify the learning procedure further so that it uses pure Hebbian learning. They report that this preserves the network's qualitative behavior. The contribution is therefore both a combined mapping approach and evidence that its characteristic organization can survive a simpler update mechanism. The stated comparison concerns self-organization in simulations, while the simplification concerns preservation of qualitative network behavior.
summary.tldr: S-Map combines self-organization with probabilistic interpretation and retains its qualitative behavior under a simplified Hebbian learning rule.

title: S-Map: A Network with a Simple Self-Organization Algorithm for Generative Topographic Mappings

abstract: Nonlinear (cid:12)ltering can solve very complex problems, but typically involve very time consuming calculations. Here we show that for (cid:12)lters that are constructed as a RBF network with Gaussian basis functions, a decomposition into linear (cid:12)lters exists, which can be computed e(cid:14)ciently in the frequency domain, yielding dramatic improvement in speed. We present an application of this idea to image processing. In electron micrograph images of photoreceptor terminals of the fruit (cid:13)y, Drosophila, synaptic vesicles containing neurotransmitter should be detected and labeled automatically. We use hand labels, provided by human experts, to learn a RBF (cid:12)lter using Support Vector Regression with Gaussian kernels. We will show that the resulting nonlinear (cid:12)lter solves the task to a degree of accuracy, which is close to what can be achieved by human experts. This allows the very time consuming task of data evaluation to be done e(cid:14)ciently.

paragraphs: Nonlinear image filters can handle difficult recognition tasks but may require expensive computation. This paper identifies a useful structure in filters represented by radial basis function networks with Gaussian basis functions. Such filters admit a decomposition into linear filters that can be computed efficiently in the frequency domain, producing a dramatic speed improvement.

The application is automatic detection and labeling of neurotransmitter-containing synaptic vesicles in electron micrographs of fruit-fly photoreceptor terminals. Human experts supply hand labels, and the authors use support vector regression with Gaussian kernels to learn the nonlinear filter. The training procedure thus connects expert judgments to a filter tailored to this image-analysis task.

The resulting filter achieves accuracy close to that of human experts, according to the paper. Coupling this recognition performance with faster computation makes a time-consuming evaluation task more efficient. The computational result applies to the specified Gaussian radial basis function filter structure, while the application demonstrates how that structure can support practical biological image analysis.
summary.tldr: A fast decomposition of Gaussian RBF filters supports near-expert detection of synaptic vesicles in electron micrographs.

title: Nonlinear Filtering of Electron Micrographs by Means of Support Vector Regression

abstract: We consider the problem of recovering an underwater image distorted by surface waves. A large amount of video data of the distorted image is acquired. The problem is posed in terms of finding an undistorted image patch at each spatial location. This challenging reconstruction task can be formulated as a manifold learning problem, such that the center of the manifold is the image of the undistorted patch. To compute the center, we present a new technique to estimate global distances on the manifold. Our technique achieves robustness through convex flow computations and solves the “leakage” problem inherent in recent manifold embedding techniques.

paragraphs: The paper tackles reconstruction of an underwater image distorted by waves at the surface. It starts with a large amount of video showing the distorted image and formulates recovery locally: at each spatial position, the task is to find the corresponding undistorted image patch.

The authors recast this reconstruction as a manifold-learning problem. In their formulation, the changing distorted observations have a manifold whose center represents the undistorted patch. Recovering the image therefore depends on locating that center. This connects the physical reconstruction task to estimating the geometry of a collection of observed patches.

To compute the center, the paper introduces a method for estimating global distances on the manifold. It uses convex flow computations to obtain robustness and is stated to solve the leakage problem in recent manifold-embedding techniques. The contribution links a new geometric distance calculation to a concrete reconstruction objective: using many wave-distorted observations to recover the undistorted image patch at each location.
summary.tldr: Wave-distorted underwater video is reconstructed through manifold centers, using a new global-distance method based on convex flow computations.

title: Seeing through water

abstract: We present a competitive analysis of Bayesian learning algorithms in the online learning setting and show that many simple Bayesian algorithms (such as Gaussian linear regression and Bayesian logistic regression) per- form favorably when compared, in retrospect, to the single best model in the model class. The analysis does not assume that the Bayesian algo- rithms’ modeling assumptions are “correct,” and our bounds hold even if the data is adversarially chosen. For Gaussian linear regression (us- ing logloss), our error bounds are comparable to the best bounds in the online learning literature, and we also provide a lower bound showing that Gaussian linear regression is optimal in a certain worst case sense. We also give bounds for some widely used maximum a posteriori (MAP) estimation algorithms, including regularized logistic regression.

The analysis does not assume that the Bayesian algo- rithms’ modeling assumptions are “correct,” and our bounds hold even if the data is adversarially chosen. paragraphs: This paper analyzes Bayesian learning as an online prediction problem. It compares an algorithm's accumulated performance with that of the single best model chosen afterward from the same model class. This retrospective benchmark asks whether sequential Bayesian predictions remain competitive even though the learner cannot know the eventual best model in advance.

The analysis does not require the Bayesian model's assumptions to describe the data correctly. Its bounds also hold for adversarially selected data. The authors show favorable comparisons for several simple Bayesian algorithms, including Gaussian linear regression and Bayesian logistic regression, giving a basis for evaluating them beyond the correctness of their probabilistic assumptions.

For Gaussian linear regression measured by logarithmic loss, the upper bounds are comparable to the best online-learning bounds discussed in the paper. A lower bound establishes optimality in a particular worst-case sense. The authors also obtain guarantees for maximum a posteriori methods, including regularized logistic regression, extending the competitive analysis to these commonly used estimation procedures.
summary.tldr: Bayesian online predictors receive competitive guarantees that hold even with incorrect modeling assumptions and adversarially chosen data.

title: Online Bounds for Bayesian Algorithms

abstract: Recently, there have been several advances in the machine learning and pattern recognition communities for developing manifold learning algo- rithms to construct nonlinear low-dimensional manifolds from sample data points embedded in high-dimensional spaces. In this paper, we de- velop algorithms that address two key issues in manifold learning: 1) the adaptive selection of the neighborhood sizes; and 2) better fitting the local geometric structure to account for the variations in the curvature of the manifold and its interplay with the sampling density of the data set. We also illustrate the effectiveness of our methods on some synthetic data sets.

In this paper, we de- velop algorithms that address two key issues in manifold learning: 1) the adaptive selection of the neighborhood sizes; and 2) better fitting the local geometric structure to account for the variations in the curvature of the manifold and its interplay with the sampling density of the data set. We also illustrate the effectiveness of our methods on some synthetic data sets.

paragraphs: Manifold learning seeks a low-dimensional description of data represented in a high-dimensional space. This paper focuses on how to recover that description when the geometry varies across the data. Its central concern is the local information used to build the representation: which nearby points to consider, and how to fit the shape they collectively describe.

The authors develop algorithms addressing two connected choices. One adaptively selects neighborhood sizes. The other improves the fit to local geometry by accounting for changes in manifold curvature and their interaction with sampling density. These issues belong together because a neighborhood contains both information about the underlying shape and evidence shaped by how densely that region was sampled.

The contribution is therefore an approach to making local modeling responsive to the data's geometry and distribution. A single treatment of all neighborhoods need not capture the variation these algorithms target. The authors illustrate effectiveness on synthetic datasets, providing evidence for the proposed adaptations in those examples without claiming universal performance across manifold-learning problems.
summary.tldr: The paper adapts neighborhood sizes and local geometric fitting to account for manifold curvature and sampling density.

title: Adaptive Manifold Learning

abstract: Previous work has demonstrated that the image variations of many ob- jects (human faces in particular) under variable lighting can be effec- tively modeled by low dimensional linear spaces. The typical linear sub- space learning algorithms include Principal Component Analysis (PCA), Linear Discriminant Analysis (LDA), and Locality Preserving Projec- tion (LPP). All of these methods consider an n1 × n2 image as a high dimensional vector in Rn1×n2, while an image represented in the plane is intrinsically a matrix. In this paper, we propose a new algorithm called Tensor Subspace Analysis (TSA). TSA considers an image as the sec- ond order tensor in Rn1 ⊗ Rn2, where Rn1 and Rn2 are two vector spaces. The relationship between the column vectors of the image ma- trix and that between the row vectors can be naturally characterized by TSA. TSA detects the intrinsic local geometrical structure of the tensor space by learning a lower dimensional tensor subspace. We compare our proposed approach with PCA, LDA and LPP methods on two standard databases. Experimental results demonstrate that TSA achieves better recognition rate, while being much more efﬁcient.

paragraphs: Many subspace methods represent an image by flattening its pixels into one long vector. This paper proposes Tensor Subspace Analysis, which instead treats an image as a second-order tensor, retaining its matrix form. That representation allows relationships among rows and among columns to be characterized naturally within the learning method.

TSA learns a lower-dimensional tensor subspace intended to capture the intrinsic local geometry of the tensor space. The motivation connects to earlier observations that image variation, particularly for faces under changing lighting, can be represented effectively in low-dimensional spaces. TSA brings the image's two-dimensional organization into the construction of such a representation.

The authors compare TSA with principal component analysis, linear discriminant analysis, and locality preserving projection on two standard databases. The reported experiments show higher recognition rates and much greater efficiency for TSA. These results support preserving matrix structure as a useful design choice for the evaluated recognition tasks, alongside the method's explicit treatment of local geometry.
summary.tldr: Tensor Subspace Analysis preserves image matrix structure and achieves better recognition and efficiency than three vector-based methods in the reported comparisons.

title: Tensor Subspace Analysis

abstract: Establishing correspondence between distinct objects is an important and nontrivial task: correctness of the correspondence hinges on properties which are difficult to capture in an a priori criterion. While previous work has used a priori criteria which in some cases led to very good results, the present paper explores whether it is possible to learn a combination of features that, for a given training set of aligned human heads, characterizes the notion of correct correspondence. By optimizing this criterion, we are then able to compute correspondence and morphs for novel heads.

They start with a set of aligned human heads and learn a combination of features that characterizes correspondence for that training set. The learned combination becomes a criterion that can be optimized when matching another pair of heads.

Using this criterion, the authors compute correspondences and morphs for previously unseen heads. The result demonstrates the possibility of transferring a correspondence criterion learned from aligned examples to new objects in this setting. The contribution centers on learning how to judge a match, then using that learned judgment to guide correspondence computation and the construction of morphs.
summary.tldr: A correspondence criterion learned from aligned human heads enables matching and morphing of new heads.

title: Learning Dense 3D Correspondence

abstract: Semi-supervised methods use unlabeled data in addition to labeled data to con- struct predictors. While existing semi-supervised methods have shown some promising empirical performance, their development has been based largely based on heuristics. In this paper we study semi-supervised learning from the viewpoint of minimax theory. Our ﬁrst result shows that some common methods based on regularization using graph Laplacians do not lead to faster minimax rates of con- vergence. Thus, the estimators that use the unlabeled data do not have smaller risk than the estimators that use only labeled data. We then develop several new approaches that provably lead to improved performance. The statistical tools of minimax analysis are thus used to offer some new perspective on the problem of semi-supervised learning.

paragraphs: Semi-supervised regression uses unlabeled observations alongside examples with known targets. Although such methods had shown promising empirical behavior, this paper asks what their benefits look like under minimax analysis. That perspective evaluates statistical performance through worst-case risk, providing a theoretical way to assess whether additional unlabeled data improves prediction.

In the analyzed setting, using unlabeled data through these methods does not yield smaller risk than using labeled data alone. This result concerns the specified methods and minimax comparison, so it does not establish that unlabeled observations are universally unhelpful.

The authors then develop several new approaches with provable performance improvements. Together, the negative and positive results distinguish between simply incorporating unlabeled data and incorporating it in a statistically beneficial way. The paper's contribution is to use minimax theory both to scrutinize existing semi-supervised techniques and to guide methods whose improvement can be established formally.
summary.tldr: Minimax analysis finds no rate improvement for some graph-based semi-supervised methods and motivates alternatives with provable benefits.

title: Statistical Analysis of Semi-Supervised Regression

abstract: Gates are a new notation for representing mixture models and context-sensitive independence in factor graphs. Factor graphs provide a natural representation for message-passing algorithms, such as expectation propagation. However, message passing in mixture models is not well captured by factor graphs unless the entire mixture is represented by one factor, because the message equations have a containment structure. Gates capture this containment structure graphically, allowing both the independences and the message-passing equations for a model to be readily visualized. Different variational approximations for mixture models can be understood as different ways of drawing the gates in a model. We present general equations for expectation propagation and variational message passing in the presence of gates.

paragraphs: Factor graphs describe probabilistic models in a form suited to message-passing inference. Mixture models create a representational difficulty because their message equations contain nested structure. Ordinary factor graphs do not capture that structure well unless the whole mixture is collapsed into one factor, which obscures its internal organization.

The paper introduces gates as a graphical notation for this containment structure. Gates express mixture models and independence relationships that depend on context. By displaying which parts of the model sit inside which contexts, the notation makes both the model's independences and its message-passing equations easier to visualize together.

The authors also present general equations for expectation propagation and variational message passing with gates. Different variational approximations can be interpreted through different placements of gates in a model. The contribution therefore goes beyond a drawing convention: it connects graphical structure to inference calculations and provides a common way to understand alternative approximations for mixtures.
summary.tldr: Gates extend factor graphs to display mixture structure and support corresponding message-passing equations.

title: Gates

abstract: Using machine learning algorithms to decode intended behavior from neural activity serves a dual purpose. First, these tools can be used to allow patients to interact with their environment through a Brain-Machine Interface (BMI). Second, analysis of the characteristics of such methods can reveal the significance of various features of neural activity, stimuli and responses to the encoding-decoding task. In this study we adapted, implemented and tested a machine learning method, called Kernel Auto-Regressive Moving Average (KARMA), for the task of inferring movements from neural activity in primary motor cortex. Our version of this algorithm is used in an on-line learning setting and is updated when feedback from the last inferred sequence become available. We first used it to track real hand movements executed by a monkey in a standard 3D motor control task. We then applied it in a closed-loop BMI setting to infer intended movement, while arms were restrained, allowing a monkey to perform the task using the BMI alone. KARMA is a recurrent method that learns a nonlinear model of output dynamics. It uses similarity functions (termed kernels) to compare between inputs. These kernels can be structured to incorporate domain knowledge into the method. We compare KARMA to various state-of-the-art methods by evaluating tracking performance and present results from the KARMA based BMI experiments.

paragraphs: The paper adapts Kernel Auto-Regressive Moving Average, or KARMA, to infer movement from activity in primary motor cortex. The method learns online, updating when feedback about the latest inferred sequence becomes available.

These functions can be designed to incorporate knowledge about the task, providing a way to connect the learning method with the domain's structure.

They then test a closed-loop interface with the monkey's arms restrained, allowing task performance through the interface alone. They compare tracking performance with other leading methods and report interface results. The study therefore examines both movement reconstruction and the use of inferred movement within an active control loop.
summary.tldr: An online recurrent kernel method decodes motor-cortex activity for hand tracking and closed-loop brain-machine control.

title: Kernel-ARMA for Hand Tracking and Brain-Machine interfacing During 3D Motor Control

abstract: We describe a primal-dual framework for the design and analysis of online strongly convex optimization algorithms. Our framework yields the tightest known logarithmic regret bounds for Follow-The-Leader and for the gradient descent algorithm proposed in HazanKaKaAg06. We then show that one can interpolate between these two extreme cases. In particular, we derive a new algorithm that shares the computational simplicity of gradient descent but achieves lower regret in many practical situations. Finally, we further extend our framework for generalized strongly convex functions.
originalAbstract: We describe a primal-dual framework for the design and analysis of online strongly convex optimization algorithms. Our framework yields the tightest known logarithmic regret bounds for Follow-The-Leader and for the gradient descent algorithm proposed in HazanKaKaAg06. We then show that one can interpolate between these two extreme cases. In particular, we derive a new algorithm that shares the computational simplicity of gradient descent but achieves lower regret in many practical situations. Finally, we further extend our framework for generalized strongly convex functions.

paragraphs: Online optimization requires making decisions as objectives are encountered over time. Regret measures the accumulated cost of those decisions relative to a comparison choice. This paper develops a primal-dual framework for designing and analyzing algorithms when the objectives are strongly convex, a structural property central to the logarithmic regret guarantees studied here.

The framework yields what the authors report as the tightest known logarithmic regret bounds for Follow-The-Leader and a previously proposed gradient-descent algorithm. It also connects these methods as endpoints of a broader range of possibilities. That connection allows the authors to derive algorithms between the endpoints, using a common analysis to understand their behavior.

One resulting algorithm retains the computational simplicity of gradient descent while achieving lower regret in many practical situations. This is a qualified advantage tied to the situations considered, rather than a claim of uniformly lower regret. The authors also extend the framework to generalized strongly convex functions. Together, the results provide both sharper analysis of existing methods and a route to new algorithms with useful computational and regret properties.
summary.tldr: A primal-dual framework sharpens logarithmic regret bounds and produces a simple online algorithm with lower regret in many practical situations.

title: Mind the Duality Gap: Logarithmic regret algorithms for online optimization

abstract: We propose an algorithm to perform multitask learning where each task has potentially distinct label sets and label correspondences are not readily available. This is in contrast with existing methods which either assume that the label sets shared by different tasks are the same or that there exists a label mapping oracle. Our method directly maximizes the mutual information among the labels, and we show that the resulting objective function can be efficiently optimized using existing algorithms. Our proposed approach has a direct application for data integration with different label spaces for the purpose of classification, such as integrating Yahoo! and DMOZ web directories.

paragraphs: Multitask learning often assumes that tasks use the same labels or that someone can supply a mapping between their label sets. This paper tackles the setting where label sets may differ and their correspondences are not readily available. The goal is to learn across tasks without requiring either of those starting conditions.

The method directly maximizes mutual information among the labels. This provides a way to express relationships between label spaces without first requiring identical label names or an externally supplied correspondence. The authors show that existing algorithms can efficiently optimize the resulting objective, connecting the proposed formulation to available optimization machinery.

A stated application is integrating classification data from differently organized web directories, such as Yahoo! and DMOZ. Their distinct label spaces illustrate why a shared-label assumption can obstruct data integration. The contribution is an algorithmic formulation for this mismatch: it makes dependence among labels the quantity to optimize, allowing the learning problem to be posed even when a label mapping is unavailable.
summary.tldr: Mutual-information optimization enables multitask learning with potentially different label sets and no supplied label correspondence.

title: Multitask Learning without Label Correspondences

abstract: Applications such as robot control and wireless communication require planning under uncertainty. Partially observable Markov decision processes (POMDPs) plan policies for single agents under uncertainty and their decentralized versions (DEC-POMDPs) find a policy for multiple agents. The policy in infinite-horizon POMDP and DEC-POMDP problems has been represented as finite state controllers (FSCs). We introduce a novel class of periodic FSCs, composed of layers connected only to the previous and next layer. Our periodic FSC method finds a deterministic finite-horizon policy and converts it to an initial periodic infinite-horizon policy. This policy is optimized by a new infinite-horizon algorithm to yield deterministic periodic policies, and by a new expectation maximization algorithm to yield stochastic periodic policies. Our method yields better results than earlier planning methods and can compute larger solutions than with regular FSCs.

paragraphs: Planning under uncertainty matters in applications such as robot control and wireless communication. Partially observable Markov decision processes describe the single-agent case, while decentralized versions handle multiple agents. For problems that continue indefinitely, policies can be represented by finite-state controllers. This paper introduces a periodic version of that representation.

The proposed controllers consist of layers connected only to the preceding and following layers. Construction begins with a deterministic policy for a finite planning horizon, which is converted into an initial periodic policy for an infinite horizon. This creates a route from a bounded planning problem to a controller intended for ongoing operation.

The authors then optimize the initial controller in two ways. A new infinite-horizon algorithm produces deterministic periodic policies, while a new expectation-maximization algorithm produces stochastic ones. The method reports better results than earlier planning approaches and can compute larger solutions than regular finite-state controllers, indicating that the periodic structure supports more capable planning within the studied framework.
summary.tldr: Periodic finite-state controllers support improved planning results and larger solutions for single-agent and decentralized partially observable problems.

title: Periodic Finite State Controllers for Efficient POMDP and DEC-POMDP Planning

abstract: A fundamental problem in the analysis of structured relational data like graphs, networks, databases, and matrices is to extract a summary of the common struc- ture underlying relations between individual entities. Relational data are typically encoded in the form of arrays; invariance to the ordering of rows and columns corresponds to exchangeable arrays. Results in probability theory due to Aldous, Hoover and Kallenberg show that exchangeable arrays can be represented in terms of a random measurable function which constitutes the natural model parameter in a Bayesian model. We obtain a ﬂexible yet simple Bayesian nonparametric model by placing a Gaussian process prior on the parameter function. Efﬁcient inference utilises elliptical slice sampling combined with a random sparse approximation to the Gaussian process. We demonstrate applications of the model to network data and clarify its relation to models in the literature, several of which emerge as special cases.

paragraphs: Relational datasets record connections among entities, often in arrays representing graphs, networks, databases, or matrices. The paper seeks a summary of the common structure behind those relationships. Its modeling basis is exchangeability: the relevant distribution is invariant to the ordering of rows and columns, so arbitrary ordering does not determine the modeled structure.

Probability results described in the abstract represent exchangeable arrays through a random measurable function. The authors treat that function as the parameter of a Bayesian model and place a Gaussian process prior on it. This yields a flexible Bayesian nonparametric model grounded in the representation of relational data through functions.

For efficient inference, the approach combines elliptical slice sampling with a random sparse approximation to the Gaussian process. The paper demonstrates applications to network data and explains connections to existing models, several of which arise as special cases. Its contribution is a simple, flexible modeling construction that also unifies established approaches within a broader function-based view of relational structure.
summary.tldr: A Gaussian process prior on the function representing an exchangeable array yields a flexible Bayesian model for networks and relational data.

title: Random function priors for exchangeable arrays with applications to graphs and relational data

abstract: Distributed learning of probabilistic models from multiple data repositories with minimum communication is increasingly important. We study a simple communication-efficient learning framework that first calculates the local maximum likelihood estimates (MLE) based on the data subsets, and then combines the local MLEs to achieve the best possible approximation to the global MLE, based on the whole dataset jointly. We study the statistical properties of this framework, showing that the loss of efficiency compared to the global setting relates to how much the underlying distribution families deviate from full exponential families, drawing connection to the theory of information loss by Fisher, Rao and Efron. We show that the full-exponential-family-ness" represents the lower bound of the error rate of arbitrary combinations of local MLEs, and is achieved by a KL-divergence-based combination method but not by a more common linear combination method. We also study the empirical properties of the KL and linear combination methods, showing that the KL method significantly outperforms linear combination in practical settings with issues such as model misspecification, non-convexity, and heterogeneous data partitions."

We study the statistical properties of this framework, showing that the loss of efficiency compared to the global setting relates to how much the underlying distribution families deviate from full exponential families, drawing connection to the theory of information loss by Fisher, Rao and Efron. paragraphs: When data are stored in separate repositories, communicating fitted models can be cheaper than collecting all observations centrally. This paper studies a two-stage framework: compute a maximum likelihood estimate at each repository, then combine those estimates to approximate the maximum likelihood estimate that joint access to all data would produce.

The analysis connects the unavoidable loss of statistical efficiency to how far the model family departs from a full exponential family. That structural property determines a lower bound on the error attainable by arbitrary combinations of the local estimates. A combination method based on KL divergence achieves the bound, whereas the more common linear combination does not.

The authors also compare the methods empirically in practical settings involving misspecified models, non-convexity, and heterogeneous data partitions. KL-based combination significantly outperforms linear combination in those evaluations. The results show why the aggregation rule matters: local fitted parameters contain a limited summary of the original data, and combining them effectively depends on the distribution family's structure.
summary.tldr: KL-based aggregation of local maximum likelihood estimates achieves an information-loss lower bound tied to exponential-family structure and outperforms linear aggregation empirically.

title: Distributed Estimation, Information Loss and Exponential Families

abstract: High dimensional regression benefits from sparsity promoting regularizations. Screening rules leverage the known sparsity of the solution by ignoring some variables in the optimization, hence speeding up solvers. When the procedure is proven not to discard features wrongly the rules are said to be safe. In this paper we derive new safe rules for generalized linear models regularized with L1 and L1/L2 norms. The rules are based on duality gap computations and spherical safe regions whose diameters converge to zero. This allows to discard safely more variables, in particular for low regularization parameters. The GAP Safe rule can cope with any iterative solver and we illustrate its performance on coordinate descent for multi-task Lasso, binary and multinomial logistic regression, demonstrating significant speed ups on all tested datasets with respect to previous safe rules.

When the procedure is proven not to discard features wrongly the rules are said to be safe. In this paper we derive new safe rules for generalized linear models regularized with L1 and L1/L2 norms. The rules are based on duality gap computations and spherical safe regions whose diameters converge to zero. This allows to discard safely more variables, in particular for low regularization parameters. paragraphs: Sparse regression models encourage many feature coefficients to become zero. If a solver can determine in advance that a feature will be unused, it can avoid spending computation on it. This paper develops screening rules that do so safely, meaning that they do not remove features that should remain in the solution.

The rules cover generalized linear models with L1 or L1/L2 regularization. They use computations of the duality gap to construct spherical safe regions whose diameters shrink to zero. As these regions become more precise, the rules can certify that additional variables are inactive. The abstract highlights this benefit particularly when regularization parameters are small.

GAP Safe screening can be combined with any iterative solver. The authors demonstrate it with coordinate descent for multi-task Lasso and for binary and multinomial logistic regression. They report significant speed improvements over earlier safe rules on every tested dataset. The contribution is a way to reduce optimization work while retaining the safety guarantee that motivates screening.
summary.tldr: GAP Safe rules use shrinking duality-gap-based regions to discard inactive variables safely and accelerate sparse-model solvers.

title: GAP Safe screening rules for sparse multi-task and multi-class models

abstract: We consider the problem of community detection or clustering in the labeled Stochastic Block Model (LSBM) with a finite number $K$ of clusters of sizes linearly growing with the global population of items $n$. Every pair of items is labeled independently at random, and label $\ell$ appears with probability $p(i,j,\ell)$ between two items in clusters indexed by $i$ and $j$, respectively. The objective is to reconstruct the clusters from the observation of these random labels. Clustering under the SBM and their extensions has attracted much attention recently. Most existing work aimed at characterizing the set of parameters such that it is possible to infer clusters either positively correlated with the true clusters, or with a vanishing proportion of misclassified items, or exactly matching the true clusters. We find the set of parameters such that there exists a clustering algorithm with at most $s$ misclassified items in average under the general LSBM and for any $s=o(n)$, which solves one open problem raised in \cite{abbe2015community}. We further develop an algorithm, based on simple spectral methods, that achieves this fundamental performance limit within $O(n \mbox{polylog}(n))$ computations and without the a-priori knowledge of the model parameters.

paragraphs: The labeled stochastic block model describes items in hidden clusters, with a random label observed for every pair. Label probabilities depend on the clusters containing the two items, and pair labels are generated independently. The paper assumes finitely many clusters, each growing linearly with the total population, and seeks to recover their memberships from the labels.

Rather than considering only exact recovery or a vanishing fraction of errors, the authors characterize when an algorithm can achieve at most s misclassified items on average for any s=o(n). This specifies an error target that grows more slowly than the population. It gives a finer account of recovery difficulty by connecting model parameters to a chosen average error allowance.

The paper also develops an algorithm based on simple spectral methods that reaches the fundamental performance limit. Its computation is O(n polylog(n)), and it does not require the model parameters in advance. The contribution therefore combines a characterization of what recovery accuracy is achievable with an efficient procedure attaining that limit under the stated model.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes attainable average clustering errors in labeled block models and gives an efficient spectral algorithm achieving that limit.

title: Optimal Cluster Recovery in the Labeled Stochastic Block Model

abstract: Batch normalization (BN) has proven to be an effective algorithm for deep neural network training by normalizing the input to each neuron and reducing the internal covariate shift. The space of weight vectors in the BN layer can be naturally interpreted as a Riemannian manifold, which is invariant to linear scaling of weights. Following the intrinsic geometry of this manifold provides a new learning rule that is more efficient and easier to analyze. We also propose intuitive and effective gradient clipping and regularization methods for the proposed algorithm by utilizing the geometry of the manifold. The resulting algorithm consistently outperforms the original BN on various types of network architectures and datasets.

The space of weight vectors in the BN layer can be naturally interpreted as a Riemannian manifold, which is invariant to linear scaling of weights. Following the intrinsic geometry of this manifold provides a new learning rule that is more efficient and easier to analyze. We also propose intuitive and effective gradient clipping and regularization methods for the proposed algorithm by utilizing the geometry of the manifold. The resulting algorithm consistently outperforms the original BN on various types of network architectures and datasets.

paragraphs: Batch normalization changes how neural-network weights relate to the computation performed by a layer. This paper focuses on the invariance to linear scaling of weights and interprets the corresponding weight space as a Riemannian manifold. That geometric view makes the scaling symmetry central to the design of the learning algorithm.

The authors derive a learning rule that follows the manifold's intrinsic geometry. They describe the resulting rule as more efficient and easier to analyze. The same geometry also guides proposed gradient clipping and regularization methods, connecting these training choices to the structure of the normalized weight space.

Experiments across multiple network architectures and datasets show that the resulting algorithm consistently outperforms original batch normalization in the evaluated settings. The contribution is therefore both conceptual and algorithmic: a geometric interpretation produces concrete changes to optimization and its supporting procedures. The reported empirical result supports those changes across the tested cases, without implying that every possible architecture or dataset must show the same advantage.
summary.tldr: A geometric treatment of batch-normalized weights yields a new learning rule, clipping method, and regularization approach with reported empirical gains.

title: Riemannian approach to batch normalization

abstract: We study the classical problem of maximizing a monotone submodular function subject to a cardinality constraint k, with two additional twists: (i) elements arrive in a streaming fashion, and (ii) m items from the algorithm’s memory are removed after the stream is finished. We develop a robust submodular algorithm STAR-T. It is based on a novel partitioning structure and an exponentially decreasing thresholding rule. STAR-T makes one pass over the data and retains a short but robust summary. We show that after the removal of any m elements from the obtained summary, a simple greedy algorithm STAR-T-GREEDY that runs on the remaining elements achieves a constant-factor approximation guarantee. In two different data summarization tasks, we demonstrate that it matches or outperforms existing greedy and streaming methods, even if they are allowed the benefit of knowing the removed subset in advance.
originalAbstract: We study the classical problem of maximizing a monotone submodular function subject to a cardinality constraint k, with two additional twists: (i) elements arrive in a streaming fashion, and (ii) m items from the algorithm’s memory are removed after the stream is finished. We develop a robust submodular algorithm STAR-T. It is based on a novel partitioning structure and an exponentially decreasing thresholding rule. STAR-T makes one pass over the data and retains a short but robust summary. We show that after the removal of any m elements from the obtained summary, a simple greedy algorithm STAR-T-GREEDY that runs on the remaining elements achieves a constant-factor approximation guarantee. In two different data summarization tasks, we demonstrate that it matches or outperforms existing greedy and streaming methods, even if they are allowed the benefit of knowing the removed subset in advance.

paragraphs: The paper studies selecting at most k items to maximize a monotone submodular objective, which captures increasing value with diminishing returns. It adds two practical complications: items arrive as a stream, and m stored items may be removed after processing finishes. A useful summary must therefore remain valuable despite those later deletions.

The proposed STAR-T algorithm processes the data once and stores a short, robust summary. Its construction combines a partitioning structure with exponentially decreasing acceptance thresholds. After any m summary elements are removed, a simple greedy procedure called STAR-T-GREEDY operates on the remaining items and achieves a constant-factor approximation guarantee.

The guarantee directly addresses the uncertainty about which stored items will disappear. The streaming stage prepares a summary that supports selection after deletion, without needing the removed subset in advance. In two data summarization tasks, the method matches or outperforms existing greedy and streaming approaches, even when those comparison methods know the deleted subset beforehand. These experiments complement the theoretical robustness guarantee with evidence on the evaluated tasks.
summary.tldr: STAR-T builds a one-pass summary that supports constant-factor submodular selection even after any specified number of stored items are deleted.

title: Streaming Robust Submodular Maximization: A Partitioned Thresholding Approach

abstract: We introduce a paradigm for understanding physical scenes without human annotations. At the core of our system is a physical world representation that is first recovered by a perception module and then utilized by physics and graphics engines. During training, the perception module and the generative models learn by visual de-animation --- interpreting and reconstructing the visual information stream. During testing, the system first recovers the physical world state, and then uses the generative models for reasoning and future prediction. Our system quickly recognizes the physical world state from appearance and motion cues, and has the flexibility to incorporate both differentiable and non-differentiable physics and graphics engines. We evaluate our system on both synthetic and real datasets involving multiple physical scenes, and demonstrate that our system performs well on both physical state estimation and reasoning problems. We further show that the knowledge learned on the synthetic dataset generalizes to constrained real images.

abstract: Deep neural networks (NNs) are powerful black box predictors that have recently achieved impressive performance on a wide spectrum of tasks. Quantifying predictive uncertainty in NNs is a challenging and yet unsolved problem. Bayesian NNs, which learn a distribution over weights, are currently the state-of-the-art for estimating predictive uncertainty; however these require significant modifications to the training procedure and are computationally expensive compared to standard (non-Bayesian) NNs. We propose an alternative to Bayesian NNs that is simple to implement, readily parallelizable, requires very little hyperparameter tuning, and yields high quality predictive uncertainty estimates. Through a series of experiments on classification and regression benchmarks, we demonstrate that our method produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates which are as good or better than approximate Bayesian NNs. To assess robustness to dataset shift, we evaluate the predictive uncertainty on test examples from known and unknown distributions, and show that our method is able to express higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution examples. We demonstrate the scalability of our method by evaluating predictive uncertainty estimates on ImageNet.

paragraphs: A neural network's prediction is more useful when accompanied by a meaningful indication of uncertainty. This paper proposes deep ensembles as a practical approach to estimating that uncertainty. The motivation is that Bayesian neural networks represent uncertainty through distributions over weights but require substantial training changes and more computation than standard neural networks.

The proposed alternative is simple to implement, readily parallelized, and requires little hyperparameter tuning. Experiments on classification and regression benchmarks show well-calibrated uncertainty estimates that match or outperform those from approximate Bayesian neural networks. Calibration concerns whether the confidence expressed by a predictor is consistent with how reliably it predicts, making it relevant beyond prediction accuracy alone.

The authors also examine dataset shift by testing examples from familiar and unfamiliar distributions. The method expresses higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution examples in these evaluations. An ImageNet evaluation demonstrates scalability. Together, the results support ensembles as an accessible way to obtain useful uncertainty estimates across predictive tasks, including a demonstrated response to inputs outside the training distribution.
summary.tldr: Deep ensembles provide scalable, well-calibrated predictive uncertainty and show higher uncertainty on unfamiliar-distribution examples.

title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles

abstract: Batch Normalization is quite effective at accelerating and improving the training of deep models. However, its effectiveness diminishes when the training minibatches are small, or do not consist of independent samples. We hypothesize that this is due to the dependence of model layer inputs on all the examples in the minibatch, and different activations being produced between training and inference. We propose Batch Renormalization, a simple and effective extension to ensure that the training and inference models generate the same outputs that depend on individual examples rather than the entire minibatch. Models trained with Batch Renormalization perform substantially better than batchnorm when training with small or non-i.i.d. minibatches. At the same time, Batch Renormalization retains the benefits of batchnorm such as insensitivity to initialization and training efficiency.

paragraphs: Batch normalization can make deep models train faster and more effectively, but its benefits weaken when training batches are small or contain dependent examples. This paper investigates an extension aimed at those conditions. The authors hypothesize that the difficulty comes from two related features: a layer's inputs depend on other examples in the batch, and activations differ between training and inference.

Batch Renormalization is designed to align the outputs produced during training and inference while making them depend on individual examples rather than the entire minibatch. The key idea is to change the normalization behavior so that the surrounding batch has less influence on how an example is processed. This directly addresses the mechanism proposed in the authors' hypothesis.

The reported models substantially outperform batch normalization when trained with small or non-independent minibatches. They also retain training efficiency and reduced sensitivity to initialization. These findings support the extension's usefulness under the batch conditions studied, while the explanation of why ordinary batch normalization struggles remains explicitly framed as a hypothesis.
summary.tldr: Batch Renormalization improves training with small or dependent minibatches by aligning training and inference behavior.

title: Batch Renormalization: Towards Reducing Minibatch Dependence in Batch-Normalized Models

abstract: We present a novel model architecture which leverages deep learning tools to perform exact Bayesian inference on sets of high dimensional, complex observations. Our model is provably exchangeable, meaning that the joint distribution over observations is invariant under permutation: this property lies at the heart of Bayesian inference. The model does not require variational approximations to train, and new samples can be generated conditional on previous samples, with cost linear in the size of the conditioning set. The advantages of our architecture are demonstrated on learning tasks that require generalisation from short observed sequences while modelling sequence variability, such as conditional image generation, few-shot learning, and anomaly detection.

The advantages of our architecture are demonstrated on learning tasks that require generalisation from short observed sequences while modelling sequence variability, such as conditional image generation, few-shot learning, and anomaly detection.

paragraphs: BRUNO is a deep recurrent architecture for reasoning about sets of complex, high-dimensional observations. Its defining property is exchangeability: changing the order of observations leaves their joint probability unchanged. This matters when the observations should be treated as a set, even though a recurrent model processes them through a sequence.

The architecture supports exact Bayesian inference within its model and does not require variational approximations for training. It can also generate new observations conditioned on examples already seen. The computational cost of that conditional generation grows linearly with the number of conditioning examples, giving a stated scaling relationship as more evidence is supplied.

The paper demonstrates the architecture on conditional image generation, few-shot learning, and anomaly detection. These tasks share a need to generalize from short observed sequences while representing variability among possible observations. BRUNO's contribution is to combine that flexibility with a provable ordering invariance, so the probabilistic treatment of a collection does not depend on which example happens to be presented first.
summary.tldr: BRUNO combines deep recurrent modeling with exact Bayesian inference and a provably order-invariant distribution over observations.

title: BRUNO: A Deep Recurrent Model for Exchangeable Data

abstract: Electronic health records provide a rich source of data for machine learning methods to learn dynamic treatment responses over time. However, any direct estimation is hampered by the presence of time-dependent confounding, where actions taken are dependent on time-varying variables related to the outcome of interest. Drawing inspiration from marginal structural models, a class of methods in epidemiology which use propensity weighting to adjust for time-dependent confounders, we introduce the Recurrent Marginal Structural Network - a sequence-to-sequence architecture for forecasting a patient's expected response to a series of planned treatments. Using simulations of a state-of-the-art pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic (PK-PD) model of tumor growth, we demonstrate the ability of our network to accurately learn unbiased treatment responses from observational data – even under changes in the policy of treatment assignments – and performance gains over benchmarks.

paragraphs: Forecasting treatment response from health records is complicated because treatment choices depend on a patient's changing condition. Those same changing variables can also influence the eventual outcome. Consequently, directly learning associations between treatments and outcomes can mix treatment effects with the reasons a treatment was selected.

The paper introduces the Recurrent Marginal Structural Network, a sequence-to-sequence model that predicts expected responses to a planned sequence of treatments. Its approach draws on marginal structural models, which use propensity weighting to adjust for time-dependent confounding. Combining this causal adjustment idea with a sequential architecture addresses both treatment-selection bias and the evolution of responses over time.

The authors evaluate the method using simulations from a pharmacokinetic-pharmacodynamic model of tumor growth. In those simulations, the network accurately learns unbiased treatment responses from observational data, including when treatment-assignment policies change, and improves on benchmarks. These findings support its ability to forecast under changing assignment rules in the studied simulation setting; the reported evaluation is not a clinical deployment.
summary.tldr: A recurrent forecasting model uses ideas from propensity weighting to learn treatment responses despite time-dependent confounding in tumor-growth simulations.

title: Forecasting Treatment Responses Over Time Using Recurrent Marginal Structural Networks

abstract: We identify a fundamental source of error in Q-learning and other forms of dynamic programming with function approximation. Delusional bias arises when the approximation architecture limits the class of expressible greedy policies. Since standard Q-updates make globally uncoordinated action choices with respect to the expressible policy class, inconsistent or even conflicting Q-value estimates can result, leading to pathological behaviour such as over/under-estimation, instability and even divergence. To solve this problem, we introduce a new notion of policy consistency and define a local backup process that ensures global consistency through the use of information sets---sets that record constraints on policies consistent with backed-up Q-values. We prove that both the model-based and model-free algorithms using this backup remove delusional bias, yielding the first known algorithms that guarantee optimal results under general conditions. These algorithms furthermore only require polynomially many information sets (from a potentially exponential support). Finally, we suggest other practical heuristics for value-iteration and Q-learning that attempt to reduce delusional bias.

paragraphs: Function approximation can restrict which greedy policies a reinforcement learning system can represent. This paper identifies a resulting error called delusional bias: separate Q-value updates may assume action choices that cannot all belong to one expressible policy. The resulting estimates can conflict, producing overestimation, underestimation, instability, or divergence.

The authors introduce policy consistency and a local backup procedure designed to maintain it globally. The procedure uses information sets that record constraints on policies compatible with backed-up Q-values. These records coordinate updates by keeping track of which action choices can coexist within the available policy class.

The paper proves that model-based and model-free algorithms using this procedure remove delusional bias and guarantee optimal results under the general conditions studied. They require only polynomially many information sets despite a potentially exponential collection of possibilities. The authors also suggest practical heuristics intended to reduce the bias. The contribution identifies representational incompatibility as a source of erroneous values and provides a principled way to keep value updates aligned with policies the architecture can actually express.
summary.tldr: Policy-consistent backups remove a source of Q-learning error caused by combining action choices that no representable policy can jointly realize.

title: Non-delusional Q-learning and value-iteration

abstract: Variational autoencoders (VAEs) are widely used deep generative models capable of learning unsupervised latent representations of data. Such representations are often difficult to interpret or control. We consider the problem of unsupervised learning of features correlated to specific labels in a dataset. We propose a VAE-based generative model which we show is capable of extracting features correlated to binary labels in the data and structuring it in a latent subspace which is easy to interpret. Our model, the Conditional Subspace VAE (CSVAE), uses mutual information minimization to learn a low-dimensional latent subspace associated with each label that can easily be inspected and independently manipulated. We demonstrate the utility of the learned representations for attribute manipulation tasks on both the Toronto Face and CelebA datasets.

paragraphs: Variational autoencoders learn hidden representations that can support data generation, but those representations are often difficult to understand or control. This paper focuses on organizing features correlated with binary labels into interpretable parts of the hidden representation. The aim is to make particular attributes easier to inspect and manipulate.

The proposed Conditional Subspace VAE, or CSVAE, learns a low-dimensional latent subspace associated with each label. Mutual-information minimization is part of the mechanism used to organize these subspaces. Instead of leaving all learned variation in an undifferentiated representation, the model gives label-associated features an explicit place within its latent structure.

The authors demonstrate attribute manipulation on the Toronto Face and CelebA datasets. These demonstrations show the utility of representations whose label-associated subspaces can be inspected and independently manipulated. The claim concerns features correlated with the labels: the paper's contribution is a controllable organization of learned variation, with practical examples of using that organization to alter attributes in generated data.
summary.tldr: CSVAE organizes features correlated with binary labels into interpretable latent subspaces that support independent attribute manipulation.

title: Learning Latent Subspaces in Variational Autoencoders

abstract: This paper introduces a model-based reinforcement learning (MBRL) framework that incorporates the underlying decision problem in learning the transition model of the environment. This is in contrast with conventional approaches to MBRL that learn the model of the environment, for example by finding the maximum likelihood estimate, without taking into account the decision problem. Value-Aware Model Learning (VAML) framework argues that this might not be a good idea, especially if the true model of the environment does not belong to the model class from which we are estimating the model. The original VAML framework, however, may result in an optimization problem that is difficult to solve. This paper introduces a new MBRL class of algorithms, called Iterative VAML, that benefits from the structure of how the planning is performed (i.e., through approximate value iteration) to devise a simpler optimization problem. The paper theoretically analyzes Iterative VAML and provides finite sample error upper bound guarantee for it.

paragraphs: Model-based reinforcement learning learns how an environment changes and then uses that model to make decisions. A conventional approach fits transitions by a statistical objective such as likelihood, without incorporating the decision problem. Value-Aware Model Learning questions this separation, especially when the available model family cannot represent the true environment.

In that setting, a model's usefulness depends on how its errors affect planning. The original value-aware formulation can lead to an optimization problem that is hard to solve. This paper introduces Iterative VAML, a class of algorithms that uses the structure of approximate value iteration to formulate a simpler model-learning problem.

The approach ties model estimation to the procedure that will use the model, allowing planning structure to inform what the learning objective emphasizes. The authors provide a theoretical analysis and a finite-sample upper bound on error. This supplies a formal guarantee for the proposed framework while addressing the optimization difficulty that motivated the iterative construction. Its central contribution is a more tractable route to decision-aware transition modeling.
summary.tldr: Iterative VAML uses approximate value iteration to simplify decision-aware transition-model learning and provides a finite-sample error bound.

title: Iterative Value-Aware Model Learning

abstract: We propose and study the known-compensation multi-arm bandit (KCMAB) problem, where a system controller offers a set of arms to many short-term players for $T$ steps. In each step, one short-term player arrives to the system. Upon arrival, the player greedily selects an arm with the current best average reward and receives a stochastic reward associated with the arm. In order to incentivize players to explore other arms, the controller provides proper payment compensation to players. The objective of the controller is to maximize the total reward collected by players while minimizing the compensation. We first give a compensation lower bound $\Theta(\sum_i {\Delta_i\log T\over KL_i})$, where $\Delta_i$ and $KL_i$ are the expected reward gap and Kullback-Leibler (KL) divergence between distributions of arm $i$ and the best arm, respectively. We then analyze three algorithms to solve the KCMAB problem, and obtain their regrets and compensations. We show that the algorithms all achieve $O(\log T)$ regret and $O(\log T)$ compensation that match the theoretical lower bound. Finally, we use experiments to show the behaviors of those algorithms.
