paragraphs: A system can benefit from exploring uncertain options even when each individual user prefers the option with the best current average reward. This paper studies that conflict in a bandit problem with a succession of short-term players. The controller offers payments to encourage exploration while seeking high total reward and low total compensation.

The authors derive a compensation lower bound involving the time horizon, each arm’s expected reward gap, and the Kullback-Leibler divergence between its reward distribution and that of the best arm. The bound connects the cost of incentives with both the reward difference and the statistical distinguishability of alternatives. It formalizes a cost that ordinary reward-focused bandit analysis does not directly capture.

They then analyze three algorithms and show that each achieves logarithmic growth in both regret and compensation, matching the stated lower-bound scaling in the horizon. Experiments illustrate the algorithms’ behavior. The results show that, in this known-compensation setting, incentives can support exploration while keeping both the accumulated reward shortfall and the required payments controlled.
summary.tldr: Three compensated bandit algorithms achieve logarithmic regret and compensation while incentivizing greedy short-term players to explore.

title: Multi-armed Bandits with Compensation

abstract: Machine learning models are often susceptible to adversarial perturbations of their inputs. Even small perturbations can cause state-of-the-art classifiers with high "standard" accuracy to produce an incorrect prediction with high confidence. To better understand this phenomenon, we study adversarially robust learning from the viewpoint of generalization. We show that already in a simple natural data model, the sample complexity of robust learning can be significantly larger than that of "standard" learning. This gap is information theoretic and holds irrespective of the training algorithm or the model family. We complement our theoretical results with experiments on popular image classification datasets and show that a similar gap exists here as well. We postulate that the difficulty of training robust classifiers stems, at least partially, from this inherently larger sample complexity.

We show that already in a simple natural data model, the sample complexity of robust learning can be significantly larger than that of "standard" learning. This gap is information theoretic and holds irrespective of the training algorithm or the model family. We complement our theoretical results with experiments on popular image classification datasets and show that a similar gap exists here as well. paragraphs: A classifier can perform well on ordinary inputs yet make confident errors after small adversarial changes. This paper examines that mismatch through generalization: how much training data is needed to perform reliably on new examples. It asks whether learning robustness can demand more information than learning accurate predictions on unmodified inputs.

The authors prove that a substantial gap in data requirements can arise even in a simple, natural data model. The gap is information theoretic, so within that setting it does not depend on choosing a particular training algorithm or model family. A different learning procedure alone cannot remove the data requirement established by the result.

Experiments on widely used image classification datasets reveal a similar gap, complementing the theoretical analysis with empirical evidence. The authors suggest that greater sample complexity explains at least part of the difficulty of training robust classifiers. This is a proposed partial explanation, while the formal result establishes that increased data requirements can be an inherent feature of robust learning in the analyzed model.
summary.tldr: Robust learning can inherently require substantially more data than standard learning, with a similar gap observed in image experiments.

title: Adversarially Robust Generalization Requires More Data

abstract: Direct democracy, where each voter casts one vote, fails when the average voter competence falls below 50%. This happens in noisy settings when voters have limited information. Representative democracy, where voters choose representatives to vote, can be an elixir in both these situations. We introduce a mathematical model for studying representative democracy, in particular understanding the parameters of a representative democracy that gives maximum decision making capability. Our main result states that under general and natural conditions, for fixed voting cost, the optimal number of representatives is linear; for polynomial cost, the optimal number of representatives is logarithmic.

Our main result states that under general and natural conditions, for fixed voting cost, the optimal number of representatives is linear; for polynomial cost, the optimal number of representatives is logarithmic.

paragraphs: This paper studies representative democracy as a mathematical decision-making system. Its starting point is a setting in which voters may have noisy or limited information. When average voter competence falls below one half, direct voting fails in the setting described by the authors. Choosing representatives can potentially improve decisions in these circumstances.

The authors introduce a model for asking which features of a representative system maximize its decision-making capability. A central design choice is how many representatives to use. The analysis connects this choice to the cost of voting, making the cost model part of the mathematical question rather than treating representation as a purely qualitative alternative.

Under conditions described as general and natural, the optimal number of representatives has linear scaling when voting cost is fixed and logarithmic scaling when cost is polynomial. These are conditional conclusions within the proposed model. Their significance is that changing the cost assumption changes the form of the optimal representative count, giving a precise way to study institutional design.
summary.tldr: A mathematical model links the optimal number of representatives to voting costs under stated conditions.

title: A Mathematical Model For Optimal Decisions In A Representative Democracy

abstract: Many classic methods have shown non-local self-similarity in natural images to be an effective prior for image restoration. However, it remains unclear and challenging to make use of this intrinsic property via deep networks. In this paper, we propose a non-local recurrent network (NLRN) as the first attempt to incorporate non-local operations into a recurrent neural network (RNN) for image restoration. The main contributions of this work are: (1) Unlike existing methods that measure self-similarity in an isolated manner, the proposed non-local module can be flexibly integrated into existing deep networks for end-to-end training to capture deep feature correlation between each location and its neighborhood. (2) We fully employ the RNN structure for its parameter efficiency and allow deep feature correlation to be propagated along adjacent recurrent states. This new design boosts robustness against inaccurate correlation estimation due to severely degraded images. (3) We show that it is essential to maintain a confined neighborhood for computing deep feature correlation given degraded images. This is in contrast to existing practice that deploys the whole image. Extensive experiments on both image denoising and super-resolution tasks are conducted. Thanks to the recurrent non-local operations and correlation propagation, the proposed NLRN achieves superior results to state-of-the-art methods with many fewer parameters.

paragraphs: Natural images contain similar structures at different locations, and classical restoration methods have used this self-similarity effectively. The paper develops a non-local recurrent network, NLRN, to incorporate that property into a trainable deep model. Its non-local module captures correlations between deep features at an image location and those in its neighborhood.

The recurrent structure reuses parameters and carries feature correlations between adjacent recurrent states. This propagation improves robustness when image degradation makes correlation estimates inaccurate. The authors also find it essential to confine the neighborhood used for correlation computation on degraded images, rather than using the whole image as in existing practice.

The module can be integrated into deep networks for end-to-end training, so similarity estimation becomes part of the learned restoration process. Experiments cover image denoising and super-resolution. The reported results exceed those of state-of-the-art methods while using many fewer parameters. Together, the findings support recurrent non-local operations and correlation propagation as an effective way to exploit image self-similarity under degradation in the evaluated restoration tasks.
summary.tldr: NLRN propagates learned image-feature correlations through recurrent states to improve restoration with fewer parameters.

title: Non-Local Recurrent Network for Image Restoration

abstract: Neural network training is usually accomplished by solving a non-convex optimization problem using stochastic gradient descent. Although one optimizes over the networks parameters, the main loss function generally only depends on the realization of the neural network, i.e. the function it computes. Studying the optimization problem over the space of realizations opens up new ways to understand neural network training. In particular, usual loss functions like mean squared error and categorical cross entropy are convex on spaces of neural network realizations, which themselves are non-convex. Approximation capabilities of neural networks can be used to deal with the latter non-convexity, which allows us to establish that for sufficiently large networks local minima of a regularized optimization problem on the realization space are almost optimal. Note, however, that each realization has many different, possibly degenerate, parametrizations. In particular, a local minimum in the parametrization space needs not correspond to a local minimum in the realization space. To establish such a connection, inverse stability of the realization map is required, meaning that proximity of realizations must imply proximity of corresponding parametrizations. We present pathologies which prevent inverse stability in general, and, for shallow networks, proceed to establish a restricted space of parametrizations on which we have inverse stability w.r.t. to a Sobolev norm. Furthermore, we show that by optimizing over such restricted sets, it is still possible to learn any function which can be learned by optimization over unrestricted sets.

Although one optimizes over the networks parameters, the main loss function generally only depends on the realization of the neural network, i.e. the function it computes. Studying the optimization problem over the space of realizations opens up new ways to understand neural network training. In particular, usual loss functions like mean squared error and categorical cross entropy are convex on spaces of neural network realizations, which themselves are non-convex. This paper examines the gap between these two viewpoints for ReLU networks. Common losses are convex as functions of predictions, but the collection of functions realizable by a network is itself nonconvex.

Transferring this statement to parameter optimization is difficult: many parameter choices can represent the same function, and a local minimum among parameters need not be a local minimum among represented functions.

The required connection is inverse stability, meaning nearby realizations admit nearby corresponding parameterizations. The authors identify pathologies that prevent this property in general. For shallow networks, they establish inverse stability on a restricted parameter space using a Sobolev norm. They also show that optimization over these restricted sets retains the ability to learn any function learnable through optimization over unrestricted sets.
summary.tldr: The paper identifies obstacles to connecting ReLU parameter optimization with function-space optimization and establishes a restricted stability result for shallow networks.

title: How degenerate is the parametrization of neural networks with the ReLU activation function?

abstract: We propose a new family of fairness definitions for classification problems that combine some of the best properties of both statistical and individual notions of fairness. We posit not only a distribution over individuals, but also a distribution over (or collection of) classification tasks. We then ask that standard statistics (such as error or false positive/negative rates) be (approximately) equalized across individuals, where the rate is defined as an expectation over the classification tasks. Because we are no longer averaging over coarse groups (such as race or gender), this is a semantically meaningful individual-level constraint. Given a sample of individuals and problems, we design an oracle-efficient algorithm (i.e. one that is given access to any standard, fairness-free learning heuristic) for the fair empirical risk minimization task. We also show that given sufficiently many samples, the ERM solution generalizes in two directions: both to new individuals, and to new classification tasks, drawn from their corresponding distributions. Finally we implement our algorithm and empirically verify its effectiveness.

For each individual, a statistic such as error rate is averaged across tasks. Fairness then asks for these averages to be approximately equal across individuals, making the individual the unit of comparison.

This combines statistical measures of prediction quality with an individual-level requirement. The averaging occurs over tasks instead of broad demographic groups, so group averages do not define the constraint. Given sampled individuals and tasks, the authors design an algorithm for minimizing empirical prediction risk while meeting this fairness requirement. It operates with access to an ordinary learning heuristic that need not itself enforce fairness.

The theoretical results show that, with sufficiently many samples, the empirical solution generalizes to new individuals and new classification tasks drawn from their respective distributions. The authors also implement the algorithm and report empirical evidence of its effectiveness. The central contribution is a fairness framework that explicitly treats performance across multiple tasks as the basis for comparing individuals.
summary.tldr: The paper defines individual fairness through performance averaged across classification tasks and develops an algorithm with conditional generalization guarantees.

title: Average Individual Fairness: Algorithms, Generalization and Experiments

abstract: We consider a generic empirical composition optimization problem, where there are empirical averages present both outside and inside nonlinear loss functions. Such a problem is of interest in various machine learning applications, and cannot be directly solved by standard methods such as stochastic gradient descent (SGD). We take a novel approach to solving this problem by reformulating the original minimization objective into an equivalent min-max objective, which brings out all the empirical averages that are originally inside the nonlinear loss functions. We exploit the rich structures of the reformulated problem and develop a stochastic primal-dual algorithms, SVRPDA-I, to solve the problem efficiently. We carry out extensive theoretical analysis of the proposed algorithm, obtaining the convergence rate, the total computation complexity and the storage complexity. In particular, the algorithm is shown to converge at a linear rate when the problem is strongly convex. Moreover, we also develop an approximate version of the algorithm, named SVRPDA-II, which further reduces the memory requirement. Finally, we evaluate the performance of our algorithms on several real-world benchmarks and experimental results show that they significantly outperform existing techniques.

paragraphs: Some learning objectives contain empirical averages both outside and inside nonlinear loss functions. This nested structure creates an empirical composition optimization problem that standard stochastic gradient descent cannot solve directly. The paper addresses the difficulty by changing the mathematical formulation so that averages hidden inside nonlinear functions become explicit in the optimization.

The authors rewrite the original minimization as an equivalent min-max problem. They exploit the resulting structure to develop SVRPDA-I, a stochastic variance-reduced primal-dual algorithm. Their theoretical analysis covers its convergence rate, total computational cost, and storage requirements. In particular, they establish linear convergence when the optimization problem is strongly convex.

The overall contribution combines an equivalent reformulation, an efficient stochastic algorithm, and a lower-memory variant for this class of objectives.
summary.tldr: Recasting nested-average objectives as min-max problems enables efficient stochastic primal-dual methods, with linear convergence under strong convexity.

title: Stochastic Variance Reduced Primal Dual Algorithms for Empirical Composition Optimization

abstract: What is the role of unlabeled data in an inference problem, when the presumed underlying distribution is adversarially perturbed? To provide a concrete answer to this question, this paper unifies two major learning frameworks: Semi-Supervised Learning (SSL) and Distributionally Robust Learning (DRL). We develop a generalization theory for our framework based on a number of novel complexity measures, such as an adversarial extension of Rademacher complexity and its semi-supervised analogue. Moreover, our analysis is able to quantify the role of unlabeled data in the generalization under a more general condition compared to the existing theoretical works in SSL. Based on our framework, we also present a hybrid of DRL and EM algorithms that has a guaranteed convergence rate. When implemented with deep neural networks, our method shows a comparable performance to those of the state-of-the-art on a number of real-world benchmark datasets.

paragraphs: This paper asks how unlabeled examples contribute to learning when the assumed data distribution can be adversarially perturbed. It joins semi-supervised learning, which uses labeled and unlabeled data, with distributionally robust learning. The resulting framework studies incomplete labeling and distributional uncertainty together, allowing their interaction to be analyzed within one learning problem.

The authors develop a generalization theory using new complexity measures, including adversarial and semi-supervised extensions of Rademacher complexity. Their analysis quantifies the role of unlabeled data under a condition more general than those used in existing semi-supervised theory. This provides a theoretical account of how unlabeled information enters generalization in the robust setting.

The paper also proposes an algorithm combining distributionally robust learning with expectation-maximization and establishes a convergence-rate guarantee. Implemented with deep neural networks, the method performs comparably to state-of-the-art approaches on several real-world benchmarks. The contributions thus connect a theoretical treatment of unlabeled data with a concrete optimization procedure and empirical evidence of competitive performance.
summary.tldr: A unified robust semi-supervised framework quantifies the role of unlabeled data and supports a convergent, empirically competitive algorithm.

title: Robustness to Adversarial Perturbations in Learning from Incomplete Data

abstract: We propose and analyze the problems of \textit{community goodness-of-fit and two-sample testing} for stochastic block models (SBM), where changes arise due to modification in community memberships of nodes. Motivated by practical applications, we consider the challenging sparse regime, where expected node degrees are constant, and the inter-community mean degree ($b$) scales proportionally to intra-community mean degree ($a$). Prior work has sharply characterized partial or full community recovery in terms of a ``signal-to-noise ratio'' ($\mathrm{SNR}$) based on $a$ and $b$. For both problems, we propose computationally-efficient tests that can succeed far beyond the regime where recovery of community membership is even possible. Overall, for large changes, $s \gg \sqrt{n}$, we need only $\mathrm{SNR}= O(1)$ whereas a na\"ive test based on community recovery with $O(s)$ errors requires $\mathrm{SNR}= \Theta(\log n)$. Conversely, in the small change regime, $s \ll \sqrt{n}$, via an information theoretic lower bound, we show that, surprisingly, no algorithm can do better than the na\"ive algorithm that first estimates the community up to $O(s)$ errors and then detects changes. We validate these phenomena numerically on SBMs and on real-world datasets as well as Markov Random Fields where we only observe node data rather than the existence of links.

paragraphs: Detecting whether network communities have changed need not require identifying every node's community accurately. This paper studies that distinction through goodness-of-fit and two-sample tests in stochastic block models. It focuses on sparse networks with constant expected node degree, where between-community connectivity scales proportionally to within-community connectivity.

The authors propose computationally efficient tests and characterize how their requirements depend on the number of changed memberships. When the number of changes is much larger than the square root of the number of nodes, their tests need only constant-order signal-to-noise ratio. A comparison method that first recovers communities with an error count proportional to the changes requires signal-to-noise ratio growing logarithmically with network size.

For changes much smaller than the square-root threshold, an information-theoretic lower bound shows that no algorithm can improve on the recovery-first approach in the stated sense. Thus, the benefit of testing directly depends on change size. Numerical studies on block models, real datasets, and Markov random fields support these phenomena, including settings where observations are node data rather than links.
summary.tldr: Large community changes can be detected with much weaker signals than community recovery requires, while small changes face a matching information-theoretic barrier.

title: Efficient Near-Optimal Testing of Community Changes in Balanced Stochastic Block Models

abstract: The transition matrix, denoting the transition relationship from clean labels to noisy labels, is essential to build statistically consistent classifiers in label-noise learning. Existing methods for estimating the transition matrix rely heavily on estimating the noisy class posterior. However, the estimation error for noisy class posterior could be large because of the randomness of label noise. The estimation error would lead the transition matrix to be poorly estimated. Therefore in this paper, we aim to solve this problem by exploiting the divide-and-conquer paradigm. Specifically, we introduce an intermediate class to avoid directly estimating the noisy class posterior. By this intermediate class, the original transition matrix can then be factorized into the product of two easy-to-estimated transition matrices. We term the proposed method as the dual $T$-estimator. Both theoretical analyses and empirical results illustrate the effectiveness of the dual $T$-estimator for estimating transition matrices, leading to better classification performances.

paragraphs: Learning from incorrect labels requires understanding how clean labels become noisy ones. A transition matrix represents these class-to-class changes and plays a central role in building statistically consistent classifiers. This paper focuses on estimating that matrix accurately, because errors in it can undermine the classifier that relies on it.

Existing approaches depend heavily on estimates of the noisy class posterior, meaning the probabilities of noisy classes given an input. Randomness in label corruption can make those probabilities difficult to estimate accurately. The proposed dual T-estimator introduces an intermediate class and factors the original transition matrix into two matrices. This divides the estimation problem into components described as easier to estimate.

The resulting method avoids directly estimating the noisy class posterior in the original way. Both theoretical analysis and empirical results support its effectiveness at estimating transition matrices, and the authors report improved classification performance. The central idea is that restructuring the estimation problem can reduce the impact of an unreliable intermediate probability estimate on learning from noisy labels.
summary.tldr: Dual T factors label-noise transitions through an intermediate class to improve transition estimates and downstream classification.

title: Dual T: Reducing Estimation Error for Transition Matrix in Label-noise Learning

abstract: As machine learning becomes prevalent in a widening array of sensitive applications such as job hiring and criminal justice, one critical aspect that machine learning classifiers should respect is to ensure fairness: guaranteeing the irrelevancy of a prediction output to sensitive attributes such as gender and race. In this work, we develop a kernel density estimation trick to quantify fairness measures that capture the degree of the irrelevancy. A key feature of our approach is that quantified fairness measures can be expressed as differentiable functions w.r.t. classifier model parameters. This then allows us to enjoy prominent gradient descent to readily solve an interested optimization problem that fully respects fairness constraints. We focus on a binary classification setting and two well-known definitions of group fairness: Demographic Parity (DP) and Equalized Odds (EO). Our experiments both on synthetic and benchmark real datasets demonstrate that our algorithm outperforms prior fair classifiers in accuracy-fairness tradeoff performance both w.r.t. DP and EO.

paragraphs: A classifier used in sensitive applications may need to balance predictive accuracy with constraints on how its outputs relate to sensitive attributes. This paper studies that problem for binary classification, focusing on demographic parity and equalized odds. These are two particular definitions of group fairness, so the optimization target is a specified statistical relationship rather than fairness in every possible sense.

The method uses kernel density estimation to quantify the relevant fairness measures. Its key computational property is that these quantities are differentiable with respect to the classifier's parameters. That connects fairness constraints to gradient descent, allowing the training procedure to adjust predictions while accounting for the chosen fairness requirement.

Experiments on synthetic and real benchmark datasets report better accuracy–fairness tradeoffs than prior fair classifiers under both definitions. The stated result concerns the balance achieved between these objectives in the experiments. The broader contribution is a way to make group fairness measures directly usable within gradient-based classifier optimization.
summary.tldr: Kernel density estimation makes two group fairness measures differentiable, enabling classifier training with improved empirical accuracy–fairness tradeoffs.

title: A Fair Classifier Using Kernel Density Estimation

abstract: Neural network training is computationally and memory intensive. Sparse training can reduce the burden on emerging hardware platforms designed to accelerate sparse computations, but it can also affect network convergence. In this work, we propose a novel CNN training algorithm called Sparse Weight Activation Training (SWAT). SWAT is more computation and memory-efficient than conventional training. SWAT modifies back-propagation based on the empirical insight that convergence during training tends to be robust to the elimination of (i) small magnitude weights during the forward pass and (ii) both small magnitude weights and activations during the backward pass. We evaluate SWAT on recent CNN architectures such as ResNet, VGG, DenseNet and WideResNet using CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100 and ImageNet datasets. For ResNet-50 on ImageNet SWAT reduces total floating-point operations (FLOPs) during training by 80% resulting in a 3.3x training speedup when run on a simulated sparse learning accelerator representative of emerging platforms while incurring only 1.63% reduction in validation accuracy. Moreover, SWAT reduces memory footprint during the backward pass by 23% to 50% for activations and 50% to 90% for weights. Code is available at https://github.com/AamirRaihan/SWAT.

paragraphs: Sparse Weight Activation Training, or SWAT, aims to reduce the computation and memory required to train convolutional networks. It builds on an empirical observation: training convergence tends to tolerate removing small-magnitude weights during the forward pass and removing both small weights and small activations during the backward pass.

The algorithm modifies backpropagation to exploit this tolerance. Evaluations cover ResNet, VGG, DenseNet, and WideResNet on CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, and ImageNet. The approach is intended to benefit hardware designed to accelerate sparse computations, connecting reduced arithmetic and storage requirements to the capabilities of emerging platforms.

For ResNet-50 on ImageNet, SWAT reduces training FLOPs by 80% with a reported 1.63% reduction in validation accuracy. A simulated sparse learning accelerator yields a 3.3-fold training speedup; that timing result specifically concerns the simulated hardware. The paper also reports backward-pass memory reductions of 23–50% for activations and 50–90% for weights, showing substantial resource savings with an evaluated accuracy tradeoff.
summary.tldr: SWAT reduces CNN training computation and memory by omitting small weights and activations, with measured accuracy tradeoffs and simulated accelerator speedups.

title: Sparse Weight Activation Training

abstract: We create a framework for bootstrapping visual representation learning from a primitive visual grouping capability. We operationalize grouping via a contour detector that partitions an image into regions, followed by merging of those regions into a tree hierarchy. A small supervised dataset suffices for training this grouping primitive. Across a large unlabeled dataset, we apply this learned primitive to automatically predict hierarchical region structure. These predictions serve as guidance for self-supervised contrastive feature learning: we task a deep network with producing per-pixel embeddings whose pairwise distances respect the region hierarchy. Experiments demonstrate that our approach can serve as state-of-the-art generic pre-training, benefiting downstream tasks. We additionally explore applications to semantic region search and video-based object instance tracking.

paragraphs: This paper learns visual features by first teaching a system a basic ability to group image regions. A contour detector partitions an image, and those regions are merged into a tree hierarchy. A small supervised dataset is sufficient to train this initial grouping component, which then supplies guidance for learning from much more unlabeled data.

Across the unlabeled dataset, the grouping system predicts hierarchical region structure automatically. A deep network learns a representation for each pixel through contrastive learning. Distances between these pixel representations are trained to respect the predicted region hierarchy, connecting the learned feature space to relationships among image regions.

Experiments show that the approach can provide state-of-the-art generic pre-training that benefits downstream tasks. The authors also explore semantic region search and tracking individual objects in video. The contribution is a way to turn limited supervision for a primitive visual task into extensive training guidance. Its self-supervised stage relies on automatically predicted structure, while the initial grouping primitive is explicitly learned with supervision.
summary.tldr: A grouping primitive trained with limited supervision generates hierarchical guidance for self-supervised pixel representation learning.

title: Self-Supervised Visual Representation Learning from Hierarchical Grouping

abstract: Recent work has indicated that, unlike humans, ImageNet-trained CNNs tend to classify images by texture rather than by shape. How pervasive is this bias, and where does it come from? We find that, when trained on datasets of images with conflicting shape and texture, CNNs learn to classify by shape at least as easily as by texture. What factors, then, produce the texture bias in CNNs trained on ImageNet? Different unsupervised training objectives and different architectures have small but significant and largely independent effects on the level of texture bias. However, all objectives and architectures still lead to models that make texture-based classification decisions a majority of the time, even if shape information is decodable from their hidden representations. The effect of data augmentation is much larger. By taking less aggressive random crops at training time and applying simple, naturalistic augmentation (color distortion, noise, and blur), we train models that classify ambiguous images by shape a majority of the time, and outperform baselines on out-of-distribution test sets. Our results indicate that apparent differences in the way humans and ImageNet-trained CNNs process images may arise not primarily from differences in their internal workings, but from differences in the data that they see.

paragraphs: ImageNet-trained convolutional networks often classify ambiguous images using texture rather than shape. This paper investigates whether that tendency reflects an inherent difficulty learning shape. When trained on images whose shape and texture conflict, the networks learn shape-based classification at least as easily as texture-based classification, showing that they can readily use shape in that setting.

The authors then vary architectures, unsupervised objectives, and data augmentation. Architecture and objective changes have small but significant, largely independent effects, yet the tested models still mostly choose texture. Shape can remain decodable from their internal representations even when it does not drive the final classification, separating the presence of information from its use.

Changing augmentation has a much larger effect. Less aggressive random cropping, together with color distortion, noise, and blur, produces models that favor shape on most ambiguous images and outperform baselines on out-of-distribution tests. The findings suggest that apparent differences between human and network image processing may arise primarily from differences in experienced data, rather than internal mechanisms.
summary.tldr: The experiments suggest that training data augmentation strongly shapes CNN texture bias and can shift decisions toward shape while improving out-of-distribution performance.

title: The Origins and Prevalence of Texture Bias in Convolutional Neural Networks

abstract: Cross-domain disentanglement is the problem of learning representations partitioned into domain-invariant and domain-specific representations, which is a key to successful domain transfer or measuring semantic distance between two domains. Grounded in information theory, we cast the simultaneous learning of domain-invariant and domain-specific representations as a joint objective of multiple information constraints, which does not require adversarial training or gradient reversal layers. We derive a tractable bound of the objective and propose a generative model named Interaction Information Auto-Encoder (IIAE). Our approach reveals insights on the desirable representation for cross-domain disentanglement and its connection to Variational Auto-Encoder (VAE). We demonstrate the validity of our model in the image-to-image translation and the cross-domain retrieval tasks. We further show that our model achieves the state-of-the-art performance in the zero-shot sketch based image retrieval task, even without external knowledge.

paragraphs: Cross-domain disentanglement separates a representation into information shared across domains and information specific to each domain. That separation is useful when transferring between domains or comparing their semantic content. This paper formulates the simultaneous learning of both parts using information theory, with several information constraints combined into a joint objective.

The authors derive a tractable bound on that objective and build a generative model called the Interaction Information Auto-Encoder, or IIAE. The approach does not require adversarial training or gradient reversal layers. Its formulation also provides insight into what the desired representations should preserve and how cross-domain disentanglement connects to the variational autoencoder framework.

The model is evaluated on image-to-image translation and cross-domain retrieval. It achieves state-of-the-art performance on zero-shot sketch-based image retrieval without using external knowledge. These findings support the usefulness of jointly organizing shared and domain-specific information. The contribution pairs a practical generative model with an information-theoretic account of the learning objective, providing a common basis for tasks that require correspondence between different kinds of visual data.
summary.tldr: IIAE uses information constraints to learn shared and domain-specific representations, with strong cross-domain retrieval results without adversarial training.

title: Variational Interaction Information Maximization for Cross-domain Disentanglement

abstract: Autonomous driving relies on a huge volume of real-world data to be labeled to high precision. Alternative solutions seek to exploit driving simulators that can generate large amounts of labeled data with a plethora of content variations. However, the domain gap between the synthetic and real data remains, raising the following important question: What are the best way to utilize a self-driving simulator for perception tasks?. In this work, we build on top of recent advances in domain-adaptation theory, and from this perspective, propose ways to minimize the reality gap. We primarily focus on the use of labels in the synthetic domain alone. Our approach introduces both a principled way to learn neural-invariant representations and a theoretically inspired view on how to sample the data from the simulator. Our method is easy to implement in practice as it is agnostic of the network architecture and the choice of the simulator. We showcase our approach on the bird's-eye-view vehicle segmentation task with multi-sensor data (cameras, lidar) using an open-source simulator (CARLA), and evaluate the entire framework on a real-world dataset (nuScenes). Last but not least, we show what types of variations (e.g. weather conditions, number of assets, map design and color diversity) matter to perception networks when trained with driving simulators, and which ones can be compensated for with our domain adaptation technique.

They also examine variations in weather, asset counts, map design, and color diversity, identifying which matter to trained perception networks and which their adaptation technique can compensate for. This connects simulator content choices with representation learning as two parts of addressing the reality gap.
summary.tldr: The paper combines invariant representation learning with principled simulator sampling to address transfer from synthetic driving data to real-world perception.

title: Towards Optimal Strategies for Training Self-Driving Perception Models in Simulation

abstract: In this paper, we comparatively analyze the Bures-Wasserstein (BW) geometry with the popular Affine-Invariant (AI) geometry for Riemannian optimization on the symmetric positive definite (SPD) matrix manifold. Our study begins with an observation that the BW metric has a linear dependence on SPD matrices in contrast to the quadratic dependence of the AI metric. We build on this to show that the BW metric is a more suitable and robust choice for several Riemannian optimization problems over ill-conditioned SPD matrices. We show that the BW geometry has a non-negative curvature, which further improves convergence rates of algorithms over the non-positively curved AI geometry. Finally, we verify that several popular cost functions, which are known to be geodesic convex under the AI geometry, are also geodesic convex under the BW geometry. Extensive experiments on various applications support our findings.

paragraphs: Optimizing over symmetric positive definite matrices requires a choice of geometry that shapes how an algorithm measures movement. This paper compares Bures-Wasserstein geometry with the widely used Affine-Invariant geometry. Its starting observation is that their metrics depend differently on the matrix: linearly for Bures-Wasserstein and quadratically for Affine-Invariant.

Building on this distinction, the authors show that Bures-Wasserstein geometry is more suitable and robust for several problems involving ill-conditioned matrices. They also establish its non-negative curvature and show convergence-rate improvements over the non-positively curved Affine-Invariant geometry in their analysis. These results explain why the geometric choice can affect optimization behavior substantially.

The paper further verifies that several commonly used objectives remain geodesically convex under Bures-Wasserstein geometry when they are already known to have that property under Affine-Invariant geometry. Thus, changing geometry can preserve useful objective structure while improving the analyzed optimization behavior. Experiments across applications support the findings, which concern the examined problems and functions rather than universal superiority for every matrix objective.
summary.tldr: Bures-Wasserstein geometry offers theoretical and empirical optimization advantages for several problems involving ill-conditioned positive definite matrices.

title: On Riemannian Optimization over Positive Definite Matrices with the Bures-Wasserstein Geometry

abstract: We consider the problem of projecting a vector onto the so-called k-capped simplex, which is a hyper-cube cut by a hyperplane.For an n-dimensional input vector with bounded elements, we found that a simple algorithm based on Newton's method is able to solve the projection problem to high precision with a complexity roughly about O(n), which has a much lower computational cost compared with the existing sorting-based methods proposed in the literature.We provide a theory for partial explanation and justification of the method.We demonstrate that the proposed algorithm can produce a solution of the projection problem with high precision on large scale datasets, and the algorithm is able to significantly outperform the state-of-the-art methods in terms of runtime (about 6-8 times faster than a commercial software with respect to CPU time for input vector with 1 million variables or more).We further illustrate the effectiveness of the proposed algorithm on solving sparse regression in a bioinformatics problem.Empirical results on the GWAS dataset (with 1,500,000 single-nucleotide polymorphisms) show that, when using the proposed method to accelerate the Projected Quasi-Newton (PQN) method, the accelerated PQN algorithm is able to handle huge-scale regression problem and it is more efficient (about 3-6 times faster) than the current state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: This paper studies projection onto a k-capped simplex, a feasible region formed by intersecting a hypercube with a hyperplane. Such a projection is a computational step inside larger optimization procedures. The authors seek a faster way to perform it when vectors are very large, reducing the cost associated with existing sorting-based approaches.

For input vectors with bounded elements, they find that a simple Newton-based algorithm reaches high precision with computational cost roughly proportional to the vector dimension. They supply theory that partially explains and justifies the method. For vectors with at least one million variables, reported CPU times are about six to eight times faster than those of commercial software.

The authors then use the projection algorithm to accelerate Projected Quasi-Newton optimization for sparse regression. On a genome-wide association dataset containing 1.5 million single-nucleotide polymorphisms, the resulting procedure handles the large regression problem and runs about three to six times faster than the compared state-of-the-art methods. This application shows how improving a recurring optimization step can benefit the full regression procedure.
summary.tldr: A Newton-based capped-simplex projection method achieves high precision at roughly linear cost and accelerates large-scale sparse regression.

title: Fast Projection onto the Capped Simplex with Applications to Sparse Regression in Bioinformatics

abstract: In this paper, we consider an inverse problem in graph learning domain -- "given the graph representations smoothed by Graph Convolutional Network (GCN), how can we reconstruct the input graph signal?" We propose Graph Deconvolutional Network (GDN) and motivate the design of GDN via a combination of inverse filters in spectral domain and de-noising layers in wavelet domain, as the inverse operation results in a high frequency amplifier and may amplify the noise. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on several tasks including graph feature imputation and graph structure generation.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we consider an inverse problem in graph learning domain -- "given the graph representations smoothed by Graph Convolutional Network (GCN), how can we reconstruct the input graph signal?" We propose Graph Deconvolutional Network (GDN) and motivate the design of GDN via a combination of inverse filters in spectral domain and de-noising layers in wavelet domain, as the inverse operation results in a high frequency amplifier and may amplify the noise. We demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method on several tasks including graph feature imputation and graph structure generation.

paragraphs: Graph convolutional networks produce smoothed representations of information attached to a graph. This paper asks how to work backward from those representations and reconstruct the original graph signal. It frames reconstruction as an inverse problem: the model must recover information from a representation that has already undergone graph-based smoothing.

The proposed Graph Deconvolutional Network combines inverse filters in the spectral domain with denoising layers in the wavelet domain. The reason for combining these operations is central to the design. Reversing the smoothing acts as an amplifier for high-frequency components, and that operation may also amplify noise. Denoising therefore accompanies the inverse operation to address an issue created by reconstruction itself.

The authors demonstrate the method on graph feature imputation and graph structure generation. These tasks provide applications for recovering or generating graph information from learned representations. The contribution is a reconstruction architecture whose design explicitly accounts for noise amplification, connecting the desired inverse transformation with a mechanism for controlling its unwanted effects.
summary.tldr: Graph Deconvolutional Networks combine inverse filtering with denoising to reconstruct graph signals from smoothed representations.

title: Deconvolutional Networks on Graph Data

abstract: Precisely annotating objects with multiple labels is costly and has become a critical bottleneck in real-world multi-label classification tasks. Instead, deciding the relative order of label pairs is obviously less laborious than collecting exact labels. However, the supervised information of pairwise relevance ordering is less informative than exact labels. It is thus an important challenge to effectively learn with such weak supervision. In this paper, we formalize this problem as a novel learning framework, called multi-label learning with pairwise relevance ordering (PRO). We show that the unbiased estimator of classification risk can be derived with a cost-sensitive loss only from PRO examples. Theoretically, we provide the estimation error bound for the proposed estimator and further prove that it is consistent with respective to the commonly used ranking loss. Empirical studies on multiple datasets and metrics validate the effectiveness of the proposed method.

paragraphs: Multi-label classification assigns several relevant labels to an object, but collecting precise annotations can be costly. This paper studies a weaker form of supervision: specifying which of two labels is more relevant. Such comparisons require less annotation effort, while also providing less information than knowing the object's exact labels.

The authors formalize this setting as learning with pairwise relevance ordering, or PRO. Their main construction derives an unbiased estimator of classification risk using a cost-sensitive loss and PRO examples alone. This connects the available relative judgments to the classification objective, providing a way to train despite not receiving complete label assignments. The loss accounts for the structure of the weaker supervision.

The theoretical results include an estimation error bound and consistency with respect to a commonly used ranking loss. These address the reliability of the estimator and its relationship to ordering labels correctly. Experiments across multiple datasets and metrics support the method's effectiveness. Together, the results establish pairwise relevance judgments as a workable supervision format for the studied multi-label learning problem.
summary.tldr: The paper learns multi-label classifiers from relative label judgments using an unbiased risk estimator with theoretical and empirical support.

title: Multi-Label Learning with Pairwise Relevance Ordering

abstract: Message passing is the core of most graph models such as Graph Convolutional Network (GCN) and Label Propagation (LP), which usually require a large number of clean labeled data to smooth out the neighborhood over the graph. However, the labeling process can be tedious, costly, and error-prone in practice. In this paper, we propose to unify active learning (AL) and message passing towards minimizing labeling costs, e.g., making use of few and unreliable labels that can be obtained cheaply. We make two contributions towards that end. First, we open up a perspective by drawing a connection between AL enforcing message passing and social influence maximization, ensuring that the selected samples effectively improve the model performance. Second, we propose an extension to the influence model that incorporates an explicit quality factor to model label noise. In this way, we derive a fundamentally new AL selection criterion for GCN and LP--reliable influence maximization (RIM)--by considering quantity and quality of influence simultaneously. Empirical studies on public datasets show that RIM significantly outperforms current AL methods in terms of accuracy and efficiency.

paragraphs: Graph models often pass information between neighboring nodes and rely on many clean labels to support that process. Obtaining labels can be expensive and error-prone. This paper studies how active learning can select useful nodes to label while accounting for the possibility that cheaply obtained labels are unreliable.

The authors connect label selection for message passing with social influence maximization. The idea is to evaluate selected samples through the influence they can exert across the graph. They extend that influence model with an explicit quality factor representing label noise, so the selection criterion considers both the amount of influence and its reliability.

The resulting criterion, reliable influence maximization or RIM, applies to graph convolutional networks and label propagation. Empirical studies on public datasets report significant gains in accuracy and efficiency over existing active-learning methods. The contribution is to make label quality part of the selection process itself, linking the goal of reducing annotation costs with the way information from labeled nodes spreads through a graph.
summary.tldr: RIM selects graph labels by balancing their influence and reliability, improving active-learning accuracy and efficiency in reported experiments.

title: RIM: Reliable Influence-based Active Learning on Graphs

abstract: Fact verification has attracted a lot of attention in the machine learning and natural language processing communities, as it is one of the key methods for detecting misinformation. Existing large-scale benchmarks for this task have focused mostly on textual sources, i.e. unstructured information, and thus ignored the wealth of information available in structured formats, such as tables. In this paper we introduce a novel dataset and benchmark, Fact Extraction and VERification Over Unstructured and Structured information (FEVEROUS), which consists of 87,026 verified claims. Each claim is annotated with evidence in the form of sentences and/or cells from tables in Wikipedia, as well as a label indicating whether this evidence supports, refutes, or does not provide enough information to reach a verdict. Furthermore, we detail our efforts to track and minimize the biases present in the dataset and could be exploited by models, e.g. being able to predict the label without using evidence. Finally, we develop a baseline for verifying claims against text and tables which predicts both the correct evidence and verdict for 18% of the claims.

paragraphs: FEVEROUS expands fact verification to include information stored in tables alongside ordinary text. The authors argue that earlier large benchmarks largely emphasize textual sources, overlooking structured information. Their dataset contains 87,026 verified claims, creating a shared setting for systems that must work with both kinds of evidence.

Each claim is linked to Wikipedia sentences, table cells, or a combination of the two. A label states whether the evidence supports the claim, refutes it, or leaves insufficient information for a verdict. This connects the final decision to identified supporting material and requires the task to accommodate different evidence formats.

The authors describe efforts to track and reduce exploitable dataset biases, including shortcuts that allow label prediction without consulting evidence. They also build a baseline that gets both the evidence and verdict correct for 18% of claims. That joint result indicates substantial difficulty in completing the full verification task, where finding the right material and reaching the right conclusion must both succeed.
summary.tldr: FEVEROUS benchmarks claim verification using Wikipedia text and tables, with a baseline solving evidence retrieval and verdict prediction jointly for 18% of claims.

title: FEVEROUS: Fact Extraction and VERification Over Unstructured and Structured information

abstract: Non-autoregressive translation (NAT) models are typically trained with the cross-entropy loss, which forces the model outputs to be aligned verbatim with the target sentence and will highly penalize small shifts in word positions. Latent alignment models relax the explicit alignment by marginalizing out all monotonic latent alignments with the CTC loss. However, they cannot handle non-monotonic alignments, which is non-negligible as there is typically global word reordering in machine translation. In this work, we explore non-monotonic latent alignments for NAT. We extend the alignment space to non-monotonic alignments to allow for the global word reordering and further consider all alignments that overlap with the target sentence. We non-monotonically match the alignments to the target sentence and train the latent alignment model to maximize the F1 score of non-monotonic matching. Extensive experiments on major WMT benchmarks show that our method substantially improves the translation performance of CTC-based models. Our best model achieves 30.06 BLEU on WMT14 En-De with only one-iteration decoding, closing the gap between non-autoregressive and autoregressive models.

paragraphs: Non-autoregressive translation produces outputs without the usual word-by-word generation process. Its training can nevertheless be sensitive to exact word positions: cross-entropy heavily penalizes even small shifts. CTC-based latent alignment relaxes that restriction, but its order-preserving alignments still cannot accommodate the global word reordering that often occurs in translation.

This paper expands the possible alignments to include non-monotonic ones, allowing words to match without preserving their order. It also considers alignments that overlap with the target sentence. The model is trained to maximize the F1 score of this non-monotonic matching, changing how candidate alignments receive credit during learning.

Experiments on major WMT benchmarks show substantial improvements over CTC-based translation models. The best reported system reaches 30.06 BLEU on WMT14 English-to-German using a single decoding iteration. The authors describe this as narrowing the performance gap between non-autoregressive and autoregressive models. The result supports a more flexible training alignment as a way to improve translation while retaining one-iteration decoding.
summary.tldr: Allowing non-monotonic latent alignments improves CTC-based translation while retaining single-iteration decoding.

title: Non-Monotonic Latent Alignments for CTC-Based Non-Autoregressive Machine Translation

abstract: We introduce SoundSpaces 2.0, a platform for on-the-fly geometry-based audio rendering for 3D environments. Given a 3D mesh of a real-world environment, SoundSpaces can generate highly realistic acoustics for arbitrary sounds captured from arbitrary microphone locations. Together with existing 3D visual assets, it supports an array of audio-visual research tasks, such as audio-visual navigation, mapping, source localization and separation, and acoustic matching. Compared to existing resources, SoundSpaces 2.0 has the advantages of allowing continuous spatial sampling, generalization to novel environments, and configurable microphone and material properties. To our knowledge, this is the first geometry-based acoustic simulation that offers high fidelity and realism while also being fast enough to use for embodied learning. We showcase the simulator's properties and benchmark its performance against real-world audio measurements. In addition, we demonstrate two downstream tasks---embodied navigation and far-field automatic speech recognition---and highlight sim2real performance for the latter. SoundSpaces 2.0 is publicly available to facilitate wider research for perceptual systems that can both see and hear.

paragraphs: SoundSpaces 2.0 generates audio from the geometry of a 3D environment while a simulation runs. Given a mesh of a real space, it can render sounds as captured at arbitrary microphone locations. Combined with visual assets, this provides a shared setting for studying systems that use both sight and hearing.

These capabilities make it useful for tasks including navigation, mapping, sound-source localization, source separation, and acoustic matching. The authors emphasize the combination of realistic geometry-based acoustics and sufficient speed for embodied learning.

The evaluation compares simulated acoustics against real-world audio measurements and demonstrates embodied navigation and far-field speech recognition. For speech recognition, the paper highlights transfer from simulation to the real world. The publicly available platform therefore contributes both an acoustic rendering resource and evidence that it can support downstream learning, including a reported application beyond the simulated setting.
summary.tldr: SoundSpaces 2.0 renders realistic audio in 3D environments fast enough for embodied learning and demonstrates simulation-to-real transfer for speech recognition.

title: SoundSpaces 2.0: A Simulation Platform for Visual-Acoustic Learning

abstract: Training deep learning models can be computationally expensive. Prior works have shown that increasing the batch size can potentially lead to better overall throughput. However, the batch size is frequently limited by the accelerator memory capacity due to the activations/feature maps stored for the training backward pass, as larger batch sizes require larger feature maps to be stored. Transformer-based models, which have recently seen a surge in popularity due to their good performance and applicability to a variety of tasks, have a similar problem. To remedy this issue, we propose Tempo, a new approach to efficiently use accelerator (e.g., GPU) memory resources for training Transformer-based models. Our approach provides drop-in replacements for the GELU, LayerNorm, and Attention layers, reducing the memory usage and ultimately leading to more efficient training. We implement Tempo and evaluate the throughput, memory usage, and accuracy/loss on the BERT Large pre-training task. We demonstrate that Tempo enables up to 2× higher batch sizes and 16% higher training throughput over the state-of-the-art baseline. We also evaluate Tempo on GPT2 and RoBERTa models, showing 19% and 26% speedup over the baseline.

paragraphs: Training a transformer requires retaining intermediate activations for the backward pass. These stored values can fill accelerator memory and restrict batch size. Because larger batches can potentially improve throughput, memory consumption can limit training speed even when the main issue appears to be computational cost.

Tempo reduces this memory burden through drop-in replacements for GELU, LayerNorm, and Attention layers. The approach targets commonly used transformer components so that their memory use becomes more efficient during training. The resulting capacity can support larger batches, linking a change in how layers use memory to improved overall training throughput.

The authors evaluate memory use, throughput, and accuracy or loss during BERT Large pretraining. Tempo enables batch sizes up to twice as large and achieves 16% higher throughput than the stated baseline. Evaluations on GPT2 and RoBERTa report speedups of 19% and 26%, respectively. These measurements demonstrate that reducing stored training data within transformer layers can translate into practical performance gains on the evaluated models.
summary.tldr: Tempo reduces transformer-layer memory use, enabling larger batches and faster training on BERT Large, GPT2, and RoBERTa.

title: Tempo: Accelerating Transformer-Based Model Training through Memory Footprint Reduction

abstract: In this work, we design differentially private hypothesis tests for the following problems in the general linear model: testing a linear relationship and testing for the presence of mixtures. The majority of our hypothesis tests are based on differentially private versions of the $F$-statistic for the general linear model framework, which are uniformly most powerful unbiased in the non-private setting. We also present another test for testing mixtures, based on the differentially private nonparametric tests of Couch, Kazan, Shi, Bray, and Groce (CCS 2019), which is especially suited for the small dataset regime. We show that the differentially private $F$-statistic converges to the asymptotic distribution of its non-private counterpart. As a corollary, the statistical power of the differentially private $F$-statistic converges to the statistical power of the non-private $F$-statistic. Through a suite of Monte Carlo based experiments, we show that our tests achieve desired \textit{significance levels} and have a high \textit{power} that approaches the power of the non-private tests as we increase sample sizes or the privacy-loss parameter. We also show when our tests outperform existing methods in the literature.

paragraphs: This paper develops differentially private hypothesis tests for detecting linear relationships and the presence of mixtures in general linear models. The aim is to preserve useful statistical inference while imposing a privacy constraint. Most proposed tests adapt the F-statistic, whose non-private form has established optimality properties in this framework.

The authors also offer a mixture test based on private nonparametric testing that is especially suitable for small datasets. For the private F-statistic, they prove convergence to the asymptotic distribution of its non-private counterpart. Consequently, its statistical power—the ability to detect an effect when one is present—also converges to that of the non-private statistic.

Monte Carlo experiments show that the tests achieve their intended significance levels and have high power. Power approaches the non-private level as sample sizes increase or the privacy-loss parameter grows, with the latter allowing weaker privacy protection. The paper also identifies cases where its tests outperform existing methods. These results connect asymptotic guarantees with empirical evidence about the privacy-inference tradeoff.
summary.tldr: Private hypothesis tests for linear models retain useful statistical power, with private F-statistic power converging to its non-private counterpart asymptotically.

title: Hypothesis Testing for Differentially Private Linear Regression

abstract: Wasserstein barycenters have become popular due to their ability to represent the average of probability measures in a geometrically meaningful way. In this paper, we present an algorithm to approximate the Wasserstein-2 barycenters of continuous measures via a generative model. Previous approaches rely on regularization (entropic/quadratic) which introduces bias or on input convex neural networks which are not expressive enough for large-scale tasks. In contrast, our algorithm does not introduce bias and allows using arbitrary neural networks. In addition, based on the celebrity faces dataset, we construct Ave, celeba! dataset which can be used for quantitative evaluation of barycenter algorithms by using standard metrics of generative models such as FID.

paragraphs: A Wasserstein barycenter averages probability distributions while respecting their geometry. This paper presents a generative-model approach to approximating Wasserstein-2 barycenters of continuous distributions. The aim is to retain a meaningful distributional average while avoiding restrictions that have made earlier approaches difficult to scale.

The authors identify two obstacles in previous methods. Entropic or quadratic regularization introduces bias, while input-convex neural networks can lack the expressiveness needed for large-scale tasks. Their proposed algorithm avoids introducing this bias and permits arbitrary neural-network architectures. That flexibility opens the choice of model beyond the input-convex networks used by earlier approaches, while the computational task remains barycenter approximation.

The paper also introduces Ave, celeba!, a dataset constructed from a celebrity-faces dataset for quantitative evaluation of barycenter methods. It enables the use of standard generative-model metrics such as FID. Together, the algorithm and dataset address both how to represent an estimated barycenter and how to evaluate barycenter algorithms using a concrete generative-model benchmark.
summary.tldr: The paper approximates Wasserstein barycenters with unrestricted neural architectures without introducing regularization bias and provides a dataset for evaluation.

title: Wasserstein Iterative Networks for Barycenter Estimation

abstract: Deep learning models struggle with compositional generalization, i.e. the ability to recognize or generate novel combinations of observed elementary concepts. In hopes of enabling compositional generalization, various unsupervised learning algorithms have been proposed with inductive biases that aim to induce compositional structure in learned representations (e.g. disentangled representation and emergent language learning). In this work, we evaluate these unsupervised learning algorithms in terms of how well they enable \textit{compositional generalization}. Specifically, our evaluation protocol focuses on whether or not it is easy to train a simple model on top of the learned representation that generalizes to new combinations of compositional factors. We systematically study three unsupervised representation learning algorithms - $\beta$-VAE, $\beta$-TCVAE, and emergent language (EL) autoencoders - on two datasets that allow directly testing compositional generalization. We find that directly using the bottleneck representation with simple models and few labels may lead to worse generalization than using representations from layers before or after the learned representation itself. In addition, we find that the previously proposed metrics for evaluating the levels of compositionality are not correlated with actual compositional generalization in our framework. Surprisingly, we find that increasing pressure to produce a disentangled representation (e.g. increasing $\beta$ in the $\beta$-VAE) produces representations with worse generalization, while representations from EL models show strong compositional generalization. Motivated by this observation, we further investigate the advantages of using EL to induce compositional structure in unsupervised representation learning, finding that it shows consistently stronger generalization than disentanglement models, especially when using less unlabeled data for unsupervised learning and fewer labels for downstream tasks. Taken together, our results shed new light onto the compositional generalization behavior of different unsupervised learning algorithms with a new setting to rigorously test this behavior, and suggest the potential benefits of developing EL learning algorithms for more generalizable representations. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/wildphoton/Compositional-Generalization .

paragraphs: Compositional generalization means handling unfamiliar combinations of concepts that were individually observed during training. This paper tests whether unsupervised methods designed to organize representations into meaningful components actually support that ability. Its evaluation asks whether a simple model trained on a learned representation can generalize to new combinations, rather than judging only how structured the representation appears.

The authors compare beta-VAE, beta-TCVAE, and emergent-language autoencoders on two datasets. With simple downstream models and few labels, the central bottleneck representation can generalize worse than representations from layers before or after it. Previously proposed compositionality metrics also fail to correlate with compositional generalization within this evaluation framework.

Increasing pressure for disentanglement produces worse generalization in the reported study, while emergent-language representations generalize strongly. Those models consistently outperform the disentanglement models, particularly with less unlabeled training data and fewer downstream labels. The findings support testing representations through their downstream ability to recombine concepts and suggest benefits from further developing emergent-language learning methods.
summary.tldr: In the studied setting, emergent-language representations generalize to new concept combinations better than disentanglement models, and compositionality metrics do not predict that ability.

title: Compositional Generalization in Unsupervised Compositional Representation Learning: A Study on Disentanglement and Emergent Language

abstract: We consider online learning with feedback graphs, a sequential decision-making framework where the learner's feedback is determined by a directed graph over the action set. We present a computationally-efficient algorithm for learning in this framework that simultaneously achieves near-optimal regret bounds in both stochastic and adversarial environments. The bound against oblivious adversaries is $\tilde{O} (\sqrt{\alpha T})$, where $T$ is the time horizon and $\alpha$ is the independence number of the feedback graph. The bound against stochastic environments is $O\big((\ln T)^2 \max_{S\in \mathcal I(G)} \sum_{i \in S} \Delta_i^{-1}\big)$ where $\mathcal I(G)$ is the family of all independent sets in a suitably defined undirected version of the graph and $\Delta_i$ are the suboptimality gaps.The algorithm combines ideas from the EXP3++ algorithm for stochastic and adversarial bandits and the EXP3.G algorithm for feedback graphs with a novel exploration scheme. The scheme, which exploits the structure of the graph to reduce exploration, is key to obtain best-of-both-worlds guarantees with feedback graphs. We also extend our algorithm and results to a setting where the feedback graphs are allowed to change over time.

paragraphs: The paper studies sequential decisions in which choosing an action reveals information according to a directed graph. This graph describes which actions provide feedback about others. The central challenge is to learn efficiently both when outcomes follow a stable stochastic process and when an adversary determines them, using a single algorithm with guarantees for both environments.

The proposed computationally efficient algorithm combines ideas from EXP3++ and EXP3.G with a new exploration strategy. Its distinctive feature is using the graph structure to reduce exploration. Because feedback from one action can inform the learner about other actions, the exploration scheme can exploit those connections instead of treating every action as an isolated information source.

The resulting regret guarantees are near-optimal in both settings. Against oblivious adversaries, regret scales roughly with the square root of the time horizon times the graph's independence number, apart from logarithmic factors. In stochastic environments, the bound depends on squared logarithmic time growth and the gaps separating suboptimal actions from the best action, aggregated over independent sets. The authors also extend their approach to feedback graphs that change over time.
summary.tldr: A graph-aware exploration algorithm achieves near-optimal regret in both stochastic and adversarial online learning, with an extension to changing feedback graphs.

title: A Near-Optimal Best-of-Both-Worlds Algorithm for Online Learning with Feedback Graphs

abstract: Much of the recent successes of deep learning can be attributed to scaling up the size of the networks to the point where they often are vastly overparameterized. Thus, understanding the role of overparameterization is of increasing importance. While predictive theories have been developed for supervised learning, little is known about the Reinforcement Learning case. In this work, we take a theoretical approach and study the role of overparameterization for off-policy Temporal Difference (TD) learning in the linear setting. We leverage tools from Random Matrix Theory and random graph theory to obtain a characterization of the spectrum of the TD operator. We use this result to study the stability and optimization dynamics of TD learning as a function of the number of parameters.

paragraphs: Increasing model size has played an important role in deep learning, motivating questions about what excess parameters do to learning dynamics. This paper examines that question in reinforcement learning, where the theoretical picture is less developed than in supervised learning. Its focus is off-policy temporal-difference learning with linear function approximation.

The authors use random matrix theory and random graph theory to characterize the spectrum of the temporal-difference operator. This spectrum provides a mathematical description of the operator underlying the learning updates. Characterizing it gives the analysis a way to connect the parameter count to the behavior of the update process.

The paper then uses that characterization to study stability and optimization dynamics as the number of parameters changes. Its contribution is a theoretical account within the linear off-policy setting, rather than a general claim that larger reinforcement-learning models always learn better. By making parameter count part of the operator analysis, the work creates a framework for examining how overparameterization affects the mechanics of temporal-difference learning.
summary.tldr: The paper analyzes how parameter count affects linear off-policy temporal-difference learning through the spectrum of its update operator.

title: On the role of overparameterization in off-policy Temporal Difference learning with linear function approximation

abstract: We show that Deep Neural Networks introduce two heteroscedastic Gumbel noise sources into Q-Learning. To account for these noise sources, we propose Double Gumbel Q-Learning, a Deep Q-Learning algorithm applicable for both discrete and continuous control. In discrete control, we derive a closed-form expression for the loss function of our algorithm. In continuous control, this loss function is intractable and we therefore derive an approximation with a hyperparameter whose value regulates pessimism in Q-Learning. We present a default value for our pessimism hyperparameter that enables DoubleGum to outperform DDPG, TD3, SAC, XQL, quantile regression, and Mixture-of-Gaussian Critics in aggregate over 33 tasks from DeepMind Control, MuJoCo, MetaWorld, and Box2D and show that tuning this hyperparameter may further improve sample efficiency.
