paragraphs: Q-learning depends on estimates of how valuable actions will be. This paper shows that using deep neural networks introduces two sources of Gumbel-distributed noise into that process. The noise is heteroscedastic, meaning its variability is not constant. Double Gumbel Q-Learning, also called DoubleGum, explicitly accounts for these two sources when constructing its learning objective.

The treatment differs between discrete and continuous action spaces. For discrete control, the authors derive a closed-form loss. For continuous control, the corresponding loss is intractable, so they derive an approximation. That approximation includes a hyperparameter controlling pessimism, allowing the learning procedure to regulate how conservatively it treats action-value estimates.

Using a proposed default setting, DoubleGum outperforms the listed comparison methods in aggregate across 33 tasks from four control suites. Aggregate superiority does not imply a win on every task. The authors also show that tuning the pessimism parameter may improve sample efficiency further. The findings connect an explicit noise model to a practical control algorithm with a usable default configuration.
summary.tldr: DoubleGum models two Gumbel noise sources in deep Q-learning and reports stronger aggregate performance across 33 control tasks.

title: Double Gumbel Q-Learning

abstract: Off-policy evaluation (OPE) is important for closing the gap between offline training and evaluation of reinforcement learning (RL), by estimating performance and/or rank of target (evaluation) policies using offline trajectories only. It can improve the safety and efficiency of data collection and policy testing procedures in situations where online deployments are expensive, such as healthcare. However, existing OPE methods fall short in estimating human feedback (HF) signals, as HF may be conditioned over multiple underlying factors and are only sparsely available; as opposed to the agent-defined environmental rewards (used in policy optimization), which are usually determined over parametric functions or distributions. Consequently, the nature of HF signals makes extrapolating accurate OPE estimations to be challenging. To resolve this, we introduce an OPE for HF (OPEHF) framework that revives existing OPE methods in order to accurately evaluate the HF signals. Specifically, we develop an immediate human reward (IHR) reconstruction approach, regularized by environmental knowledge distilled in a latent space that captures the underlying dynamics of state transitions as well as issuing HF signals. Our approach has been tested over *two real-world experiments*, adaptive *in-vivo* neurostimulation and intelligent tutoring, and a simulation environment (visual Q&A). Results show that our approach significantly improves the performance toward estimating HF signals accurately, compared to directly applying (variants of) existing OPE methods.

paragraphs: Off-policy evaluation estimates how a policy would perform using previously collected trajectories instead of new deployments. Human feedback makes this difficult because it can depend on multiple underlying factors and appear only sparsely. Methods designed around environmental rewards may therefore struggle to estimate policies' performance according to human feedback.

The proposed OPEHF framework reconstructs immediate human rewards so that existing evaluation methods can better use the available feedback. Reconstruction is regularized using environmental knowledge represented in a latent space. That representation captures both state-transition dynamics and the process associated with issuing feedback, tying the inferred reward signal to information about the environment.

The authors test the approach in two real-world experiments, adaptive in-vivo neurostimulation and intelligent tutoring, plus a visual question-answering simulation. They report significantly more accurate human-feedback estimation than directly applying existing off-policy evaluation methods or their variants. The findings support reconstruction as a way to make sparse feedback more useful for offline policy assessment, which matters when testing policies through fresh deployments is expensive.
summary.tldr: OPEHF reconstructs immediate human rewards using latent environmental knowledge to improve policy evaluation from sparse offline feedback.

title: Off-Policy Evaluation for Human Feedback

abstract: Deep learning models have progressively advanced time series forecasting due to their powerful capacity in capturing sequence dependence. Nevertheless, it is still challenging to make accurate predictions due to the existence of non-stationarity in real-world data, denoting the data distribution rapidly changes over time. To mitigate such a dilemma, several efforts have been conducted by reducing the non-stationarity with normalization operation. However, these methods typically overlook the distribution discrepancy between the input series and the horizon series, and assume that all time points within the same instance share the same statistical properties, which is too ideal and may lead to suboptimal relative improvements. To this end, we propose a novel slice-level adaptive normalization, referred to \textbf{SAN}, which is a novel scheme for empowering time series forecasting with more flexible normalization and denormalization. SAN includes two crucial designs. First, SAN tries to eliminate the non-stationarity of time series in units of a local temporal slice (i.e., sub-series) rather than a global instance. Second, SAN employs a slight network module to independently model the evolving trends of statistical properties of raw time series. Consequently, SAN could serve as a general model-agnostic plugin and better alleviate the impact of the non-stationary nature of time series data. We instantiate the proposed SAN on four widely used forecasting models and test their prediction results on benchmark datasets to evaluate its effectiveness. Also, we report some insightful findings to deeply analyze and understand our proposed SAN. We make our codes publicly available.

paragraphs: Time series forecasting becomes difficult when the statistical properties of a sequence change over time. Normalization can reduce this variation, but existing approaches often treat an entire input sequence as statistically uniform. They can also overlook differences between the observed sequence and the future interval being predicted. This paper addresses both issues through slice-level adaptive normalization, or SAN.

SAN operates on local sections of a sequence rather than applying one statistical treatment to the whole instance. This makes normalization more flexible when different parts of the input have different properties. A separate lightweight network models how the raw series’ statistical properties evolve, supporting adaptive normalization and the corresponding conversion of predictions back to their original scale.

The framework is designed as a model-agnostic plugin, and the authors instantiate it with four widely used forecasting models on benchmark datasets. Its central contribution is to make changing local statistics an explicit part of forecasting. The evaluation investigates its effectiveness, while additional analyses examine how the proposed normalization approach behaves.
summary.tldr: SAN normalizes local time-series slices and models evolving statistics to help forecasting models handle changing data distributions.

title: Adaptive Normalization for Non-stationary Time Series Forecasting: A Temporal Slice Perspective

abstract: Despite the proliferation of generative models, achieving fast sampling during inference without compromising sample diversity and quality remains challenging. Existing models such as Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DDPM) deliver high-quality, diverse samples but are slowed by an inherently high number of iterative steps. The Denoising Diffusion Generative Adversarial Networks (DDGAN) attempted to circumvent this limitation by integrating a GAN model for larger jumps in the diffusion process. However, DDGAN encountered scalability limitations when applied to large datasets. To address these limitations, we introduce a novel approach that tackles the problem by matching implicit and explicit factors. More specifically, our approach involves utilizing an implicit model to match the marginal distributions of noisy data and the explicit conditional distribution of the forward diffusion. This combination allows us to effectively match the joint denoising distributions. Unlike DDPM but similar to DDGAN, we do not enforce a parametric distribution for the reverse step, enabling us to take large steps during inference. Similar to the DDPM but unlike DDGAN, we take advantage of the exact form of the diffusion process. We demonstrate that our proposed method obtains comparable generative performance to diffusion-based models and vastly superior results to models with a small number of sampling steps.

paragraphs: Diffusion models can generate diverse, high-quality samples, but many sequential denoising steps slow inference. Earlier diffusion-GAN hybrids allowed larger steps, yet encountered difficulties scaling to large datasets. Semi-Implicit Denoising Diffusion Models aim to combine larger inference steps with useful information from the known forward diffusion process.

The method combines an implicit model for the marginal distributions of noisy data with the explicit conditional distribution of forward diffusion. Matching these factors allows it to match the joint denoising distributions. It does not impose a parametric distribution on each reverse step, which permits larger sampling steps, while still using the exact form of the forward process.

This construction draws on properties emphasized separately by the preceding approaches: flexible reverse transitions and explicit knowledge of how noise is introduced. The authors report generative performance comparable to diffusion-based models and substantially better results than models using few sampling steps. The findings support the proposed factor-matching strategy as a way to address the tension between sampling efficiency and generated-sample quality.
summary.tldr: SIDDMs combine implicit noisy-data modeling with explicit forward diffusion to enable large sampling steps and strong generative performance.

title: Semi-Implicit Denoising Diffusion Models (SIDDMs)

abstract: In-context learning (ICL) is one of the most powerful and most unexpected capabilities to emerge in recent transformer-based large language models (LLMs). Yet the mechanisms that underlie it are poorly understood. In this paper, we demonstrate that comparable ICL capabilities can be acquired by an alternative sequence prediction learning method using clone-structured causal graphs (CSCGs). Moreover, a key property of CSCGs is that, unlike transformer-based LLMs, they are {\em interpretable}, which considerably simplifies the task of explaining how ICL works. Specifically, we show that it uses a combination of (a) learning template (schema) circuits for pattern completion, (b) retrieving relevant templates in a context-sensitive manner, and (c) rebinding of novel tokens to appropriate slots in the templates. We go on to marshall evidence for the hypothesis that similar mechanisms underlie ICL in LLMs. For example, we find that, with CSCGs as with LLMs, different capabilities emerge at different levels of overparameterization, suggesting that overparameterization helps in learning more complex template (schema) circuits. By showing how ICL can be achieved with small models and datasets, we open up a path to novel architectures, and take a vital step towards a more general understanding of the mechanics behind this important capability.

paragraphs: In-context learning is a striking capability of large language models, but its underlying mechanisms remain difficult to explain. This paper studies an alternative sequence-prediction method, clone-structured causal graphs, that acquires comparable in-context learning capabilities while providing a more interpretable view of how those capabilities arise.

The authors identify three interacting mechanisms in these models. They learn reusable template circuits for completing patterns, retrieve templates appropriate to the current context, and bind unfamiliar tokens to suitable positions within those templates. This account explains how a previously learned pattern can be reused when the particular tokens appearing in a new context have changed.

The paper also gathers evidence for the hypothesis that related mechanisms operate in language models. In both model families, different capabilities emerge at different degrees of overparameterization, suggesting that extra capacity helps learn more complex templates. This supports a possible explanation rather than proving an identical mechanism in transformers. Demonstrating these behaviors with small models and datasets also points toward alternative architectures for studying in-context learning.
summary.tldr: Interpretable sequence models exhibit in-context learning through reusable templates and token rebinding, offering evidence for a possible mechanism in language models.

title: Schema-learning and rebinding as mechanisms of in-context learning and emergence

abstract: User modeling, which aims to capture users' characteristics or interests, heavily relies on task-specific labeled data and suffers from the data sparsity issue. Several recent studies tackled this problem by pre-training the user model on massive user behavior sequences with a contrastive learning task. Generally, these methods assume different views of the same behavior sequence constructed via data augmentation are semantically consistent, i.e., reflecting similar characteristics or interests of the user, and thus maximizing their agreement in the feature space. However, due to the diverse interests and heavy noise in user behaviors, existing augmentation methods tend to lose certain characteristics of the user or introduce noisy behaviors. Thus, forcing the user model to directly maximize the similarity between the augmented views may result in a negative transfer. To this end, we propose to replace the contrastive learning task with a new pretext task: Augmentation-Adaptive SelfSupervised Ranking (AdaptSSR), which alleviates the requirement of semantic consistency between the augmented views while pre-training a discriminative user model. Specifically, we adopt a multiple pairwise ranking loss which trains the user model to capture the similarity orders between the implicitly augmented view, the explicitly augmented view, and views from other users. We further employ an in-batch hard negative sampling strategy to facilitate model training. Moreover, considering the distinct impacts of data augmentation on different behavior sequences, we design an augmentation-adaptive fusion mechanism to automatically adjust the similarity order constraint applied to each sample based on the estimated similarity between the augmented views. Extensive experiments on both public and industrial datasets with six downstream tasks verify the effectiveness of AdaptSSR.

Moreover, considering the distinct impacts of data augmentation on different behavior sequences, we design an augmentation-adaptive fusion mechanism to automatically adjust the similarity order constraint applied to each sample based on the estimated similarity between the augmented views. Extensive experiments on both public and industrial datasets with six downstream tasks verify the effectiveness of AdaptSSR.

paragraphs: AdaptSSR addresses how to learn useful user representations when labeled examples are scarce. Existing approaches pretrain on behavior sequences by making augmented versions of the same sequence similar in representation space. That assumes both versions retain the same interests. Diverse interests and noisy behavior can break this assumption, making enforced agreement harmful to later tasks.

The proposed method instead learns relative similarity rankings. Its multiple pairwise ranking loss compares implicitly augmented views, explicitly augmented views, and views belonging to other users. This gives the model a way to distinguish users without requiring every augmented pair to express identical characteristics. Hard negative sampling within a training batch supplies challenging comparisons.

AdaptSSR also adjusts its ranking constraints for individual samples. An adaptive fusion mechanism uses the estimated similarity between augmented views to account for how differently augmentation affects different behavior sequences. Experiments on public and industrial datasets across six downstream tasks support its effectiveness. The central contribution is a pretraining objective that accommodates imperfect preservation of user interests during augmentation.
summary.tldr: AdaptSSR learns user representations through adaptive similarity rankings that accommodate noisy or semantically altered augmentations.

title: AdaptSSR: Pre-training User Model with Augmentation-Adaptive Self-Supervised Ranking

abstract: Images generated by diffusion models like Stable Diffusion are increasingly widespread. Recent works and even lawsuits have shown that these models are prone to replicating their training data, unbeknownst to the user. In this paper, we first analyze this memorization problem in text-to-image diffusion models. While it is widely believed that duplicated images in the training set are responsible for content replication at inference time, we observe that the text conditioning of the model plays a similarly important role. In fact, we see in our experiments that data replication often does not happen for unconditional models, while it is common in the text-conditional case. Motivated by our findings, we then propose several techniques for reducing data replication at both training and inference time by randomizing and augmenting image captions in the training set. Code is available at https://github.com/somepago/DCR.

paragraphs: This paper investigates why text-to-image diffusion models sometimes reproduce images from their training data. Such copying can occur without users realizing that an output closely replicates an existing example. The authors examine memorization with particular attention to the role of text conditioning, extending the discussion beyond repeated images in the training collection.

Their experiments indicate that text conditioning plays a role comparable in importance to image duplication. Replication often does not occur in the unconditional models they study, while it is common in the text-conditioned case. This is an empirical pattern rather than a claim that unconditional generation cannot copy or that every text-conditioned model will do so.

The approach makes the textual side of generation part of the mitigation strategy. Its significance is to identify caption information as a useful intervention point alongside concerns about duplicate training images, broadening how the copying problem can be addressed.
summary.tldr: Experiments identify text conditioning as an important contributor to diffusion-model copying and motivate caption-based mitigation techniques.

title: Understanding and Mitigating Copying in Diffusion Models

abstract: Learning to detect and encode temporal regularities (TRs) in events is a prerequisite for human-like intelligence. These regularities should be formed from limited event samples and stored as easily retrievable representations. Existing event embeddings, however, cannot effectively decode TR validity with well-trained vectors, let alone satisfy the efficiency requirements. We develop Noether Embedding (NE) as the first efficient TR learner with event embeddings. Specifically, NE possesses the intrinsic time-translation symmetries of TRs indicated as conserved local energies in the embedding space. This structural bias reduces the calculation of each TR validity to embedding each event sample, enabling NE to achieve data-efficient TR formation insensitive to sample size and time-efficient TR retrieval in constant time complexity. To comprehensively evaluate the TR learning capability of embedding models, we define complementary tasks of TR detection and TR query, formulate their evaluation metrics, and assess embeddings on classic ICEWS14, ICEWS18, and GDELT datasets. Our experiments demonstrate that NE consistently achieves about double the F1 scores for detecting valid TRs compared to classic embeddings, and it provides over ten times higher confidence scores for querying TR intervals. Additionally, we showcase NE's potential applications in social event prediction, personal decision-making, and memory-constrained scenarios.

It treats learning a pattern and later querying it as connected representation problems.

This structural constraint reduces checking a regularity's validity to embedding individual event samples. Evaluation separates detection of valid regularities from queries about their intervals, using ICEWS14, ICEWS18, and GDELT. Noether Embedding achieves roughly twice the detection F1 scores of classic embeddings and more than ten times their interval-query confidence scores. These are distinct reported measures, supporting both detection and retrieval capabilities. The authors also illustrate potential uses in social-event prediction, personal decisions, and memory-constrained settings.
summary.tldr: Noether Embedding encodes time-translation symmetry to learn temporal regularities efficiently and retrieve them in constant time.

title: Noether Embedding: Efficient Learning of Temporal Regularities

abstract: We tackle the task of scene flow estimation from point clouds. Given a source and a target point cloud, the objective is to estimate a translation from each point in the source point cloud to the target, resulting in a 3D motion vector field. Previous dominant scene flow estimation methods require complicated coarse-to-fine or recurrent architectures as a multi-stage refinement. In contrast, we propose a significantly simpler single-scale one-shot global matching to address the problem. Our key finding is that reliable feature similarity between point pairs is essential and sufficient to estimate accurate scene flow. We thus propose to decompose the feature extraction step via a hybrid local-global-cross transformer architecture which is crucial to accurate and robust feature representations. Extensive experiments show that the proposed Global Matching Scene Flow (GMSF) sets a new state-of-the-art on multiple scene flow estimation benchmarks. On FlyingThings3D, with the presence of occlusion points, GMSF reduces the outlier percentage from the previous best performance of 27.4% to 5.6%. On KITTI Scene Flow, without any fine-tuning, our proposed method shows state-of-the-art performance. On the Waymo-Open dataset, the proposed method outperforms previous methods by a large margin. The code is available at https://github.com/ZhangYushan3/GMSF.

Many leading approaches build this estimate through repeated refinement or multiple scales. GMSF instead uses a single-scale, one-shot global matching procedure, simplifying the structure of the estimation process.

The authors identify reliable feature similarity between pairs of points as essential and sufficient for accurate scene flow in their approach. They focus the model on producing these features through a hybrid local-global-cross transformer architecture. This combines several forms of feature processing to support accurate and robust representations for the global matching step.

Experiments report leading performance across multiple scene-flow benchmarks. On FlyingThings3D with occluded points, the outlier percentage falls from the previous best of 27.4% to 5.6%. The method also achieves state-of-the-art results on KITTI Scene Flow without fine-tuning and substantially outperforms previous methods on Waymo-Open. These findings support the effectiveness of improving correspondence features within a comparatively simple matching pipeline.
summary.tldr: GMSF estimates point-cloud motion through one-shot global matching and reports leading results using strong transformer-based correspondence features.

title: GMSF: Global Matching Scene Flow

abstract: Clustering is a fundamental problem in unsupervised machine learning with many applications in data analysis. Popular clustering algorithms such as Lloyd's algorithm and $k$-means++ can take $\Omega(ndk)$ time when clustering $n$ points in a $d$-dimensional space (represented by an $n\times d$ matrix $X$) into $k$ clusters. On massive datasets with moderate to large $k$, the multiplicative $k$ factor can become very expensive. We introduce a simple randomized clustering algorithm that provably runs in expected time $O(\mathsf{nnz}(X) + n\log n)$ for arbitrary $k$. Here $\mathsf{nnz}(X)$ is the total number of non-zero entries in the input dataset $X$, which is upper bounded by $nd$ and can be significantly smaller for sparse datasets. We prove that our algorithm achieves approximation ratio $\widetilde{O}(k^4)$ on any input dataset for the $k$-means objective, and our experiments show that the quality of the clusters found by our algorithm is usually much better than this worst-case bound. We use our algorithm for $k$-means clustering and for coreset construction; our experiments show that it gives a new tradeoff between running time and cluster quality compared to previous state-of-the-art methods for these tasks. Our theoretical analysis is based on novel results of independent interest. We show that the approximation ratio achieved after a random one-dimensional projection can be lifted to the original points and that $k$-means++ seeding can be implemented in expected time $O(n\log n)$ in one dimension.

summary.tldr: Random one-dimensional projections enable clustering with fast expected runtime and a provable approximation bound, with stronger quality observed empirically.

title: Simple, Scalable and Effective Clustering via One-Dimensional Projections

abstract: The representation gap between teacher and student is an emerging topic in knowledge distillation (KD). To reduce the gap and improve the performance, current methods often resort to complicated training schemes, loss functions, and feature alignments, which are task-specific and feature-specific. In this paper, we state that the essence of these methods is to discard the noisy information and distill the valuable information in the feature, and propose a novel KD method dubbed DiffKD, to explicitly denoise and match features using diffusion models. Our approach is based on the observation that student features typically contain more noises than teacher features due to the smaller capacity of student model. To address this, we propose to denoise student features using a diffusion model trained by teacher features. This allows us to perform better distillation between the refined clean feature and teacher feature. Additionally, we introduce a light-weight diffusion model with a linear autoencoder to reduce the computation cost and an adaptive noise matching module to improve the denoising performance. Extensive experiments demonstrate that DiffKD is effective across various types of features and achieves state-of-the-art performance consistently on image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation tasks. Code is available at https://github.com/hunto/DiffKD.

paragraphs: Knowledge distillation transfers information from a larger teacher model to a smaller student, but their internal features can differ substantially. DiffKD approaches this mismatch as a denoising problem. It builds on the observation that a student's smaller capacity typically produces noisier features than those of its teacher.

The method trains a diffusion model using teacher features and uses it to denoise the student's features. Distillation then compares the refined student representation with the teacher representation. This makes removal of unwanted feature information an explicit step, matching the authors' interpretation of what more elaborate feature-alignment methods seek to accomplish.

Experiments report consistent state-of-the-art performance across image classification, object detection, and semantic segmentation, using various feature types. The breadth of those results supports feature denoising as a useful distillation strategy across the evaluated vision tasks.
summary.tldr: DiffKD uses diffusion-based denoising to make student features better match a teacher during knowledge distillation.

title: Knowledge Diffusion for Distillation

abstract: Dataset condensation (DC) distills a large real-world dataset into a small synthetic dataset, with the goal of training a network from scratch on the latter that performs similarly to the former. State-of-the-art (SOTA) DC methods have achieved satisfactory results through techniques such as accuracy, gradient, training trajectory, or distribution matching. However, these works all perform matching in the high-dimension pixel spaces, ignoring that natural images are usually locally connected and have lower intrinsic dimensions, resulting in low condensation efficiency. In this work, we propose a simple-yet-efficient dataset condensation plugin that matches the raw and synthetic datasets in a low-dimensional manifold. Specifically, our plugin condenses raw images into two low-rank matrices instead of parameterized image matrices. Our plugin can be easily incorporated into existing DC methods, thereby containing richer raw dataset information at limited storage costs to improve the downstream applications' performance. We verify on multiple public datasets that when the proposed plugin is combined with SOTA DC methods, the performance of the network trained on synthetic data is significantly improved compared to traditional DC methods. Moreover, when applying the DC methods as a plugin to continual learning tasks, we observed that our approach effectively mitigates catastrophic forgetting of old tasks under limited memory buffer constraints and avoids the problem of raw data privacy leakage.

summary.tldr: A low-rank dataset condensation plugin improves synthetic-data training and reduces continual-learning forgetting under limited memory.

title: An Efficient Dataset Condensation Plugin and Its Application to Continual Learning

abstract: Variable importance assessment has become a crucial step in machine-learning applications when using complex learners, such as deep neural networks, on large-scale data. Removal-based importance assessment is currently the reference approach, particularly when statistical guarantees are sought to justify variable inclusion. It is often implemented with variable permutation schemes. On the flip side, these approaches risk misidentifying unimportant variables as important in the presence of correlations among covariates. Here we develop a systematic approach for studying Conditional Permutation Importance (CPI) that is model agnostic and computationally lean, as well as reusable benchmarks of state-of-the-art variable importance estimators. We show theoretically and empirically that \textit{CPI} overcomes the limitations of standard permutation importance by providing accurate type-I error control. When used with a deep neural network, \textit{CPI} consistently showed top accuracy across benchmarks. An experiment on real-world data analysis in a large-scale medical dataset showed that \textit{CPI} provides a more parsimonious selection of statistically significant variables. Our results suggest that \textit{CPI} can be readily used as drop-in replacement for permutation-based methods.

paragraphs: Variable importance methods help determine which inputs matter to a complex predictive model. A common strategy removes information through variable permutations and measures the consequences. However, when input variables are correlated, standard permutation approaches can incorrectly label an unimportant variable as important, undermining statistical conclusions about variable inclusion.

The paper develops a systematic treatment of Conditional Permutation Importance, or CPI. The approach is model agnostic and computationally lean, and the work also introduces reusable benchmarks for comparing leading importance estimators. The authors show theoretically and empirically that CPI addresses the false-positive problem through accurate type-I error control, linking importance assessment to a statistical guarantee.

When paired with a deep neural network, CPI consistently achieves top accuracy across the benchmarks. In a large medical dataset, it selects a smaller set of statistically significant variables. These results suggest that conditional permutation methods can provide more selective assessments while preserving strong accuracy, and support CPI as a practical replacement for existing permutation-based importance methods.
summary.tldr: Conditional Permutation Importance controls false positives from correlated inputs and yields accurate, more selective variable importance assessments.

title: Statistically Valid Variable Importance Assessment through Conditional Permutations

abstract: Graph Neural Networks (GNNs) have emerged as a powerful technique for learning on relational data. Owing to the relatively limited number of message passing steps they perform—and hence a smaller receptive field—there has been significant interest in improving their expressivity by incorporating structural aspects of the underlying graph. In this paper, we explore the use of affinity measures as features in graph neural networks, in particular measures arising from random walks, including effective resistance, hitting and commute times. We propose message passing networks based on these features and evaluate their performance on a variety of node and graph property prediction tasks. Our architecture has low computational complexity, while our features are invariant to the permutations of the underlying graph. The measures we compute allow the network to exploit the connectivity properties of the graph, thereby allowing us to outperform relevant benchmarks for a wide variety of tasks, often with significantly fewer message passing steps. On one of the largest publicly available graph regression datasets, OGB-LSC-PCQM4Mv1, we obtain the best known single-model validation MAE at the time of writing.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks often exchange information through only a few rounds of message passing. This limits how much of the surrounding graph directly informs a prediction. The paper investigates whether features describing graph connectivity can supply useful structural information without requiring many additional rounds.

The proposed networks use affinity measures associated with random walks, including effective resistance, hitting times, and commute times. These features characterize relationships through the graph's connectivity and are incorporated into message passing. They also remain unchanged when the graph's nodes are relabeled, so their meaning does not depend on an arbitrary numbering of the nodes. The authors describe the architecture as having low computational complexity.

Across node and graph property prediction tasks, the approach outperforms relevant benchmarks, often using substantially fewer message passing steps. On OGB-LSC-PCQM4Mv1, it achieves the best known single-model validation mean absolute error at the time of writing. The findings support connectivity-aware features as an effective way to strengthen graph predictions while keeping message passing relatively shallow.
summary.tldr: Random-walk affinity features help graph networks capture connectivity and improve predictions, often with fewer message passing steps.

title: Affinity-Aware Graph Networks

abstract: Flexible models for probability distributions are an essential ingredient in many machine learning tasks. We develop and investigate a new class of probability distributions, which we call a Squared Neural Family (SNEFY), formed by squaring the 2-norm of a neural network and normalising it with respect to a base measure. Following the reasoning similar to the well established connections between infinitely wide neural networks and Gaussian processes, we show that SNEFYs admit closed form normalising constants in many cases of interest, thereby resulting in flexible yet fully tractable density models. SNEFYs strictly generalise classical exponential families, are closed under conditioning, and have tractable marginal distributions. Their utility is illustrated on a variety of density estimation, conditional density estimation, and density estimation with missing data tasks.

We develop and investigate a new class of probability distributions, which we call a Squared Neural Family (SNEFY), formed by squaring the 2-norm of a neural network and normalising it with respect to a base measure. Following the reasoning similar to the well established connections between infinitely wide neural networks and Gaussian processes, we show that SNEFYs admit closed form normalising constants in many cases of interest, thereby resulting in flexible yet fully tractable density models. SNEFYs strictly generalise classical exponential families, are closed under conditioning, and have tractable marginal distributions. Their utility is illustrated on a variety of density estimation, conditional density estimation, and density estimation with missing data tasks.

paragraphs: Probability models need both expressive shapes and a way to ensure their total probability is one. Squared Neural Families, or SNEFYs, construct distributions by taking the squared Euclidean norm of a neural network’s output and normalizing it relative to a base measure. Squaring provides the non-negative quantity needed to form a density.

The difficult part of this construction is computing the normalizing constant. Using reasoning related to connections between infinitely wide neural networks and Gaussian processes, the authors obtain closed-form constants in many cases of interest. This allows flexible neural-network-based densities whose normalization can still be handled exactly in those cases.

The paper also establishes useful structural properties: SNEFYs strictly generalize classical exponential families, remain within the family under conditioning, and have tractable marginal distributions. These properties support working with partially observed variables and distributions conditioned on available information. Applications illustrate density estimation, conditional density estimation, and estimation with missing data. The main contribution is a probability-model family that combines neural flexibility with tractable operations needed for these statistical tasks.
summary.tldr: SNEFYs turn squared neural-network outputs into flexible probability models with closed-form normalization in many cases and tractable conditioning and marginals.

title: Squared Neural Families: A New Class of Tractable Density Models

abstract: We propose a simple generalization of standard and empirically successful decision tree learning algorithms such as ID3, C4.5, and CART. These algorithms, which have been central to machine learning for decades, are greedy in nature: they grow a decision tree by iteratively splitting on the best attribute. Our algorithm, Top-$k$, considers the $k$ best attributes as possible splits instead of just the single best attribute. We demonstrate, theoretically and empirically, the power of this simple generalization. We first prove a greediness hierarchy theorem showing that for every $k\in \mathbb{N}$, Top-$(k+1)$ can be dramatically more powerful than Top-$k$: there are data distributions for which the former achieves accuracy $1-\epsilon$, whereas the latter only achieves accuracy $\frac{1}{2}+\epsilon$. We then show, through extensive experiments, that Top-$k$ outperforms the two main approaches to decision tree learning: classic greedy algorithms and more recent ``optimal decision tree'' algorithms. On one hand, Top-$k$ consistently enjoys significant accuracy gains over greedy algorithms across a wide range of benchmarks. On the other hand, Top-$k$ is markedly more scalable than optimal decision tree algorithms and is able to handle dataset and feature set sizes that remain far beyond the reach of these algorithms. The code to reproduce our results is available at https://github.com/SullivanC19/pydl8.5-topk.

The code to reproduce our results is available at https://github.com/SullivanC19/pydl8.5-topk.

paragraphs: Classic decision-tree algorithms grow a tree by repeatedly choosing the attribute that looks best for the next split. That greedy choice keeps learning manageable but restricts which alternatives are considered. This paper proposes Top-k, a generalization that considers the k best candidate attributes instead of committing to just one.

The theoretical contribution shows that increasing this choice budget can fundamentally change what the algorithm achieves. For every k, there are data distributions where Top-(k+1) reaches accuracy close to one while Top-k stays close to one-half. This is an existence result about particular distributions, showing that even one additional candidate can sometimes matter dramatically.

Experiments compare Top-k with both conventional greedy learners and algorithms that search for optimal decision trees. It achieves substantial accuracy gains over greedy methods across many benchmarks while scaling to dataset and feature-set sizes beyond the tested optimal-tree approaches. The resulting contribution is a useful tradeoff: a modest expansion of the choices considered can improve predictive performance without taking on the full computational burden of optimal-tree learning.
summary.tldr: Considering several candidate tree splits yields strong accuracy and scalability results, with theory showing that each extra choice can sometimes provide a dramatic advantage.

title: Harnessing the power of choices in decision tree learning

abstract: Event-intensity asymmetric stereo systems have emerged as a promising approach for robust 3D perception in dynamic and challenging environments by integrating event cameras with frame-based sensors in different views. However, existing methods often suffer from overfitting and poor generalization due to limited dataset sizes and lack of scene diversity in the event domain. To address these issues, we propose a zero-shot framework that utilizes monocular depth estimation and stereo matching models pretrained on diverse image datasets. Our approach introduces a visual prompting technique to align the representations of frames and events, allowing the use of off-the-shelf stereo models without additional training. Furthermore, we introduce a monocular cue-guided disparity refinement module to improve robustness across static and dynamic regions by incorporating monocular depth information from foundation models. Extensive experiments on real-world datasets demonstrate the superior zero-shot evaluation performance and enhanced generalization ability of our method compared to existing approaches.

Such systems can help in dynamic or challenging environments, but limited event datasets can lead to overfitting and weak generalization. The proposed framework draws on models pre-trained with diverse image datasets to address that shortage.

A visual-prompting technique aligns the representations of events and frames, allowing an off-the-shelf stereo-matching model to operate without additional training. The framework also uses a pre-trained monocular depth model. Its depth information guides a disparity-refinement module, helping improve robustness in both static and moving parts of a scene.

Experiments on real-world datasets report stronger zero-shot performance and improved generalization compared with existing approaches. The contribution is a way to connect event-based observations with image-domain models through representation alignment and depth-guided refinement. The findings support transferring existing image-model capabilities into this mixed-sensor setting without training a new stereo model for the event domain.
summary.tldr: Visual prompting and monocular depth cues enable pre-trained image models to perform event–frame stereo estimation without additional training.

title: Zero-Shot Event-Intensity Asymmetric Stereo via Visual Prompting from Image Domain

abstract: Continual Imitation Learning (CiL) involves extracting and accumulating task knowledge from demonstrations across multiple stages and tasks to achieve a multi-task policy. With recent advancements in foundation models, there has been a growing interest in adapter-based CiL approaches, where adapters are established parameter-efficiently for tasks newly demonstrated. While these approaches isolate parameters for specific tasks and tend to mitigate catastrophic forgetting, they limit knowledge sharing among different demonstrations. We introduce IsCiL, an adapter-based CiL framework that addresses this limitation of knowledge sharing by incrementally learning shareable skills from different demonstrations, thus enabling sample-efficient task adaptation using the skills particularly in non-stationary CiL environments. In IsCiL, demonstrations are mapped into the state embedding space, where proper skills can be retrieved upon input states through prototype-based memory. These retrievable skills are incrementally learned on their corresponding adapters. Our CiL experiments with complex tasks in the Franka-Kitchen and Meta-World demonstrate the robust performance of IsCiL in both task adaptation and sample-efficiency. We also show a simple extension of IsCiL for task unlearning scenarios.

paragraphs: Continual imitation learning builds a policy from demonstrations that arrive across different tasks and stages. Adapter-based methods add relatively few parameters for each new task and tend to reduce forgetting by separating task-specific parameters. That separation can also restrict how much knowledge is shared between demonstrations, limiting reuse when new tasks arrive.

IsCiL organizes adaptation around shareable skills that are learned incrementally. Demonstrations are mapped into a state representation space, where a prototype-based memory helps retrieve suitable skills for an input state. Each skill is learned through its corresponding adapter. This creates a mechanism for reusing relevant knowledge across demonstrations while retaining the parameter-efficient adapter structure.

Experiments on complex Franka-Kitchen and Meta-World tasks show robust task adaptation and sample efficiency, including the changing environments emphasized by the framework. The authors also demonstrate a simple extension for task unlearning. The results support treating reusable skills as the units of accumulated knowledge, allowing new tasks to draw on previously learned behavior instead of relying entirely on isolated task-specific adaptation.
summary.tldr: IsCiL incrementally learns retrievable, shareable skills in adapters to improve continual imitation learning and sample-efficient task adaptation.

title: Incremental Learning of Retrievable Skills For Efficient Continual Task Adaptation

abstract: Optimal transport (OT) has profoundly impacted machine learning by providing theoretical and computational tools to realign datasets.In this context, given two large point clouds of sizes $n$ and $m$ in $\mathbb{R}^d$, entropic OT (EOT) solvers have emerged as the most reliable tool to either solve the Kantorovich problem and output a $n\times m$ coupling matrix, or to solve the Monge problem and learn a vector-valued push-forward map. While the robustness of EOT couplings/maps makes them a go-to choice in practical applications, EOT solvers remain difficult to tune because of a small but influential set of hyperparameters, notably the omnipresent entropic regularization strength $\varepsilon$. Setting $\varepsilon$ can be difficult, as it simultaneously impacts various performance metrics, such as compute speed, statistical performance, generalization, and bias. In this work, we propose a new class of EOT solvers (ProgOT), that can estimate both plans and transport maps.We take advantage of several opportunities to optimize the computation of EOT solutions by *dividing* mass displacement using a time discretization, borrowing inspiration from dynamic OT formulations, and *conquering* each of these steps using EOT with properly scheduled parameters. We provide experimental evidence demonstrating that ProgOT is a faster and more robust alternative to *standard solvers* when computing couplings at large scales, even outperforming neural network-based approaches. We also prove statistical consistency of our approach for estimating OT maps.

paragraphs: Optimal transport provides ways to realign datasets, either through a matrix describing how mass moves between points or through a map that moves points directly. Entropic optimal transport is widely useful, but its regularization strength is difficult to tune. The same parameter affects computational speed, statistical behavior, generalization, and bias, creating several interacting design considerations.

ProgOT divides the overall displacement into a sequence of smaller steps inspired by dynamic optimal transport. Each step is solved with entropic optimal transport using appropriately scheduled parameters. This progressive formulation can estimate both transport plans and transport maps, distributing the work of alignment across time-discretized stages instead of treating displacement as one operation.

Experiments show that ProgOT computes large-scale couplings faster and more robustly than standard solvers, including outperforming the evaluated neural-network approaches. The paper also proves statistical consistency for its transport-map estimates. These are complementary findings: the experiments establish practical advantages in the tested computations, while the consistency result supplies a theoretical foundation for the map-estimation approach.
summary.tldr: ProgOT solves transport progressively with scheduled entropic parameters, improving large-scale coupling computation and providing consistent transport-map estimates.

title: Progressive Entropic Optimal Transport Solvers

abstract: Most large multimodal models (LMMs) are implemented by feeding visual tokens as a sequence into the first layer of a large language model (LLM). The resulting architecture is simple but significantly increases computation and memory costs, as it has to handle a large number of additional tokens in its input layer. This paper presents a new architecture *DeepStack* for LMMs. Considering $N$ layers in the language and vision transformer of LMMs, we stack the visual tokens into $N$ groups and feed each group to its aligned transformer layer from bottom to top. Surprisingly, this simple method greatly enhances the power of LMMs to model interactions among visual tokens across layers but with minimal additional cost. We apply *DeepStack* to both language and vision transformer in LMMs, and validate the effectiveness of *DeepStack* LMMs with extensive empirical results. Using the same context length, our DeepStack 7B and 13B parameters surpass their counterparts by 2.7 and 2.9 on average across 9 benchmarks, respectively. Using only one-fifth of the context length, DeepStack rivals closely to the counterparts that use the full context length. These gains are particularly pronounced on high-resolution tasks, *e.g.*, 4.2, 11.0, and 4.0 improvements on TextVQA, DocVQA, and InfoVQA compared to LLaVA-1.5-7B, respectively. We further apply *DeepStack* to vision transformer layers, which brings us a similar amount of improvements, 3.8 on average compared with LLaVA-1.5-7B.

paragraphs: Many large multimodal models pass all visual tokens into the first layer of a language model. This simple design increases input sequence length and therefore computation and memory costs. DeepStack changes where visual information enters the network, distributing it across layers instead of concentrating its introduction at the bottom.

The architecture divides visual tokens into N groups and feeds each group into its corresponding transformer layer. The authors apply this idea to both language and vision transformers. Their central finding is that this straightforward change strengthens interactions among visual tokens across layers with minimal additional cost, making depth another way to organize visual input.

At the same context length, the 7B and 13B models improve average results across nine benchmarks by 2.7 and 2.9, respectively. With one-fifth of the context length, DeepStack performs close to counterparts using the full length. Gains are particularly pronounced on high-resolution tasks, including TextVQA, DocVQA, and InfoVQA. These results suggest that how visual tokens are distributed through a model can materially affect their usefulness.
summary.tldr: DeepStack distributes visual tokens across transformer layers, improving multimodal performance and achieving competitive results with much shorter context.

title: DeepStack: Deeply Stacking Visual Tokens is Surprisingly Simple and Effective for LMMs

abstract: Localized receptive fields—neurons that are selective for certain contiguous spatiotemporal features of their input—populate early sensory regions of the mammalian brain. Unsupervised learning algorithms that optimize explicit sparsity or independence criteria replicate features of these localized receptive fields, but fail to explain directly how localization arises through learning without efficient coding, as occurs in early layers of deep neural networks and might occur in early sensory regions of biological systems. We consider an alternative model in which localized receptive fields emerge without explicit top-down efficiency constraints—a feed-forward neural network trained on a data model inspired by the structure of natural images. Previous work identified the importance of non-Gaussian statistics to localization in this setting but left open questions about the mechanisms driving dynamical emergence. We address these questions by deriving the effective learning dynamics for a single nonlinear neuron, making precise how higher-order statistical properties of the input data drive emergent localization, and we demonstrate that the predictions of these effective dynamics extend to the many-neuron setting. Our analysis provides an alternative explanation for the ubiquity of localization as resulting from the nonlinear dynamics of learning in neural circuits

paragraphs: Localized receptive fields make neurons selective for contiguous regions of their inputs. They are common in early sensory processing and can also emerge in neural networks. Existing explanations based on explicitly encouraging sparse or independent representations reproduce such fields, but do not directly explain localization when those efficiency objectives are absent.

The authors study a feed-forward network trained on a data model inspired by natural-image structure. They derive effective learning dynamics for a single nonlinear neuron to explain how localization develops during learning. Their analysis makes precise the contribution of higher-order input statistics, building on earlier work that identified non-Gaussian statistics as important.

The paper also demonstrates that predictions from the single-neuron dynamics extend to networks with many neurons. This provides an alternative account of localization based on the interaction between input structure and nonlinear learning dynamics. Its explanatory scope is the studied model and demonstrated extension, offering a possible mechanism relevant to neural circuits without requiring an explicit top-down objective for efficient coding.
summary.tldr: The paper explains how higher-order input statistics and nonlinear learning dynamics can produce localized receptive fields without explicit efficiency objectives.

title: Nonlinear dynamics of localization in neural receptive fields

abstract: In recent years, there has been a surge of interest in the use of machine-learned predictions to bypass worst-case lower bounds for classical problems in combinatorial optimization. So far, the focus has mostly been on online algorithms, where information-theoretic barriers are overcome using predictions about the unknown future. In this paper, we consider the complementary question of using learned information to overcome computational barriers in the form of approximation hardness of polynomial-time algorithms for NP-hard (offline) problems. We show that noisy predictions about the optimal solution can be used to break classical hardness results for maximization problems such as the max-cut problem and more generally, maximization versions of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs).

So far, the focus has mostly been on online algorithms, where information-theoretic barriers are overcome using predictions about the unknown future. In this paper, we consider the complementary question of using learned information to overcome computational barriers in the form of approximation hardness of polynomial-time algorithms for NP-hard (offline) problems. We show that noisy predictions about the optimal solution can be used to break classical hardness results for maximization problems such as the max-cut problem and more generally, maximization versions of constraint satisfaction problems (CSPs).

paragraphs: This paper investigates whether learned predictions can improve algorithms for difficult offline optimization problems. Earlier work largely studied online problems, where predictions offer information about a future that has not yet been observed. Here, the obstacle is computational: even with the problem instance available, finding sufficiently good solutions can face approximation-hardness barriers.

The authors consider supplying an algorithm with noisy predictions about an optimal solution. Their results show that this extra information can enable approximation performance beyond classical hardness thresholds for maximum cut and, more generally, maximization versions of constraint satisfaction problems. The predictions need not be perfectly correct for the paper’s approach to provide an advantage.

The significance lies in changing what information the optimization algorithm receives. Classical hardness results concern their original computational setting; learned guidance supplies additional information about the solution. The paper therefore establishes a role for predictions in addressing offline computational barriers, extending the learning-augmented perspective beyond its more common use in handling uncertainty about future inputs.
summary.tldr: Noisy predictions about optimal solutions can help approximation algorithms surpass classical hardness thresholds for maximum cut and related problems.

title: Learning-Augmented Approximation Algorithms for Maximum Cut and Related Problems

abstract: Many algorithms and observed phenomena in deep learning appear to be affected by parameter symmetries --- transformations of neural network parameters that do not change the underlying neural network function. These include linear mode connectivity, model merging, Bayesian neural network inference, metanetworks, and several other characteristics of optimization or loss-landscapes. However, theoretical analysis of the relationship between parameter space symmetries and these phenonmena is difficult. In this work, we empirically investigate the impact of neural parameter symmetries by introducing new neural network architectures that have reduced parameter space symmetries. We develop two methods, with some provable guarantees, of modifying standard neural networks to reduce parameter space symmetries. With these new methods, we conduct a comprehensive experimental study consisting of multiple tasks aimed at assessing the effect of removing parameter symmetries. Our experiments reveal several interesting observations on the empirical impact of parameter symmetries; for instance, we observe linear mode connectivity between our networks without alignment of weight spaces, and we find that our networks allow for faster and more effective Bayesian neural network training.

paragraphs: Different neural-network parameter settings can represent exactly the same function. These parameter symmetries are thought to influence phenomena such as model merging, connectivity between solutions, and Bayesian inference, but their effects are difficult to analyze theoretically. This paper studies them empirically by modifying networks to reduce their symmetries.

The authors introduce two modification methods with some provable guarantees, then use the resulting architectures across multiple tasks. Reducing symmetries provides a way to investigate how training behavior and relationships between learned solutions change when fewer equivalent parameter arrangements are available. The experimental design turns symmetry reduction into a practical tool for studying these questions.

Among the findings, the modified networks exhibit linear mode connectivity without first aligning their weight spaces. They also support faster and more effective Bayesian neural-network training. These observations show concrete consequences of the architectural changes and provide evidence about symmetry’s role in the evaluated phenomena. The contribution combines methods for reducing parameter symmetries with an empirical examination of what that reduction changes.
summary.tldr: The paper reduces neural parameter symmetries to study their empirical effects, finding connectivity without weight alignment and improved Bayesian network training.

title: The Empirical Impact of Neural Parameter Symmetries, or Lack Thereof

abstract: Recent advances in multi-modal algorithms have driven and been driven by the increasing availability of large image-text datasets, leading to significant strides in various fields, including computational pathology. However, in most existing medical image-text datasets, the text typically provides high-level summaries that may not sufficiently describe sub-tile regions within a large pathology image. For example, an image might cover an extensive tissue area containing cancerous and healthy regions, but the accompanying text might only specify that this image is a cancer slide, lacking the nuanced details needed for in-depth analysis. In this study, we introduce STimage-1K4M, a novel dataset designed to bridge this gap by providing genomic features for sub-tile images. STimage-1K4M contains 1,149 images derived from spatial transcriptomics data, which captures gene expression information at the level of individual spatial spots within a pathology image. Specifically, each image in the dataset is broken down into smaller sub-image tiles, with each tile paired with $15,000-30,000$ dimensional gene expressions. With $4,293,195$ pairs of sub-tile images and gene expressions, STimage-1K4M offers unprecedented granularity, paving the way for a wide range of advanced research in multi-modal data analysis an innovative applications in computational pathology, and beyond.

Such summaries provide little detail about individual regions. STimage-1K4M addresses this mismatch by pairing small tissue-image tiles with gene-expression information associated with their spatial locations.

The authors present it as a foundation for further multimodal analysis and computational-pathology applications that need information about specific regions within larger tissue images.
summary.tldr: STimage-1K4M provides over four million tissue-image tiles paired with spatially matched gene-expression measurements.

title: STimage-1K4M: A histopathology image-gene expression dataset for spatial transcriptomics

abstract: Real-world data deviating from the independent and identically distributed (\textit{i.i.d.}) assumption of in-distribution training data poses security threats to deep networks, thus advancing out-of-distribution (OOD) detection algorithms. Detection methods in generative language models (GLMs) mainly focus on uncertainty estimation and embedding distance measurement, with the latter proven to be most effective in traditional linguistic tasks like summarization and translation. However, another complex generative scenario mathematical reasoning poses significant challenges to embedding-based methods due to its high-density feature of output spaces, but this feature causes larger discrepancies in the embedding shift trajectory between different samples in latent spaces. Hence, we propose a trajectory-based method TV score, which uses trajectory volatility for OOD detection in mathematical reasoning. Experiments show that our method outperforms all traditional algorithms on GLMs under mathematical reasoning scenarios and can be extended to more applications with high-density features in output spaces, such as multiple-choice questions.

paragraphs: Out-of-distribution detection asks whether an input differs from the data a model was trained to handle. For generative language models, existing approaches often examine uncertainty or distances between internal representations, called embeddings. This paper studies why embedding-based detection becomes difficult in mathematical reasoning, where the output space has a high-density structure.

The authors argue that this same structure creates useful differences in how embeddings shift through latent space. Their proposed TV score measures the volatility of an embedding trajectory. The approach therefore uses variation along a trajectory as its detection signal, drawing on information that a distance measurement alone may fail to capture.

In the reported mathematical reasoning experiments, TV score outperforms all traditional detection algorithms evaluated on the generative language models. The authors also describe extension to other applications with similarly dense output spaces, including multiple-choice questions. The central finding is that tracking changes in representations can improve detection in a setting where conventional embedding distances face particular challenges.
summary.tldr: TV score detects unfamiliar mathematical reasoning inputs by measuring volatility in embedding trajectories.

title: Embedding Trajectory for Out-of-Distribution Detection in Mathematical Reasoning

abstract: Prior Unsupervised Domain Adaptation (UDA) methods often aim to train a domain-invariant feature extractor, which may hinder the model from learning sufficiently discriminative features. To tackle this, a line of works based on prompt learning leverages the power of large-scale pre-trained vision-language models to learn both domain-invariant and specific features through a set of domain-agnostic and domain-specific learnable prompts. Those studies typically enforce invariant constraints on representation, output, or prompt space to learn such prompts. Differently, we cast UDA as a multiple-objective optimization problem in which each objective is represented by a domain loss. Under this new framework, we propose aligning per-objective gradients to foster consensus between them. Additionally, to prevent potential overfitting when fine-tuning this deep learning architecture, we penalize the norm of these gradients. To achieve these goals, we devise a practical gradient update procedure that can work under both single-source and multi-source UDA. Empirically, our method consistently surpasses other vision language model adaptation methods by a large margin on a wide range of benchmarks. The implementation is available at https://github.com/VietHoang1512/PGA.

paragraphs: Unsupervised domain adaptation aims to transfer a model across domains without labeled target-domain data. The paper addresses a tension in learning features that are shared across domains: enforcing invariance can interfere with retaining distinctions useful for prediction. Prompt-based adaptation of pretrained vision-language models provides a way to learn both shared and domain-specific information.

The authors formulate adaptation as a multiple-objective problem, assigning a loss to each domain. Their method aligns the gradients of these objectives so that the updates they request are more consistent with one another. It also penalizes gradient norms to help prevent potential overfitting during fine-tuning. A practical update procedure supports both single-source and multiple-source adaptation.

This approach places the coordination mechanism in the optimization process, where domain objectives determine how prompts are updated. The paper reports consistent improvements by a large margin over other vision-language adaptation methods across a wide range of benchmarks. These empirical findings support gradient agreement as a useful way to coordinate domain learning while preserving the flexibility of prompt-based adaptation.
summary.tldr: Aligning domain-loss gradients improves prompt-based domain adaptation while gradient-norm penalties help control potential overfitting.

title: Enhancing Domain Adaptation through Prompt Gradient Alignment

abstract: Existing Goal-Conditioned Reinforcement Learning (GCRL) algorithms are built upon Hindsight Experience Replay (HER), which densifies rewards through hindsight replay and leverages historical goal-achieving information to construct a learning curriculum. However, when the task is characterized by a non-Markovian reward (NMR), whose computation depends on multiple steps of states and actions, HER can no longer densify rewards by treating a single encountered state as the hindsight goal. The lack of informative rewards hinders policy learning, resulting in rolling out failed trajectories. Consequently, the replay buffer is overwhelmed with failed trajectories, impeding the establishment of an applicable curriculum. To circumvent these limitations, we deviate from existing HER-based methods and propose an on-policy GCRL framework, GCPO, which is applicable to both multi-goal Markovian reward (MR) and NMR problems.GCPO consists of (1) Pre-training from Demonstrations, which pre-trains the policy to possess an initial goal-achieving capability, thereby diminishing the difficulty of subsequent online learning. (2) Online Self-Curriculum Learning, which first estimates the policy's goal-achieving capability based on historical evaluation information and then selects progressively challenging goals for learning based on its current capability. We evaluate GCPO on a challenging multi-goal long-horizon task: fixed-wing UAV velocity vector control. Experimental results demonstrate that GCPO is capable of effectively addressing both multi-goal MR and NMR problems.

paragraphs: Goal-conditioned reinforcement learning trains a policy to pursue different goals. Hindsight Experience Replay helps by reinterpreting encountered states as goals that were achieved. This becomes problematic when rewards depend on several states and actions across time: a single encountered state cannot provide the required hindsight goal, leaving learning with too little useful feedback.

The proposed GCPO framework uses an on-policy approach with two components. It first pretrains the policy on demonstrations to establish an initial ability to achieve goals. During online learning, it estimates the policy's current capabilities from historical evaluations and selects progressively harder goals. This creates a curriculum tied to what the policy can currently accomplish.

The authors evaluate GCPO on fixed-wing UAV velocity vector control, a long-horizon task with multiple goals. Results show that it can address both Markovian rewards and rewards that depend on a longer history. The contribution connects an initial demonstration-based foundation with adaptive goal selection, addressing the curriculum difficulties that arise when hindsight replay accumulates unsuccessful trajectories.
summary.tldr: GCPO combines demonstration pretraining and an adaptive goal curriculum to learn tasks with both immediate-state and history-dependent rewards.

title: Goal-Conditioned On-Policy Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Uncertainty quantification, once a singular task, has evolved into a spectrum of tasks, including abstained prediction, out-of-distribution detection, and aleatoric uncertainty quantification. The latest goal is disentanglement: the construction of multiple estimators that are each tailored to one and only one source of uncertainty. This paper presents the first benchmark of uncertainty disentanglement. We reimplement and evaluate a comprehensive range of uncertainty estimators, from Bayesian over evidential to deterministic ones, across a diverse range of uncertainty tasks on ImageNet. We find that, despite recent theoretical endeavors, no existing approach provides pairs of disentangled uncertainty estimators in practice. We further find that specialized uncertainty tasks are harder than predictive uncertainty tasks, where we observe saturating performance. Our results provide both practical advice for which uncertainty estimators to use for which specific task, and reveal opportunities for future research toward task-centric and disentangled uncertainties. All our reimplementations and Weights & Biases logs are available at https://github.com/bmucsanyi/untangle.

paragraphs: A model's uncertainty can serve several purposes: deciding when to withhold a prediction, detecting unfamiliar inputs, or estimating ambiguity inherent in the data. Uncertainty disentanglement asks for something more specific than an overall confidence score. It seeks separate estimators, each responding to only one source of uncertainty.

This paper introduces a benchmark for testing whether existing methods achieve that separation in practice. The authors reimplement a broad selection of Bayesian, evidential, and deterministic uncertainty estimators and evaluate them across multiple uncertainty tasks on ImageNet. This shared evaluation makes it possible to compare both task performance and whether pairs of estimators actually isolate different uncertainty sources.

Among the approaches evaluated, none produces successfully disentangled estimator pairs in practice. Specialized uncertainty tasks also prove harder than general predictive uncertainty tasks, where performance appears to be leveling off. The findings support choosing estimators according to the particular task, while identifying a remaining gap between theoretical approaches to separating uncertainty and the behavior observed in this benchmark.
summary.tldr: An ImageNet benchmark finds that evaluated uncertainty methods do not successfully separate uncertainty sources in practice.

title: Benchmarking Uncertainty Disentanglement: Specialized Uncertainties for Specialized Tasks

abstract: Planning in real-world settings often entails addressing partial observability while aligning with users' requirements. We present a novel framework for expressing users' constraints and preferences about agent behavior in a partially observable setting using parameterized belief-state query (BSQ) policies in the setting of goal-oriented partially observable Markov decision processes (gPOMDPs). We present the first formal analysis of such constraints and prove that while the expected cost function of a parameterized BSQ policy w.r.t its parameters is not convex, it is piecewise constant and yields an implicit discrete parameter search space that is finite for finite horizons. This theoretical result leads to novel algorithms that optimize gPOMDP agent behavior with guaranteed user alignment. Analysis proves that our algorithms converge to the optimal user-aligned behavior in the limit. Empirical results show that parameterized BSQ policies provide a computationally feasible approach for user-aligned planning in partially observable settings.

paragraphs: An agent planning under partial observability must act without knowing the full state of its environment. It must also respect what a user wants or forbids. This paper introduces parameterized belief-state query policies as a way to express such preferences and constraints in goal-oriented partially observable Markov decision processes.

The key theoretical finding concerns how a policy's expected cost changes with its parameters. Although this objective is not convex, it is piecewise constant: different parameter values can produce the same cost over regions of the search space. For finite planning horizons, this structure induces a finite discrete search space, providing a basis for optimization despite the lack of convexity.

The authors use that structure to develop algorithms with guaranteed alignment to the expressed user requirements. They prove convergence to optimal user-aligned behavior in the limit, rather than claiming that every finite run reaches the optimum. Empirical results indicate that these policies are computationally feasible, connecting the formal analysis to practical planning under uncertainty.
summary.tldr: Belief-state query policies make user-constrained planning under partial observability optimizable, with alignment guarantees and convergence to optimal behavior in the limit.

title: Belief-State Query Policies for User-Aligned POMDPs

abstract: Despite satisfactory results on ``easy'' cases of single image reflection separation, prior dual-stream methods still suffer from considerable performance degradation when facing complex ones, i.e, the transmission layer is densely entangled with the reflection having a wide distribution of spatial intensity. The main reasons come from the lack of concern on the feature correlation during interaction, and the limited receptive field. To remedy these deficiencies, this paper presents a Dual-Stream Interactive Transformer (DSIT) design. Specifically, we devise a dual-attention interactive structure that embraces a dual-stream self-attention and a layer-aware dual-stream cross-attention mechanism to simultaneously capture intra-layer and inter-layer feature correlations. Meanwhile, the introduction of attention mechanisms can also mitigate the receptive field limitation. We modulate single-stream pre-trained Transformer embeddings with dual-stream convolutional features through cross-architecture interactions to provide richer semantic priors, thereby further relieving the ill-posedness of the problem. Extensive experimental results reveal the merits of the proposed DSIT over other state-of-the-art alternatives. Our code is publicly available at https://github.com/mingcv/DSIT.
