paragraphs: Separating a scene from its reflection in a single image becomes especially difficult when the two are densely mixed and reflection intensity varies widely across the image. The paper attributes weaknesses in earlier dual-stream methods to limited spatial context and insufficient modeling of relationships between the features exchanged by the streams.

The proposed Dual-Stream Interactive Transformer addresses relationships both within and between the two image layers. Dual-stream self-attention captures correlations inside each layer, while layer-aware cross-attention captures correlations across them. Attention also expands the spatial context available to the model, helping address the limited receptive field identified in earlier designs.

The method further combines pretrained Transformer embeddings with convolutional features from both streams through cross-architecture interactions. This supplies richer semantic information to help resolve an inherently ambiguous separation problem. Extensive experiments show advantages over the compared state-of-the-art alternatives. The contribution is a coordinated interaction design that uses layer relationships, wider context, and pretrained semantic features to improve reflection separation.
summary.tldr: DSIT improves single-image reflection separation by combining within-layer and cross-layer attention with pretrained semantic features.

title: Single Image Reflection Separation via Dual-Stream Interactive Transformers

abstract: We study Bandits with Knapsacks (Bwk) in a piecewise-stationary environment. We propose a novel inventory reserving algorithm which draws new insights into the problem. Suppose parameters $\eta_{\min}, \eta_{\max} \in (0,1]$ respectively lower and upper bound the reward earned and the resources consumed in a time round. Our algorithm achieves a provably near-optimal competitive ratio of $O(\log(\eta_{\max}/\eta_{\min}))$, with a matching lower bound provided. Our performance guarantee is based on a dynamic benchmark, distinguishing our work from existing works on adversarial Bwk who compare with the static benchmark. Furthermore, different from existing non-stationary Bwk work, we do not require a bounded global variation.

Suppose parameters $\eta_{\min}, \eta_{\max} \in (0,1]$ respectively lower and upper bound the reward earned and the resources consumed in a time round. Our algorithm achieves a provably near-optimal competitive ratio of $O(\log(\eta_{\max}/\eta_{\min}))$, with a matching lower bound provided. Our performance guarantee is based on a dynamic benchmark, distinguishing our work from existing works on adversarial Bwk who compare with the static benchmark. paragraphs: Bandits with Knapsacks studies sequential decisions that earn rewards while consuming limited resources. This paper considers a piecewise-stationary environment, where conditions can change between otherwise stable periods. Resource use is especially consequential in this setting because spending inventory now affects what remains available after conditions change.

The authors propose an inventory-reserving algorithm and analyze it against a dynamic benchmark. This comparison differs from the static benchmark used in existing adversarial Bandits with Knapsacks work: the reference used to assess performance can reflect changing conditions. The analysis assumes parameters η_min and η_max in (0,1] that bound per-round reward and resource consumption as specified in the problem.

Under those assumptions, the algorithm achieves a competitive ratio of O(log(η_max/η_min)), with a matching lower bound supporting near-optimality. The guarantee also avoids requiring bounded global variation, an assumption used in existing non-stationary work. The contribution is a resource-reservation strategy whose performance is theoretically characterized against a changing benchmark, without placing that global bound on how much the environment varies.
summary.tldr: An inventory-reserving bandit algorithm achieves a near-optimal logarithmic competitive ratio against a dynamic benchmark in piecewise-stationary environments.

title: Piecewise-Stationary Bandits with Knapsacks

abstract: We study a data pricing problem, where a seller has access to $N$ homogeneous data points (e.g. drawn i.i.d. from some distribution).There are $m$ types of buyers in the market, where buyers of the same type $i$ have the same valuation curve $v_i:[N]\rightarrow [0,1]$, where $v_i(n)$ is the value for having $n$ data points.*A priori*, the seller is unaware of thedistribution of buyers, but can repeat the market for $T$ rounds so as to learn the revenue-optimal pricing curve $p:[N] \rightarrow [0, 1]$.To solve this online learning problem,we first develop novel discretization schemes to approximate any pricing curve.When compared to prior work,the size of our discretization schemes scales gracefully with the approximation parameter, which translates to better regret in online learning.Under assumptions like smoothness and diminishing returns which are satisfied by data, the discretization size can be reduced further.We then turn to the online learning problem, both in the stochastic and adversarial settings.On each round, the seller chooses an *anonymous* pricing curve $p_t$.A new buyer appears and may choose to purchase some amount of data.She then reveals her type *only if* she makes a purchase.Our online algorithms build on classical algorithms such as UCB and FTPL, but require novel ideas to account for the asymmetric nature of this feedback and to deal with the vastness of the space of pricing curves.Using the improved discretization schemes previously developed, we are able to achieve $\widetilde{O}(m\sqrt{T})$ regret in the stochastic setting and $\widetilde{\mathcal{O}}(m^{3/2}\sqrt{T})$ regret in the adversarial setting.

paragraphs: The paper studies a seller who repeatedly offers quantities of homogeneous data to buyers. Buyers belong to different types, each with its own valuation for a given number of data points. The seller does not initially know the distribution of buyer types and must learn a revenue-maximizing pricing curve over repeated market rounds.

Two features make learning difficult. There is a vast space of possible pricing curves, and a buyer reveals their type only after making a purchase. The authors develop discretization schemes that approximate pricing curves using manageable collections of candidates. Under additional assumptions such as smoothness and diminishing returns, those collections can be reduced further.

The resulting online algorithms build on UCB and follow-the-perturbed-leader methods while accounting for the asymmetric feedback. With m buyer types over T rounds, they achieve regret scaling as m√T in the stochastic setting and m^(3/2)√T in the adversarial setting, up to logarithmic factors. These guarantees connect a better representation of the pricing choices to improved revenue-learning performance under both market models.
summary.tldr: Improved approximations of pricing curves enable stronger online revenue-learning guarantees when buyer types are revealed only after purchases.

title: Learning to Price Homogeneous Data

abstract: Neural ordinary differential equations (Neural ODEs) is a family of continuous-depth neural networks where the evolution of hidden states is governed by learnable temporal derivatives. We identify a significant limitation in applying traditional Batch Normalization (BN) to Neural ODEs, due to a fundamental mismatch --- BN was initially designed for discrete neural networks with no temporal dimension, whereas Neural ODEs operate continuously over time. To bridge this gap, we introduce temporal adaptive Batch Normalization (TA-BN), a novel technique that acts as the continuous-time analog to traditional BN. Our empirical findings reveal that TA-BN enables the stacking of more layers within Neural ODEs, enhancing their performance. Moreover, when confined to a model architecture consisting of a single Neural ODE followed by a linear layer, TA-BN achieves 91.1\% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 with 2.2 million parameters, making it the first \texttt{unmixed} Neural ODE architecture to approach MobileNetV2-level parameter efficiency. Extensive numerical experiments on image classification and physical system modeling substantiate the superiority of TA-BN compared to baseline methods.

paragraphs: Neural ordinary differential equations describe a network's hidden state as evolving continuously according to learned derivatives. Traditional batch normalization was designed for discrete networks without this temporal dimension. The paper identifies that mismatch as a significant obstacle to applying batch normalization effectively within Neural ODE models.

The authors introduce temporal adaptive batch normalization, or TA-BN, as a continuous-time counterpart to ordinary batch normalization. It brings the temporal dimension into the normalization approach. Their empirical findings show that TA-BN supports stacking more layers within Neural ODEs and improves performance, connecting the normalization change to the ability to build more capable models.

In an architecture containing a single Neural ODE followed by a linear layer, TA-BN reaches 91.1% test accuracy on CIFAR-10 using 2.2 million parameters. The authors describe this as the first unmixed Neural ODE architecture to approach MobileNetV2-level parameter efficiency. Experiments on image classification and physical-system modeling also show advantages over the evaluated baselines, providing evidence across both visual and dynamical modeling tasks.
summary.tldr: TA-BN adapts batch normalization to continuous-time Neural ODEs, enabling deeper models and improving reported accuracy and parameter efficiency.

title: Improving Neural ODE Training with Temporal Adaptive Batch Normalization

abstract: The discovery and identification of molecules in biological and environmental samples is crucial for advancing biomedical and chemical sciences. Tandem mass spectrometry (MS/MS) is the leading technique for high-throughput elucidation of molecular structures. However, decoding a molecular structure from its mass spectrum is exceptionally challenging, even when performed by human experts. As a result, the vast majority of acquired MS/MS spectra remain uninterpreted, thereby limiting our understanding of the underlying (bio)chemical processes. Despite decades of progress in machine learning applications for predicting molecular structures from MS/MS spectra, the development of new methods is severely hindered by the lack of standard datasets and evaluation protocols. To address this problem, we propose MassSpecGym -- the first comprehensive benchmark for the discovery and identification of molecules from MS/MS data. Our benchmark comprises the largest publicly available collection of high-quality MS/MS spectra and defines three MS/MS annotation challenges: \textit{de novo} molecular structure generation, molecule retrieval, and spectrum simulation. It includes new evaluation metrics and a generalization-demanding data split, therefore standardizing the MS/MS annotation tasks and rendering the problem accessible to the broad machine learning community. MassSpecGym is publicly available at \url{https://github.com/pluskal-lab/MassSpecGym}.

paragraphs: Tandem mass spectrometry provides high-throughput measurements used to investigate molecular structures, but interpreting a spectrum remains difficult even for experts. Most acquired spectra therefore remain uninterpreted. MassSpecGym addresses a development bottleneck for machine learning in this area: the lack of shared datasets and evaluation protocols for comparing methods.

The benchmark brings together what the authors describe as the largest publicly available collection of high-quality tandem mass spectra. It organizes evaluation around three tasks: generating molecular structures from scratch, retrieving molecules, and simulating spectra. These tasks provide distinct ways to study the relationship between molecular structures and their measured spectral information.

MassSpecGym also supplies new evaluation metrics and a data split designed to demand generalization. Together, the dataset, tasks, and evaluation rules establish a common framework for method development. Its contribution is research infrastructure for molecular discovery and identification, making these problems more accessible to the broader machine learning community and giving researchers a standardized basis for evaluating progress.
summary.tldr: MassSpecGym standardizes molecular structure generation, molecule retrieval, and spectrum simulation with shared mass-spectrometry data and evaluation protocols.

title: MassSpecGym: A benchmark for the discovery and identification of molecules

abstract: Today's best language models still struggle with "hallucinations", factually incorrect generations, which impede their ability to reliably retrieve information seen during training. The *reversal curse*, where models cannot recall information when probed in a different order than was encountered during training, exemplifies limitations in information retrieval. To better understand these limitations, we reframe the reversal curse as a *factorization curse* --- a failure of models to learn the same joint distribution under different factorizations.We more closely simulate finetuning workflows which train pretrained models on specialized knowledge by introducing*WikiReversal*, a realistic testbed based on Wikipedia knowledge graphs. Through a series of controlled experiments with increasing levels of realism, including non-reciprocal relations, we find that reliable information retrieval is an inherent failure of the next-token prediction objective used in popular large language models. Moreover, we demonstrate reliable information retrieval cannot be solved with scale, reversed tokens, or even naive bidirectional-attention training. Consequently, various approaches to finetuning on specialized data would necessarily provide mixed results on downstream tasks, unless the model has already seen the right sequence of tokens. Across five tasks of varying levels of complexity, our results uncover a promising path forward: factorization-agnostic objectives can significantly mitigate the reversal curse and hint at improved knowledge storage and planning capabilities.

paragraphs: A language model may encounter a fact during training yet fail to retrieve it when the question presents the relationship in a different order. This paper reframes that reversal problem as a factorization problem: learning one ordering of conditional predictions does not reliably teach the same joint information under another ordering.

The authors introduce WikiReversal, a testbed built from Wikipedia knowledge graphs that resembles fine-tuning pretrained models on specialized knowledge. Controlled experiments become progressively more realistic and include non-reciprocal relations. The findings identify next-token prediction as an inherent obstacle to reliable retrieval and show that scaling, reversed tokens, and naive bidirectional-attention training do not resolve the problem.

The paper argues that specialized fine-tuning can consequently yield mixed downstream results unless the model has already encountered the appropriate token sequence. Across five tasks, objectives that are agnostic to factorization significantly mitigate the reversal curse. Those results suggest a promising objective-level change, with potential benefits for knowledge storage and planning rather than an established complete solution to either.
summary.tldr: The paper links retrieval failures to prediction factorization and finds that factorization-agnostic objectives substantially mitigate the reversal curse.

title: The Factorization Curse: Which Tokens You Predict Underlie the Reversal Curse and More

abstract: In many reinforcement learning (RL) applications, incorporating heuristic rewards alongside the task reward is crucial for achieving desirable performance. Heuristics encode prior human knowledge about how a task should be done, providing valuable hints for RL algorithms. However, such hints may not be optimal, limiting the performance of learned policies. The currently established way of using heuristics is to modify the heuristic reward in a manner that ensures that the optimal policy learned with it remains the same as the optimal policy for the task reward (i.e., optimal policy invariance). However, these methods often fail in practical scenarios with limited training data. We found that while optimal policy invariance ensures convergence to the best policy based on task rewards, it doesn't guarantee better performance than policies trained with biased heuristics under a finite data regime, which is impractical. In this paper, we introduce a new principle tailored for finite data settings. Instead of enforcing optimal policy invariance, we train a policy that combines task and heuristic rewards and ensures it outperforms the heuristic-trained policy. As such, we prevent policies from merely exploiting heuristic rewards without improving the task reward. Our experiments on robotic locomotion, helicopter control, and manipulation tasks demonstrate that our method consistently outperforms the heuristic policy, regardless of the heuristic rewards' quality.Code is available at https://github.com/Improbable-AI/hepo.

paragraphs: Heuristic rewards give reinforcement-learning systems human guidance about how to perform a task, but that guidance can favor imperfect behavior. A common approach modifies those rewards to preserve the task’s optimal policy. This paper argues that preserving the eventual optimum does not ensure better performance when training data are limited.

The authors propose a principle centered on improvement over a policy trained using the heuristic. Their method trains with both task and heuristic rewards while imposing a constraint that the resulting policy outperform the heuristic-trained policy. This makes improvement in the actual task reward the relevant comparison and prevents success from consisting solely of exploiting heuristic rewards.

Experiments cover robotic locomotion, helicopter control, and manipulation. Across these evaluations, the method consistently improves on the heuristic policy despite variation in heuristic quality. The contribution is therefore directed at finite-data learning: it changes the objective from preserving an asymptotic optimum to enforcing improvement relative to the policy supplied by the available guidance.
summary.tldr: The method uses a policy-improvement constraint to turn heuristic guidance into better task performance in finite-data reinforcement learning.

title: Going Beyond Heuristics by Imposing Policy Improvement as a Constraint

abstract: With the rapid development of the big data era, Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) has been widely applied to enable data collaboration while ensuring privacy protection. However, the ultrahigh dimensionality of features and the sparse data structures inherent in large-scale datasets introduce significant computational complexity. In this paper, we propose the Vertical Federated Feature Screening (VFS) algorithm, which effectively reduces computational, communication, and encryption costs. VFS is a two-stage feature screening procedure that proceeds from coarse to fine: the first stage quickly filters out irrelevant feature groups, followed by a more refined screening of individual features. It significantly reduces the resource demands of downstream tasks such as secure joint modeling or federated feature selection. This efficiency is particularly beneficial in scenarios with ultrahigh feature dimensionality or severe class imbalance in the response variable. The statistical and computational properties of VFS are rigorously established. Numerical simulations and real-world applications demonstrate its superior performance.

paragraphs: Vertical federated learning enables collaborative analysis while protecting participating data. When datasets contain extremely many features and sparse structure, however, the associated computation can become expensive. This paper focuses on reducing the feature-processing burden before downstream secure modeling or federated feature selection takes place.

The proposed Vertical Federated Feature Screening algorithm works in two stages. It first performs a coarse screening that quickly removes irrelevant groups of features. It then examines individual features more finely. Group screening narrows the set that needs detailed attention, making the overall procedure a progression from broad elimination to more selective assessment.

The authors establish statistical and computational properties of the method and evaluate it through numerical simulations and real-world applications. They report reduced computation, communication, and encryption costs, alongside superior performance in those evaluations. The efficiency is particularly useful with ultrahigh feature dimensionality or severe response-class imbalance. The contribution is a screening procedure that reduces resource demands for later collaborative analysis, placing feature reduction before more costly downstream operations.
summary.tldr: VFS screens feature groups and then individual features to reduce computation, communication, and encryption costs in vertical federated analysis.

title: Vertical Federated Feature Screening

abstract: Multimodal Large Language Models (MLLMs) are increasingly deployed in fine-tuning-as-a-service (FTaaS) settings, where user-submitted datasets adapt general-purpose models to downstream tasks. This flexibility, however, introduces serious security risks, as malicious fine-tuning can implant backdoors into MLLMs with minimal effort. In this paper, we observe that backdoor triggers systematically disrupt cross-modal processing by causing abnormal attention concentration on non-semantic regions—a phenomenon we term **attention collapse**. Based on this insight, we propose **Believe Your Eyes (BYE)**, a data filtering framework that leverages attention entropy patterns as self-supervised signals to identify and filter backdoor samples. BYE operates via a three-stage pipeline: (1) extracting attention maps using the fine-tuned model, (2) computing entropy scores and profiling sensitive layers via bimodal separation, and (3) performing unsupervised clustering to remove suspicious samples. Unlike prior defenses, BYE equires no clean supervision, auxiliary labels, or model modifications. Extensive experiments across various datasets, models, and diverse trigger types validate BYE's effectiveness: it achieves near-zero attack success rates while maintaining clean-task performance, offering a robust and generalizable solution against backdoor threats in MLLMs.

paragraphs: Fine-tuning services let users adapt multimodal language models with their own datasets, but malicious training examples can implant backdoors. The paper identifies an observable sign of these attacks: triggers cause attention to concentrate abnormally on regions that do not carry meaningful content. The authors call this disruption of cross-modal processing attention collapse.

It first extracts attention maps from the fine-tuned model, then computes entropy scores describing attention patterns. These findings support attention patterns as a practical signal for cleaning backdoor-contaminated fine-tuning data in the tested settings. The contribution combines an explanation of a recurring attack behavior with a filtering procedure that does not require external guidance.
summary.tldr: BYE filters backdoor training samples using abnormal attention patterns, achieving near-zero attack success in the reported experiments without external supervision.

title: Backdoor Cleaning without External Guidance in MLLM Fine-tuning

abstract: Identifying and measuring biases associated with sensitive attributes is a crucial consideration in healthcare to prevent treatment disparities. One prominent issue is inaccurate pulse oximeter readings, which tend to overestimate oxygen saturation for dark-skinned patients and misrepresent supplemental oxygen needs. Most existing research has revealed *statistical disparities* linking device measurement errors to patient outcomes in intensive care units (ICUs) without causal formalization. This study *causally* investigates how racial discrepancies in oximetry measurements affect invasive ventilation in ICU settings. We employ a causal inference-based approach using *path-specific effects* to isolate the impact of bias by race on clinical decision-making. To estimate these effects, we leverage a doubly robust estimator, propose its self-normalized variant for improved sample efficiency, and provide novel finite-sample guarantees. Our methodology is validated on semi-synthetic data and applied to two large real-world health datasets: MIMIC-IV and eICU. Contrary to prior work, our analysis reveals minimal impact of racial discrepancies on invasive ventilation rates. However, path-specific effects mediated by oxygen saturation disparity are more pronounced on ventilation duration, and the severity differs by dataset. Our work provides a novel pipeline for investigating potential disparities in clinical decision-making and, more importantly, highlights the necessity of causal methods to robustly assess fairness in healthcare.

summary.tldr: A causal analysis finds minimal effects of racial oximetry discrepancies on ventilation rates, with more pronounced, dataset-dependent effects on duration.

title: Path-specific effects for pulse-oximetry guided decisions in critical care

abstract: In recent years, vision-based end-to-end autonomous driving has emerged as a new paradigm. However, popular end-to-end approaches typically rely on visual feature extraction networks trained under label supervision. This limited supervision framework restricts the generality and applicability of driving models. In this paper, we propose a novel paradigm termed $E^{3}AD$, which advocates for comparative learning between visual feature extraction networks and the general EEG large model, in order to learn latent human driving cognition for enhancing end-to-end planning. In this work, we collected a cognitive dataset for the mentioned contrastive learning process. Subsequently, we investigated the methods and potential mechanisms for enhancing end-to-end planning with human driving cognition, using popular driving models as baselines on publicly available autonomous driving datasets. Both open-loop and closed-loop tests are conducted for a comprehensive evaluation of planning performance. Experimental results demonstrate that the $E^{3}AD$ paradigm significantly enhances the end-to-end planning performance of baseline models. Ablation studies further validate the contribution of driving cognition and the effectiveness of comparative learning process. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first work to integrate human driving cognition for improving end-to-end autonomous driving planning. It represents an initial attempt to incorporate embodied cognitive data into end-to-end autonomous driving, providing valuable insights for future brain-inspired autonomous driving systems. Our code will be made available at https://github.com/AIR-DISCOVER/E-cubed-AD.

The reported results show significant planning improvements over the baseline models. Ablation studies support contributions from the cognitive information and the comparative learning process. The paper frames this as an initial attempt to incorporate embodied cognitive data into driving systems, with evidence for improving planning in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: E³AD uses contrastive learning with EEG-derived representations of human driving cognition to improve autonomous driving planning.

title: Embodied Cognition Augmented End2End Autonomous Driving

abstract: We address the problem of language-guided 3D affordance prediction, a core capability for embodied agents interacting with unstructured environments. Existing methods often rely on fixed affordance categories or require external expert prompts, limiting their ability to generalize across different objects and interpret multi-step instructions. In this work, we introduce $\textit{ViSPLA}$, a novel iterative self-prompting framework that leverages the intrinsic geometry of predicted masks for continual refinement. We redefine affordance detection as a language-conditioned segmentation task: given a 3D point cloud and language instruction, our model predicts a sequence of refined affordance masks, each guided by differential geometric feedback including Laplacians, normal derivatives, and curvature fields. This feedback is encoded into visual prompts that drive a multi-stage refinement decoder, enabling the model to self-correct and adapt to complex spatial structures. To further enhance precision and coherence, we introduce Implicit Neural Affordance Fields, which define continuous probabilistic regions over the 3D surface without additional supervision. Additionally, our Spectral Convolutional Self-Prompting module operates in the frequency domain of the point cloud, enabling multi-scale refinement that captures both coarse and fine affordance structures. Extensive experiments demonstrate that $\textit{ViSPLA}$ achieves state-of-the-art results on both seen and unseen objects on two benchmark datasets. Our framework establishes a new paradigm for open-world 3D affordance reasoning by unifying language comprehension with low-level geometric perception through iterative refinement.

paragraphs: ViSPLA predicts which parts of a three-dimensional object are relevant to a language instruction. It treats this affordance problem as language-conditioned segmentation: given a point cloud and an instruction, the model produces masks over the object's surface. This formulation addresses limitations associated with fixed affordance categories and reliance on external expert prompts.

Signals including Laplacians, normal derivatives, and curvature become visual prompts for a multistage decoder. This feedback lets earlier predictions guide subsequent correction. Implicit Neural Affordance Fields add continuous probabilistic regions over the surface without requiring additional supervision, aiming to improve precision and coherence.

A spectral self-prompting module also operates in the point cloud's frequency domain to refine structures at coarse and fine scales. Experiments report state-of-the-art results on two benchmarks for both seen and unseen objects. Together, the components connect language interpretation with local geometry through iterative refinement, providing an evaluated approach to identifying instruction-relevant regions across varied object structures.
summary.tldr: ViSPLA uses geometric feedback from its own predictions to iteratively refine language-guided affordance regions on 3D objects.

title: ViSPLA: Visual Iterative Self-Prompting for Language-Guided 3D Affordance Learning

abstract: Large Language Models (LLMs) have demonstrated impressive performance across various tasks, yet they remain vulnerable to generating toxic content, necessitating detoxification strategies to ensure safe and responsible deployment. Test-time detoxification methods, which typically introduce static or dynamic interventions into LLM representations, offer a promising solution due to their flexibility and minimal invasiveness. However, current approaches often suffer from imprecise interventions, primarily due to their insufficient exploration of the transition space between toxic and non-toxic outputs. To address this challenge, we propose \textsc{A}utoregressive \textsc{R}eward \textsc{G}uided \textsc{R}epresentation \textsc{E}diting (ARGRE), a novel test-time detoxification framework that explicitly models toxicity transitions within the latent representation space, enabling stable and precise reward-guided editing. ARGRE identifies non-toxic semantic directions and interpolates between toxic and non-toxic representations to reveal fine-grained transition trajectories. These trajectories transform sparse toxicity annotations into dense training signals, enabling the construction of an autoregressive reward model that delivers stable and precise editing guidance. At inference, the reward model guides an adaptive two-step editing process to obtain detoxified representations: it first performs directional steering based on expected reward gaps to shift representations toward non-toxic regions, followed by lightweight gradient-based refinements. Extensive experiments across 8 widely used LLMs show that ARGRE significantly outperforms leading baselines in effectiveness (-62.21\% toxicity) and efficiency (-47.58\% inference time), while preserving the core capabilities of the original model with minimal degradation. Our code is available at the \href{https://anonymous.4open.science/r/ARGRE-6291}{anonymous website}.

paragraphs: Editing a language model's internal representations during generation can reduce toxic outputs, but choosing an effective intervention requires knowing how those representations relate to toxicity. The paper argues that existing approaches insufficiently explore the transitions between toxic and non-toxic outputs. ARGRE learns from those transitions to provide more precise guidance for test-time editing.

The framework first identifies semantic directions associated with non-toxic outputs and interpolates between toxic and non-toxic representations. These intermediate trajectories turn sparse toxicity annotations into denser training signals for an autoregressive reward model. During inference, editing proceeds in two stages: expected reward differences guide an initial directional shift, followed by lightweight gradient-based refinement.

Experiments across eight language models report a 62.21% reduction in toxicity and a 47.58% reduction in inference time relative to leading baselines, with minimal degradation of the models' core capabilities. The findings suggest that modeling the transition between output behaviors can improve both the effectiveness and efficiency of representation editing, rather than relying only on a coarse direction of intervention.
summary.tldr: ARGRE learns toxicity transitions in internal representations to guide faster, more effective test-time detoxification across eight evaluated language models.

title: Detoxifying Large Language Models via Autoregressive Reward Guided Representation Editing

abstract: Deep State Space Models (SSMs) reignite physics-grounded compute paradigms, as RNNs could natively be embodied into dynamical systems. This calls for dedicated learning algorithms obeying to core physical principles, with efficient techniques to simulate these systems and guide their design. We propose \emph{Recurrent Hamiltonian Echo Learning} (RHEL), an algorithm which provably computes loss gradients as finite differences of physical trajectories of non-dissipative, \emph{Hamiltonian systems}. In ML terms, RHEL only requires three ``forward passes'' irrespective of model size, without explicit Jacobian computation, nor incurring any variance in the gradient estimation. Motivated by the potential to implement our algorithm in non-digital physical systems, we first introduce RHEL in \emph{continuous time} and demonstrate its formal equivalence with the continuous adjoint state method. To facilitate the simulation of Hamiltonian systems trained by RHEL, we propose a \emph{discrete-time} version of RHEL which is equivalent to Backpropagation Through Time (BPTT) when applied to a class of recurrent modules which we call \emph{Hamiltonian Recurrent Units} (HRUs). This setting allows us to demonstrate the scalability of RHEL by generalizing these results to hierarchies of HRUs, which we call \emph{Hamiltonian SSMs} (HSSMs). We apply RHEL to train HSSMs with linear and nonlinear dynamics on a variety of time-series tasks ranging from mid-range to long-range classification and regression with sequence length reaching $\sim 50k$. We show that RHEL consistently matches the performance of BPTT across all models and tasks. This work opens new doors for the design of scalable, energy-efficient physical systems endowed with self-learning capabilities for sequence modelling.

paragraphs: Recurrent models can be viewed as dynamical systems, raising the possibility of learning directly through physical dynamics. RHEL consistently matches backpropagation-through-time performance across the tested models and tasks. The results establish a learning route compatible with these Hamiltonian dynamics; energy-efficient, self-learning physical implementations remain a possibility opened by the work.
summary.tldr: RHEL obtains gradients through Hamiltonian trajectories and matches backpropagation performance in the reported long-sequence experiments.

title: Learning long range dependencies through time reversal symmetry breaking

abstract: We study the problem of infrequent exploration in linear bandits, addressing a significant yet overlooked gap between fully adaptive exploratory methods (e.g., UCB and Thompson Sampling), which explore potentially at every time step, and purely greedy approaches, which require stringent diversity assumptions to succeed. Continuous exploration can be impractical or unethical in safety-critical or costly domains, while purely greedy strategies typically fail without adequate contextual diversity. To bridge these extremes, we introduce a simple and practical framework, INFEX, explicitly designed for infrequent exploration. INFEX executes a base exploratory policy according to a given schedule while predominantly choosing greedy actions in between. Despite its simplicity, our theoretical analysis demonstrates that INFEX achieves instance-dependent regret matching standard provably efficient algorithms, provided the exploration frequency exceeds a logarithmic threshold. Additionally, INFEX is a general, modular framework that allows seamless integration of any fully adaptive exploration method, enabling wide applicability and ease of adoption. By restricting intensive exploratory computations to infrequent intervals, our approach can also enhance computational efficiency. Empirical evaluations confirm our theoretical findings, showing state-of-the-art regret performance and runtime improvements over existing methods.

paragraphs: INFEX studies decision-making when exploration is useful but too costly or impractical to perform continually. In linear bandits, an algorithm must choose actions while learning their rewards. Fully adaptive methods may explore at every step, whereas purely greedy choices can fail without strong contextual diversity. The paper investigates a middle ground with explicitly scheduled exploration.

The framework runs a chosen exploratory policy at selected times and predominantly takes greedy actions between them. It is modular, allowing an existing fully adaptive exploration method to serve as the underlying policy. This separates the choice of exploration strategy from the decision about how frequently to invoke it, making the schedule a central part of the method.

The theoretical guarantee is conditional: when exploration frequency exceeds a logarithmic threshold, INFEX matches the instance-dependent regret of standard provably efficient algorithms. Restricting expensive exploration computations to selected intervals can also improve efficiency. Experiments support the analysis and report state-of-the-art regret performance with runtime improvements. The result supports infrequent exploration under the stated frequency condition, rather than arbitrarily rare exploration.
summary.tldr: INFEX combines scheduled exploration with mostly greedy actions, matching strong regret guarantees when exploration exceeds a logarithmic threshold.

title: Infrequent Exploration in Linear Bandits

abstract: Accurate polyp sizing during endoscopy is crucial for cancer risk assessment but is hindered by subjective methods and inadequate datasets lacking integrated 2D appearance, 3D structure, and real-world size information. We introduce PolypSense3D, the first multi-source benchmark dataset specifically targeting depth-aware polyp size measurement. It uniquely integrates over 43,000 frames from virtual simulations, physical phantoms, and clinical sequences, providing synchronized RGB, dense/sparse depth, segmentation masks, camera parameters, and millimeter-scale size labels derived via a novel forceps-assisted in-vivo annotation technique. To establish its value, we benchmark state-of-the-art segmentation and depth estimation models. Results quantify significant domain gaps between simulated/phantom and clinical data and reveal substantial error propagation from perception stages to final size estimation, with the best fully automated pipelines achieving an average Mean Absolute Error (MAE) of 0.95 mm on the clinical data subset. Publicly released under CC BY-SA 4.0 with code and evaluation protocols, PolypSense3D offers a standardized platform to accelerate research in robust, clinically relevant quantitative endoscopic vision. The benchmark dataset and code are available at: https://github.com/HNUicda/PolypSense3D and https://doi.org/10.7910/DVN/K13H89.

paragraphs: PolypSense3D provides a benchmark for measuring polyp size from endoscopic images using depth information. The paper identifies a dataset gap: appearance, three-dimensional structure, and real physical size have not been adequately integrated. Bringing these measurements together supports evaluation of the full path from visual perception to size estimation.

The dataset contains more than 43,000 frames from virtual simulations, physical phantoms, and clinical sequences. It combines RGB images, dense or sparse depth, segmentation masks, camera parameters, and size labels in millimeters. A forceps-assisted annotation technique supplies in-vivo size information. These sources enable comparisons across controlled settings and clinical imagery.

Benchmarking segmentation and depth-estimation models reveals substantial differences between simulated or phantom data and clinical data. It also shows how perception errors propagate into final size estimates. The best fully automated pipelines achieve an average mean absolute error of 0.95 mm on the clinical subset. Released with code and evaluation protocols, the dataset provides a shared basis for studying these connected sources of measurement error.
summary.tldr: PolypSense3D links endoscopic appearance, depth, and physical size to benchmark polyp measurement and expose domain gaps and error propagation.

title: PolypSense3D: A Multi-Source Benchmark Dataset for Depth-Aware Polyp Size Measurement in Endoscopy

abstract: Masked diffusion models have demonstrated competitive results on various tasks including language generation. However, due to its iterative refinement process, the inference is often bottlenecked by slow and static sampling speed. To overcome this problem, we introduce `KL-Adaptive Stability Sampling' (KLASS), a fast yet effective sampling method that exploits token-level KL divergence to identify stable, high-confidence predictions. By unmasking multiple tokens in each iteration without any additional model training, our approach speeds up generation significantly while maintaining sample quality. On reasoning benchmarks, KLASS achieves up to $2.78\times$ wall-clock speedups while improving performance over standard greedy decoding, attaining state-of-the-art results among diffusion-based samplers. We further validate KLASS across diverse domains, including text, image, and molecular generation, showing its effectiveness as a broadly applicable sampler across different models.

paragraphs: Masked diffusion models produce outputs through iterative refinement, which can make generation slow when sampling follows a static schedule. KLASS changes the sampling procedure to recognize predictions that are already stable and confident. Its aim is to spend fewer iterations completing an output while retaining sample quality.

The method uses token-level KL divergence to identify those stable predictions and unmasks multiple tokens within an iteration. Because this adjustment happens during sampling, it requires no additional model training. The central idea is to let evidence about prediction stability determine which tokens can be resolved together, accelerating the existing model’s generation process.

On reasoning benchmarks, the authors report wall-clock speedups of up to 2.78 times while improving performance relative to standard greedy decoding. They also report state-of-the-art results among diffusion-based samplers. Additional evaluations cover text, image, and molecular generation, supporting applicability across the tested domains and models. The speed figure is a reported maximum, while the broader contribution is a training-free adaptive sampler.
summary.tldr: KLASS accelerates masked diffusion sampling by unmasking multiple stable tokens at once, with reported speedups of up to 2.78 times.

title: KLASS: KL-Guided Fast Inference in Masked Diffusion Models

abstract: The primate visual system is typically divided into two streams — the ventral stream, responsible for object recognition, and the dorsal stream, responsible for encoding spatial relations and motion. Recent studies have shown that convolutional neural networks (CNNs) pretrained on object recognition tasks are remarkably effective at predicting neuronal responses in the ventral stream, shedding light on the neural mechanisms underlying object recognition. However, similar models of the dorsal stream remain underdeveloped due to the lack of large scale datasets encompassing dorsal stream areas. To address this gap, we present STSBench, a dataset of large-scale, single neuron recordings from over 2,000 neurons in the superior temporal sulcus (STS), a nearly 50-fold increase over existing dorsal stream datasets, collected while Rhesus macaques viewed thousands of unique, natural videos. We show that our dataset can be used for benchmarking encoding models of dorsal stream neuronal responses and reconstructing visual input from neural activity.

paragraphs: Models trained for object recognition have helped explain neuronal activity in the primate visual system's ventral stream. Comparable modeling of the dorsal stream, associated with spatial relationships and motion, has been held back by limited datasets. STSBench addresses that gap by providing substantially more neural recordings during natural video viewing.

The dataset contains single-neuron recordings from more than 2,000 neurons in the superior temporal sulcus of rhesus macaques watching thousands of distinct natural videos. The authors describe its scale as nearly fifty times that of existing dorsal-stream datasets. This pairs varied visual input with measured neuronal responses, providing material for studying how the recorded areas represent visual information.

The paper demonstrates two uses: benchmarking models that predict neuronal responses and reconstructing visual input from neural activity. These directions examine the relationship between videos and responses from opposite sides. STSBench's contribution is therefore both a larger empirical resource and a basis for evaluating models of a visual-processing stream whose computational characterization remains less developed.
summary.tldr: STSBench provides large-scale primate neural recordings during natural video viewing for response prediction and visual reconstruction.

title: STSBench: A Large-Scale Dataset for Modeling Neuronal Activity in the Dorsal Stream of Primate Visual Cortex

abstract: We propose and study Hierarchical Ego Graph Neural Networks (HE-GNNs), an expressive extension of graph neural networks (GNNs) with hierarchical node individualization, inspired by the Individualization-Refinement paradigm for isomorphism testing. HE-GNNs generalize subgraph-GNNs and form a hierarchy of increasingly expressive models that, in the limit, distinguish graphs up to isomorphism. We show that, over graphs of bounded degree, the separating power of HE-GNN node classifiers equals that of graded hybrid logic. This characterization enables us to relate the separating power of HE-GNNs to that of higher-order GNNs, GNNs enriched with local homomorphism count features, and color refinement algorithms based on Individualization-Refinement. Our experimental results confirm the practical feasibility of HE-GNNs and show benefits in comparison with traditional GNN architectures, both with and without local homomorphism count features.

paragraphs: Graph neural networks differ in their ability to distinguish graph structures. This paper introduces Hierarchical Ego Graph Neural Networks, which use hierarchical node individualization inspired by methods for testing graph isomorphism. The architecture extends subgraph-based networks into a family with progressively greater distinguishing power.

In the limit, the hierarchy can distinguish graphs up to isomorphism: structures that differ only in node naming remain equivalent. The authors also give a precise logical characterization for node classification on graphs of bounded degree. In that setting, the architecture's separating power matches graded hybrid logic, providing a formal language for describing which distinctions it can express.

This characterization supports comparisons with higher-order graph networks, networks augmented with local homomorphism counts, and refinement algorithms based on individualization. Experiments establish practical feasibility and report benefits over traditional graph architectures, both with and without those count features. The paper thus connects an architectural hierarchy to formal expressiveness results while also showing that the proposed models can be used in practice.
summary.tldr: HE-GNNs form an increasingly expressive graph-network hierarchy with a logical characterization on bounded-degree graphs and demonstrated practical benefits.

title: Logical Expressiveness of Graph Neural Networks with Hierarchical Node Individualization

abstract: Recent advances in language modeling have demonstrated the effectiveness of State Space Models (SSMs) for efficient sequence modeling. While hybrid architectures such as Samba and the decoder-decoder architecture, YOCO, have shown promising performance gains over Transformers, prior works have not investigated the efficiency potential of representation sharing between SSM layers. In this paper, we introduce the Gated Memory Unit (GMU), a simple yet effective mechanism for efficient memory sharing across layers. We apply it to create SambaY, a decoder-hybrid-decoder architecture that incorporates GMUs in the cross-decoder to share memory readout states from a Samba-based self-decoder. SambaY significantly enhances decoding efficiency, preserves linear pre-filling time complexity, and boosts long-context performance, all while eliminating the need for explicit positional encoding. Through extensive scaling experiments, we demonstrate that our model exhibits a significantly lower irreducible loss compared to a strong YOCO baseline, indicating superior performance scalability under large-scale compute regimes. Our largest model enhanced with Differential Attention, Phi4-mini-Flash-Reasoning, achieves significantly better performance than Phi4-mini-Reasoning on reasoning tasks such as Math500, AIME24/25, and GPQA Diamond without any reinforcement learning, while delivering up to 10× higher decoding throughput on 2K-length prompts with 32K generation length under the vLLM inference framework. We release our training codebase on open-source data at https://github.com/microsoft/ArchScale.

paragraphs: Generating long reasoning outputs places substantial demands on a language model's decoding process. This paper investigates whether layers in a state space model can share representations to reduce that cost. Its central component is the Gated Memory Unit, a mechanism for sharing memory across layers.

The resulting SambaY architecture uses a Samba-based self-decoder and a cross-decoder that shares memory readout states through these units. The authors report improved decoding efficiency and long-context performance, while prompt processing retains linear time complexity and requires no explicit positional encoding. The largest version adds Differential Attention and is called Phi4-mini-Flash-Reasoning. Without reinforcement learning, it outperforms Phi4-mini-Reasoning on Math500, AIME24/25, and GPQA Diamond. Under vLLM, it delivers up to ten times the decoding throughput for 2K-token prompts followed by 32K-token generations. That speed figure describes this particular generation setup, illustrating the architecture's potential for long outputs.
summary.tldr: SambaY shares state space memory across layers to improve long-generation efficiency, with its largest model showing stronger reasoning and setup-specific throughput gains.

title: Decoder-Hybrid-Decoder Architecture for Efficient Reasoning with Long Generation

abstract: Deep Neural Networks (DNNs) have demonstrated remarkable performance across various domains, including computer vision and natural language processing. However, they often struggle to accurately quantify their predictions' uncertainty, limiting their broader adoption in critical industrial applications. Uncertainty Quantification (UQ) for Deep Learning seeks to address this challenge by providing methodologies to improve the reliability of uncertainty estimates. While numerous techniques have been proposed, a unified tool remains lacking that offers a seamless workflow for evaluating and integrating these methods. To bridge this gap, we introduce **Torch-Uncertainty**, a *PyTorch* and *Lightning* framework designed to streamline the training and evaluation of DNNs with UQ techniques. In this paper, we outline the foundational principles of our library and present comprehensive experimental results that benchmark a diverse set of UQ methods across classification, segmentation, and regression tasks. Our library is available at: https://github.com/ENSTA-U2IS-AI/torch-uncertainty.

paragraphs: Torch-Uncertainty addresses the practical problem of assessing how uncertain a neural network is about its predictions. High predictive performance does not by itself ensure reliable uncertainty estimates. The paper frames this gap as an obstacle to wider use in critical industrial applications, where the reliability of a prediction matters alongside its value.

The contribution is a framework built on PyTorch and Lightning that streamlines training and evaluation with uncertainty-quantification methods. Rather than presenting a single uncertainty estimator, it provides a unified workflow for integrating and examining a diverse set of techniques. This makes the experimental process around uncertainty a central part of the software's purpose.

The paper explains the library's foundational principles and presents extensive benchmark experiments across classification, segmentation, and regression. Covering these task types allows the framework to address uncertainty in several forms of neural prediction. The stated contribution is the shared tooling and comparative experimental coverage; the abstract does not identify one method as universally best. The library is also made publicly available.
summary.tldr: Torch-Uncertainty provides a unified PyTorch and Lightning workflow for training and benchmarking neural-network uncertainty methods.

title: Torch-Uncertainty: Deep Learning Uncertainty Quantification

abstract: We present in this paper a novel post-training quantization (PTQ) method, dubbed AccuQuant, for diffusion models. We show analytically and empirically that quantization errors for diffusion models are accumulated over denoising steps in a sampling process. To alleviate the error accumulation problem, AccuQuant minimizes the discrepancies between outputs of a full-precision diffusion model and its quantized version within a couple of denoising steps. That is, it simulates multiple denoising steps of a diffusion sampling process explicitly for quantization, accounting the accumulated errors over multiple denoising steps, which is in contrast to previous approaches to imitating a training process of diffusion models, namely, minimizing the discrepancies independently for each step. We also present an efficient implementation technique for AccuQuant, together with a novel objective, which reduces a memory complexity significantly from $\mathcal{O}(n)$ to $\mathcal{O}(1)$, where $n$ is the number of denoising steps. We demonstrate the efficacy and efficiency of AccuQuant across various tasks and diffusion models on standard benchmarks.

paragraphs: AccuQuant addresses a problem that arises when diffusion models are converted to lower numerical precision after training. These models generate samples through repeated denoising, so an error introduced at one step can influence later steps. The paper supports this accumulation effect with both analysis and experiments, making the full sampling process central to its quantization approach.

The method calibrates the quantized model by explicitly simulating several connected denoising steps and comparing its outputs with those of the full-precision model. This lets calibration account for errors carried forward through sampling. Previous approaches described in the abstract compare steps independently, which does not directly capture how their errors combine over time.

The paper also introduces an implementation technique and objective that reduce memory complexity from linear to constant in the number of denoising steps. Evaluations across multiple tasks and diffusion models support its effectiveness and efficiency. The contribution is therefore both a better match between quantization and actual generation, and a way to make that calibration computationally practical.
summary.tldr: AccuQuant calibrates quantized diffusion models across connected denoising steps to address accumulating errors with constant memory complexity.

title: AccuQuant: Simulating Multiple Denoising Steps for Quantizing Diffusion Models

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) is a critical component of large language model (LLM) post-training. However, on-policy algorithms used for post-training are not naturally robust to a diversified content of experience replay buffers, which asynchronous off-policy actors can efficiently populate in parallel to training. We propose efficiently learning on such off-policy data via Trajectory Balance with Asynchrony (TBA), an approach to asynchronous RL for LLMs that leverages the principled off-policy TB objective. On math, preference-tuning, and automated red-teaming tasks, we post-train models ranging from Pythia 410M to Qwen 2.5 7B, finding TBA offers speed and performance boosts over strong baselines like Online DPO and Dr. GRPO. Beyond TBA's performance benefits (high accuracy even as asynchrony grows) and speedups ($4\times$ or more), we show its reward- and recency-prioritizing sampling enable further gains as data generation is scaled. Our code is available at https://github.com/bbartoldson/TBA.

We propose efficiently learning on such off-policy data via Trajectory Balance with Asynchrony (TBA), an approach to asynchronous RL for LLMs that leverages the principled off-policy TB objective. On math, preference-tuning, and automated red-teaming tasks, we post-train models ranging from Pythia 410M to Qwen 2.5 7B, finding TBA offers speed and performance boosts over strong baselines like Online DPO and Dr. GRPO. Beyond TBA's performance benefits (high accuracy even as asynchrony grows) and speedups ($4\times$ or more), we show its reward- and recency-prioritizing sampling enable further gains as data generation is scaled. paragraphs: Language-model reinforcement learning can generate experience in parallel with training, but that experience may come from policies that differ from the current learner. Standard on-policy methods are not naturally robust to the resulting diversity in replay buffers. This makes efficient asynchronous data generation difficult to exploit fully.

Trajectory Balance with Asynchrony, or TBA, uses an off-policy trajectory-balance objective to learn from such data. It decouples exploration from learning so that actors can keep supplying experience while training proceeds. Sampling that prioritizes reward and recency provides another way to select useful experience as the amount of generated data grows.

The authors evaluate math, preference-tuning, and automated red-teaming tasks with models ranging from Pythia 410M to Qwen 2.5 7B. They report speed and performance gains over Online DPO and Dr. GRPO, including speedups of four times or more and high accuracy as asynchrony increases. Reward- and recency-based sampling brings further gains when data generation scales, supporting the value of coordinating off-policy learning with asynchronous experience collection.
summary.tldr: TBA uses off-policy trajectory balance to learn efficiently from asynchronously generated experience, reporting speedups of four times or more.

title: Trajectory Balance with Asynchrony: Decoupling Exploration and Learning for Fast, Scalable LLM Post-Training

abstract: We study a fundamental question of domain generalization: given a family of domains (i.e., data distributions), how many randomly sampled domains do we need to collect data from in order to learn a model that performs reasonably well on every seen and unseen domain in the family? We model this problem in the PAC framework and introduce a new combinatorial measure, which we call the domain shattering dimension. We show that this dimension characterizes the domain sample complexity. Furthermore, we establish a tight quantitative relationship between the domain shattering dimension and the classic VC dimension, demonstrating that every hypothesis class that is learnable in the standard PAC setting is also learnable in our setting.

paragraphs: Domain generalization asks whether training across several data distributions can produce a model that works on distributions it has not seen. This paper focuses on the number of domains needed, rather than only the amount of data. Its target is reasonable performance on every domain in a specified family, including those absent from training.

The authors formalize this question in the probably approximately correct, or PAC, framework, with training domains sampled randomly. They introduce the domain shattering dimension, a combinatorial measure that characterizes domain sample complexity. This gives the question a mathematical answer tied to a measure of complexity, rather than a fixed number of domains that would apply to every learning problem.

The paper also establishes a tight quantitative relationship with the classical VC dimension. Through that connection, it shows that every hypothesis class learnable in the standard PAC setting is learnable in this domain-generalization setting. The conclusion concerns the stated family of distributions and sampling formulation, giving a theoretical learnability result within that framework.
summary.tldr: The domain shattering dimension tightly characterizes how many randomly sampled domains suffice for learning across a specified domain family.

title: How Many Domains Suffice for Domain Generalization? A Tight Characterization via the Domain Shattering Dimension

abstract: We present STARFlow, a scalable generative model based on normalizing flows that achieves strong performance on high-resolution image synthesis. STARFlow's main building block is Transformer Autoregressive Flow (TARFlow), which combines normalizing flows with Autoregressive Transformer architectures and has recently achieved impressive results in image modeling. In this work, we first establish the theoretical universality of TARFlow for modeling continuous distributions. Building on this foundation, we introduce a set of architectural and algorithmic innovations that significantly enhance the scalability: (1) a deep-shallow design where a deep Transformer block captures most of the model’s capacity, followed by a few shallow Transformer blocks that are computationally cheap yet contribute non-negligibly, (2) learning in the latent space of pretrained autoencoders, which proves far more effective than modeling pixels directly, and (3) a novel guidance algorithm that substantially improves sample quality. Crucially, our model remains a single, end-to-end normalizing flow, allowing exact maximum likelihood training in continuous space without discretization. STARFlow achieves competitive results in both class- and text-conditional image generation, with sample quality approaching that of state-of-the-art diffusion models. To our knowledge, this is the **first** successful demonstration of normalizing flows at this scale and resolution. Code and weights available at https://github.com/apple/ml-starflow.

paragraphs: STARFlow develops normalizing flows for high-resolution image generation using Transformer Autoregressive Flow, or TARFlow, as its building block. The authors first establish TARFlow’s theoretical universality for modeling continuous distributions. They then address the architectural and computational choices needed to scale that foundation into a competitive image generator.

The model places most capacity in a deep Transformer block and follows it with a few cheaper, shallow blocks that still contribute meaningfully. It learns in the latent space of pretrained autoencoders, which the authors find substantially more effective than direct pixel modeling. A new guidance algorithm further improves sample quality.

Despite these changes, STARFlow remains a single end-to-end normalizing flow, retaining exact maximum-likelihood training in continuous space without discretization. It achieves competitive class-conditional and text-conditional image generation, with sample quality approaching leading diffusion models. The authors characterize it as the first successful normalizing-flow demonstration at this scale and resolution, to their knowledge, connecting practical scalability with the model family’s likelihood-training framework.
summary.tldr: STARFlow scales latent normalizing flows to high-resolution image synthesis while preserving exact continuous-space maximum-likelihood training.

title: STARFlow: Scaling Latent Normalizing Flows for High-resolution Image Synthesis

abstract: Vertical Federated Learning (VFL) enables participants to collaboratively train models on aligned samples while keeping their heterogeneous features private and distributed. Despite their utility, VFL models remain vulnerable to adversarial attacks during inference. Adversarial Training (AT), which generates adversarial examples at each training iteration, stands as the most effective defense for improving model robustness. However, applying AT in VFL settings (VFAL) faces significant computational efficiency challenges, as the distributed training framework necessitates iterative propagations across participants. To this end, we propose **_DecVFAL_** framework, which substantially accelerates **_VFAL_** training through a dual-level ***Dec***oupling mechanism applied during adversarial sample generation. Specifically, we first decouple the bottom modules of clients (directly responsible for adversarial updates) from the remaining networks, enabling efficient _lazy sequential propagations_ that reduce communication frequency through delayed gradients. We further introduce _decoupled parallel backpropagation_ to accelerate delayed gradient computation by eliminating idle waiting through parallel processing across modules. Additionally, we are the first to establish convergence analysis for VFAL, rigorously characterizing how our decoupling mechanism interacts with existing VFL dynamics, and prove that _DecVFAL_ achieves an $\mathcal{O}(1/\sqrt{K})$ convergence rate matching that of standard VFLs. Experimental results show that _DecVFAL_ ensures competitive robustness while significantly achieving about $3\sim10\times$ speed up.

paragraphs: Vertical federated learning lets participants train together on aligned examples while retaining different features locally. Making these models robust through adversarial training is expensive because generating adversarial examples requires repeated computations across participants. The resulting communication and waiting add substantial overhead to an already distributed training process.

DecVFAL reduces this overhead by separating dependencies at two levels during adversarial example generation. It first separates the clients' bottom modules, which directly handle adversarial updates, from the remaining network. Delayed gradients then allow less frequent communication. A second mechanism computes delayed gradients through parallel backpropagation across modules, reducing time spent waiting for other modules to finish.

The paper also analyzes how these changes interact with vertical federated learning dynamics. It proves a convergence rate of order one over the square root of K, matching the stated rate for standard vertical federated learning. Experiments report approximately threefold to tenfold speedups while retaining competitive robustness. The contribution therefore combines a faster distributed training procedure with theoretical analysis of its convergence.
summary.tldr: DecVFAL reduces communication and waiting during federated adversarial training, reporting roughly 3–10× speedups with competitive robustness.

title: Accelerated Vertical Federated Adversarial Learning through Decoupling Layer-Wise Dependencies

abstract: We consider matroid allocation problems under \textit{opportunity fairness} constraints: resources need to be allocated to a set of agents under matroid constraints (which includes classical problems such as bipartite matching). Agents are divided into $C$ groups according to a sensitive attribute, and an allocation is opportunity-fair if each group receives the same share proportional to the maximum feasible allocation it could achieve in isolation. We study the Price of Fairness (PoF), i.e., the ratio between maximum size allocations and maximum size opportunity-fair allocations. We first provide a characterization of the PoF leveraging the underlying polymatroid structure of the allocation problem. Based on this characterization, we prove bounds on the PoF in various settings from fully adversarial (worst-case) to fully random. Notably, one of our main results considers an arbitrary matroid structure with agents randomly divided into groups. In this setting, we prove a PoF bound as a function of the (relative) size of the largest group. Our result implies that, as long as there is no dominant group (i.e., the largest group is not too large), opportunity fairness constraints do not induce any loss of social welfare (defined as the allocation size). Overall, our results give insights into which aspects of the problem's structure affect the trade-off between opportunity fairness and social welfare.

Notably, one of our main results considers an arbitrary matroid structure with agents randomly divided into groups. Our result implies that, as long as there is no dominant group (i.e., the largest group is not too large), opportunity fairness constraints do not induce any loss of social welfare (defined as the allocation size). Overall, our results give insights into which aspects of the problem's structure affect the trade-off between opportunity fairness and social welfare.

paragraphs: This paper studies resource allocation under matroid constraints, a mathematical setting that includes bipartite matching. Agents belong to groups defined by a sensitive attribute. Opportunity fairness requires each group to receive the same proportion of the maximum allocation it could obtain on its own, so fairness is measured relative to each group's feasible opportunity.

The authors quantify the cost of that requirement through the Price of Fairness: the largest unconstrained allocation divided by the largest opportunity-fair allocation. They characterize this ratio using the problem's underlying polymatroid structure. That characterization supports bounds across settings ranging from adversarially chosen problems to random ones, connecting fairness costs to structural properties of the allocation problem.

One main result allows an arbitrary matroid but assumes agents are randomly divided into groups. In that setting, the bound depends on the relative size of the largest group. The authors conclude that, when no group is too dominant under these conditions, opportunity fairness causes no loss in allocation size. This identifies a setting where fairness and the stated social-welfare objective can coexist without a trade-off.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes opportunity fairness costs and identifies random-group settings where fairness preserves maximum allocation size.

title: The Price of Opportunity Fairness in Matroid Allocation Problems

abstract: Large-scale pre-trained models hold significant potential for learning universal EEG representations. However, most existing methods, particularly autoregressive (AR) frameworks, primarily rely on straightforward temporal sequencing of multi-channel EEG data, which fails to capture the rich physiological characteristics inherent to EEG signals. Moreover, their time-centered modeling approach also limits the effective representation of the dynamic spatial topology of brain activity. To address these challenges and fully exploit the potential of large-scale EEG models, we propose a novel Topology Hierarchical Derived Brain Autoregressive Modeling (THD-BAR) for EEG generic representations. The core innovation of THD-BAR lies in the introduction of the Brain Topology Hierarchy (BTH), which establishes a multi-scale spatial order for EEG channels. This hierarchical structure enables a redefinition of autoregressive learning as a "next-scale-time prediction" problem, effectively capturing both spatial and temporal dynamics. Based on BTH, we design a Topology-Hierarchical Vector Quantized-Variational Autoencoder (THVQ-VAE) for multi-scale tokenization and develop an enhanced Brain Autoregressive (BAR) module with specialized masking strategies for prediction. Through extensive large-scale pre-training on 17 datasets, followed by rigorous validation on 10 downstream datasets spanning 5 distinct tasks, THD-BAR consistently outperforms existing methods. These results highlight the superior generalization and modeling capabilities of our proposed approach.

title: THD-BAR: Topology Hierarchical Derived Brain Autoregressive Modeling for EEG Generic Representations

abstract: We introduce Open-Reasoner-Zero, the first open source implementation of large-scale reasoning-oriented RL training on the base model focusing on scalability, simplicity and accessibility. Through extensive experiments, we demonstrate that a minimalist approach, vanilla PPO with GAE ($\lambda=1$, $\gamma=1$) and straightforward rule-based rewards, without any KL regularization, is sufficient to scale up both benchmark performance and response length, replicating the scaling phenomenon observed in DeepSeek-R1-Zero. Using the same base model as DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B, our implementation achieves superior performance across AIME2024, MATH500, and GPQA Diamond, while demonstrating remarkable efficiency—requiring only 1/10 of the training steps compared to the DeepSeek-R1-Zero pipeline. We validate that this recipe generalizes well across diverse training domains and different model families without algorithmic modifications. Moreover, our analysis not only covers training dynamics and ablation for critical design choices, but also quantitatively show how the learned critic in Reasoner-Zero training effectively identifies and devalues repetitive response patterns, yielding more robust advantage estimations and enhancing training stability. Embracing the principles of open-source, we release our source code, parameter settings, training data, and model weights across various sizes, fostering reproducibility and encouraging further exploration of the properties of related models.

paragraphs: Open-Reasoner-Zero presents an accessible implementation of large-scale reinforcement learning for reasoning directly from a base language model. The authors investigate whether a simple training recipe can reproduce the growth in benchmark performance and response length seen in prior reasoning-oriented reinforcement learning. Their experiments show that vanilla PPO with rule-based rewards is sufficient in the studied settings.

The recipe uses generalized advantage estimation with both lambda and gamma set to one and omits KL regularization. Using the same base model as DeepSeek-R1-Zero-Qwen-32B, it surpasses that comparison on AIME2024, MATH500, and GPQA Diamond while requiring one tenth as many training steps. The authors also validate the recipe across different model families and training domains without changing the algorithm.

Their analysis finds that the learned critic identifies and devalues repetitive response patterns, improving advantage estimation and training stability. This helps explain a useful role for the critic within the simple recipe. The release includes code, settings, training data, and model weights at multiple sizes, supporting reproduction and further investigation of the training behavior.
summary.tldr: Open-Reasoner-Zero shows that a simple PPO recipe can scale reasoning performance efficiently and releases the resources needed to study it.

title: Open-Reasoner-Zero: An Open Source Approach to Scaling Up Reinforcement Learning on the Base Model

abstract: We study the target node prediction problem: given two social networks, identify those nodes/users from one network (called the source network) who are likely to join another (called the target network, with nodes called target nodes). Although this problem can be solved using existing techniques in the field of cross domain classification, we observe that in many real-world situations the cross-domain classifiers perform sub-optimally due to the heterogeneity between source and target networks that prevents the knowledge from being transferred. In this paper, we propose learning the consistent behavior of common users to help the knowledge transfer. We first present the Consistent Incidence Co-Factorization (CICF) for identifying the consistent users, i.e., common users that behave consistently across networks. Then we introduce the Domain-UnBiased (DUB) classifiers that transfer knowledge only through those consistent users. Extensive experiments are conducted and the results show that our proposal copes with heterogeneity and improves prediction accuracy.
