paragraphs: The paper asks which users in one social network are likely to join another. Cross-domain classifiers can approach this prediction problem, but differences between networks can make transferred knowledge unreliable. Even users present in both networks may behave differently across them, complicating their role as a bridge.

The proposed approach identifies common users whose behavior is consistent across the two networks. A method called Consistent Incidence Co-Factorization finds these users. Domain-UnBiased classifiers then transfer knowledge only through that selected group, making behavioral consistency the criterion for deciding which shared users should support cross-network prediction.

This design directly addresses heterogeneity between the source and target networks. Shared membership provides potential connections, while consistent behavior determines which connections the method uses. Extensive experiments show that the approach handles heterogeneity and improves prediction accuracy. The findings support selective transfer based on user behavior as a useful strategy for the target-node prediction problem studied.
summary.tldr: The method improves cross-network user prediction by transferring knowledge through shared users whose behavior remains consistent across networks.

title: Learning the Consistent Behavior of Common Users for Target Node Prediction across Social Networks

abstract: In this paper, we consider the problem of column subset selection. We present a novel analysis of the spectral norm reconstruction for a simple randomized algorithm and establish a new bound that depends explicitly on the sampling probabilities. The sampling dependent error bound (i) allows us to better understand the tradeoff in the reconstruction error due to sampling probabilities, (ii) exhibits more insights than existing error bounds that exploit specific probability distributions, and (iii) implies better sampling distributions. In particular, we show that a sampling distribution with probabilities proportional to the square root of the statistical leverage scores is better than uniform sampling, and is better than leverage-based sampling when the statistical leverage scores are very nonuniform. And by solving a constrained optimization problem related to the error bound with an efficient bisection search we are able to achieve better performance than using either the leverage-based distribution or that proportional to the square root of the statistical leverage scores. Numerical simulations demonstrate the benefits of the new sampling distributions for low-rank matrix approximation and least square approximation compared to state-of-the art algorithms.

paragraphs: Column subset selection approximates a matrix using a selection of its columns. This paper analyzes a simple randomized selection algorithm, measuring reconstruction quality with spectral-norm error. Its main contribution is an error bound that explicitly depends on the probabilities used to sample columns, making the consequences of different sampling choices visible in the analysis.

The bound guides the design of improved sampling distributions. The authors show that probabilities proportional to square roots of statistical leverage scores improve on uniform sampling. They also improve on leverage-score sampling when the leverage scores are very uneven. That latter comparison is conditional on the score distribution, rather than a universal preference between the two choices.

The authors further formulate a constrained optimization problem connected to their bound and solve it using efficient bisection search. This produces better performance than either leverage-based or square-root-leverage sampling. Numerical simulations demonstrate benefits for low-rank matrix approximation and least-squares approximation. The work turns an error analysis into a practical tool for choosing how to sample.
summary.tldr: An explicit sampling-dependent error bound guides improved column-selection probabilities for matrix and least-squares approximation.

title: An Explicit Sampling Dependent Spectral Error Bound for Column Subset Selection

abstract: With a growing need to understand large-scale networks, factorial relational models, such as binary matrix factorization models (BMFs), have become important in many applications. Although BMFs have a natural capability to uncover overlapping group structures behind network data, existing inference techniques have issues of either high computational cost or lack of model selection capability, and this limits their applicability. For scalable model selection of BMFs, this paper proposes stochastic factorized asymptotic Bayesian (sFAB) inference that combines concepts in two recently-developed techniques: stochastic variational inference (SVI) and FAB inference. sFAB is a highly-efficient algorithm, having both scalability and an inherent model selection capability in a single inference framework. Empirical results show the superiority of sFAB/BMF in both accuracy and scalability over state-of-the-art inference methods for overlapping relational models.

paragraphs: Binary matrix factorization can uncover overlapping groups in network data, allowing entities to belong to more than one group. Applying these models to large networks creates an inference challenge. Existing techniques may be computationally expensive or lack a way to select the model's structure, restricting their usefulness as network size grows.

The paper proposes stochastic factorized asymptotic Bayesian inference, abbreviated sFAB. It combines ideas from stochastic variational inference and factorized asymptotic Bayesian inference. The resulting framework is designed to offer scalability and inherent model selection together, addressing both the cost of fitting a relational model and the choice of its complexity.

Empirical comparisons report better accuracy and scalability for sFAB with binary matrix factorization than for state-of-the-art inference methods for overlapping relational models. The contribution matters because discovering overlapping network structure requires more than a representationally suitable model. The authors provide an inference approach that can also make model-selection decisions while handling large-scale data efficiently.
summary.tldr: sFAB combines scalable inference and model selection for binary matrix factorization, improving reported accuracy and scalability on relational data.

title: Scalable Model Selection for Large-Scale Factorial Relational Models

abstract: This paper develops differentially private mechanisms for $\chi^2$ test of independence. While existing works put their effort into properly controlling the type-I error, in addition to that, we investigate the type-II error of differentially private mechanisms. Based on the analysis, we present unit circle mechanism: a novel differentially private mechanism based on the geometrical property of the test statistics. Compared to existing output perturbation mechanisms, our mechanism improves the dominated term of the type-II error from $O(1)$ to $O(\exp(-\sqrt{N}))$ where $N$ is the sample size. Furthermore, we introduce novel procedures for multiple $\chi^2$ tests by incorporating the unit circle mechanism into the sparse vector technique and the exponential mechanism. These procedures can control the family-wise error rate (FWER) properly, which has never been attained by existing mechanisms.

paragraphs: A chi-squared independence test asks whether two variables show evidence of a relationship. Making that test differentially private introduces an additional statistical challenge: privacy protection should preserve useful decisions. This paper examines both type-I errors, which falsely indicate dependence, and type-II errors, which miss dependence that is present.

The proposed unit circle mechanism uses geometric properties of the test statistics. Compared with existing output-perturbation mechanisms, the authors report improving the specified term in the type-II error from O(1) to O(exp(-sqrt(N))), where N is sample size. That term therefore decreases with more data instead of remaining constant in order. This is a claim about a component of the error analysis, not a statement that every source of testing error disappears.

The paper also develops procedures for multiple chi-squared tests by combining the mechanism with the sparse vector technique and the exponential mechanism. These procedures control the family-wise error rate, addressing false positives across a collection of tests. The contribution connects privacy-preserving testing with both sensitivity to real relationships and error control across multiple decisions.
summary.tldr: A geometry-based private chi-squared mechanism improves a type-II error term and supports family-wise error control for multiple tests.

title: Differentially Private Chi-squared Test by Unit Circle Mechanism

abstract: In this paper, a new theory is developed for first-order stochastic convex optimization, showing that the global convergence rate is sufficiently quantified by a local growth rate of the objective function in a neighborhood of the optimal solutions. In particular, if the objective function $F(\mathbf{w})$ in the $\epsilon$-sublevel set grows as fast as $\|\mathbf{w} - \mathbf{w}_*\|_2^{1/\theta}$, where $\mathbf{w}_*$ represents the closest optimal solution to $\mathbf{w}$ and $\theta\in(0,1]$ quantifies the local growth rate, the iteration complexity of first-order stochastic optimization for achieving an $\epsilon$-optimal solution can be $\widetilde O(1/\epsilon^{2(1-\theta)})$, which is optimal at most up to a logarithmic factor. This result is fundamentally better in contrast with the previous works that either assume a global growth condition in the entire domain or achieve a local faster convergence under the local faster growth condition. To achieve the faster global convergence, we develop two different accelerated stochastic subgradient methods by iteratively solving the original problem approximately in a local region around a historical solution with the size of the local region gradually decreasing as the solution approaches the optimal set. Besides the theoretical improvements, this work also include new contributions towards making the proposed algorithms practical: (i) we present practical variants of accelerated stochastic subgradient methods that can run without the knowledge of multiplicative growth constant and even the growth rate $\theta$; (ii) we consider a broad family of problems in machine learning to demonstrate that the proposed algorithms enjoy faster convergence than traditional stochastic subgradient method. For example, when applied to the $\ell_1$ regularized empirical polyhedral loss minimization (e.g., hinge loss, absolute loss), the proposed stochastic methods have a logarithmic iteration complexity.

paragraphs: This paper connects the shape of a convex objective near its optimal solutions with the global efficiency of stochastic optimization. Its key result uses a local growth condition rather than requiring comparable growth throughout the entire domain. Faster growth near the optimum can therefore support faster overall convergence under the stated condition.

When growth is characterized by an exponent theta between zero and one, the iteration complexity can scale as 1/epsilon raised to 2(1-theta), apart from logarithmic factors. Their two accelerated stochastic subgradient methods repeatedly solve approximate problems inside local regions whose sizes shrink as optimization approaches the solution set.

In particular, l1-regularized empirical objectives with polyhedral losses, including hinge and absolute loss, admit logarithmic iteration complexity for the proposed stochastic methods.
summary.tldr: Local objective growth can yield near-optimal faster global convergence for stochastic convex optimization through progressively shrinking search regions.

title: Stochastic Convex Optimization: Faster Local Growth Implies Faster Global Convergence

abstract: We give the first provably efficient algorithm for learning a one hidden layer convolutional network with respect to a general class of (potentially overlapping) patches under mild conditions on the underlying distribution. We prove that our framework captures commonly used schemes from computer vision, including one-dimensional and two-dimensional “patch and stride” convolutions. Our algorithm– Convotron – is inspired by recent work applying isotonic regression to learning neural networks. Convotron uses a simple, iterative update rule that is stochastic in nature and tolerant to noise (requires only that the conditional mean function is a one layer convolutional network, as opposed to the realizable setting). In contrast to gradient descent, Convotron requires no special initialization or learning-rate tuning to converge to the global optimum. We also point out that learning one hidden convolutional layer with respect to a Gaussian distribution and just one disjoint patch $P$ (the other patches may be arbitrary) is easy in the following sense: Convotron can efficiently recover the hidden weight vector by updating only in the direction of $P$.

paragraphs: This paper studies provably efficient learning of a convolutional network with one hidden layer when input patches may overlap. Its framework covers a general class of patches, including familiar one-dimensional and two-dimensional patch-and-stride arrangements. The guarantees apply under mild conditions on the input distribution.

The proposed Convotron algorithm uses a simple stochastic iterative update inspired by work connecting isotonic regression to neural-network learning. It tolerates noise by requiring the conditional mean of the output to be a one-layer convolutional network; individual observations need not fit that network exactly. Within the stated setting, it converges to the global optimum without special initialization or learning-rate tuning.

The authors also identify a particular simplification for Gaussian inputs. If there is one disjoint patch, while the other patches may be arbitrary, Convotron can efficiently recover the hidden weights by updating only along that patch's direction. Together, these results clarify circumstances in which overlap and noisy observations remain compatible with efficient learning, while keeping the scope to the specified one-layer networks and distributional conditions.
summary.tldr: Convotron provably learns one-layer convolutional networks with potentially overlapping patches under stated distributional conditions and tolerates noisy observations.

title: Learning One Convolutional Layer with Overlapping Patches

abstract: In this paper, we introduce DICOD, a convolutional sparse coding algorithm which builds shift invariant representations for long signals. This algorithm is designed to run in a distributed setting, with local message passing, making it communication efficient. It is based on coordinate descent and uses locally greedy updates which accelerate the resolution compared to greedy coordinate selection. We prove the convergence of this algorithm and highlight its computational speed-up which is super-linear in the number of cores used. We also provide empirical evidence for the acceleration properties of our algorithm compared to state-of-the-art methods.
originalAbstract: In this paper, we introduce DICOD, a convolutional sparse coding algorithm which builds shift invariant representations for long signals. This algorithm is designed to run in a distributed setting, with local message passing, making it communication efficient. It is based on coordinate descent and uses locally greedy updates which accelerate the resolution compared to greedy coordinate selection. We prove the convergence of this algorithm and highlight its computational speed-up which is super-linear in the number of cores used. We also provide empirical evidence for the acceleration properties of our algorithm compared to state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Convolutional sparse coding represents long signals using patterns that can recur at different positions. Solving the associated optimization problem efficiently is important when signals are large enough to benefit from multiple processors. This paper introduces DICOD, a distributed coordinate-descent algorithm designed around the local structure of that computation.

DICOD uses local message passing, reducing the need for broad communication between workers. Its updates are locally greedy: workers make useful coordinate choices within their own regions. The authors argue that this choice can accelerate optimization compared with a globally greedy coordinate-selection strategy, so parallelism changes more than simply how many updates happen at once.

The paper proves convergence and highlights a speedup that can be super-linear in the number of cores. Empirical comparisons with existing methods support its acceleration properties. The contribution is specifically an efficient solver for convolutional sparse coding; the abstract does not attribute the gains to a new signal representation or report an improvement in downstream predictive accuracy.
summary.tldr: DICOD uses local, distributed coordinate updates to accelerate convolutional sparse coding with a convergence guarantee.

title: DICOD: Distributed Convolutional Coordinate Descent for Convolutional Sparse Coding

abstract: The Variational Autoencoder (VAE) has proven to be an effective model for producing semantically meaningful latent representations for natural data. However, it has thus far seen limited application to sequential data, and, as we demonstrate, existing recurrent VAE models have difficulty modeling sequences with long-term structure. To address this issue, we propose the use of a hierarchical decoder, which first outputs embeddings for subsequences of the input and then uses these embeddings to generate each subsequence independently. This structure encourages the model to utilize its latent code, thereby avoiding the "posterior collapse" problem which remains an issue for recurrent VAEs. We apply this architecture to modeling sequences of musical notes and find that it exhibits dramatically better sampling, interpolation, and reconstruction performance than a "flat" baseline model. An implementation of our "MusicVAE" is available online at https://goo.gl/magenta/musicvae-code.

To address this issue, we propose the use of a hierarchical decoder, which first outputs embeddings for subsequences of the input and then uses these embeddings to generate each subsequence independently. This structure encourages the model to utilize its latent code, thereby avoiding the "posterior collapse" problem which remains an issue for recurrent VAEs. paragraphs: Music contains structure that extends beyond the next note. This paper examines why recurrent variational autoencoders struggle to represent that longer structure, even though variational autoencoders can learn meaningful compact representations of other kinds of data. The central problem is making the representation useful throughout a generated sequence.

The proposed MusicVAE uses a hierarchical decoder. It first produces an embedding for each subsequence, then generates the individual subsequences independently from those embeddings. This creates a level of organization between the overall latent code and the notes. The structure encourages the decoder to use the latent code, addressing posterior collapse, where that code ceases to contribute useful information.

In experiments on musical note sequences, the authors report dramatically better sampling, interpolation, and reconstruction than a flat baseline. These results concern generating music, moving between latent representations, and recovering existing sequences. Together, they support the value of organizing sequence generation into multiple levels when learning longer musical structure.
summary.tldr: MusicVAE uses a hierarchical decoder to encourage useful latent representations and improve the modeling of long-term musical structure.

title: A Hierarchical Latent Vector Model for Learning Long-Term Structure in Music

abstract: Reinforcement learning (RL) has been successfully used to solve many continuous control tasks. Despite its impressive results however, fundamental questions regarding the sample complexity of RL on continuous problems remain open. We study the performance of RL in this setting by considering the behavior of the Least-Squares Temporal Difference (LSTD) estimator on the classic Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) problem from optimal control. We give the first finite-time analysis of the number of samples needed to estimate the value function for a fixed static state-feedback policy to within epsilon-relative error. In the process of deriving our result, we give a general characterization for when the minimum eigenvalue of the empirical covariance matrix formed along the sample path of a fast-mixing stochastic process concentrates above zero, extending a result by Koltchinskii and Mendelson in the independent covariates setting. Finally, we provide experimental evidence indicating that our analysis correctly captures the qualitative behavior of LSTD on several LQR instances.

Despite its impressive results however, fundamental questions regarding the sample complexity of RL on continuous problems remain open. We study the performance of RL in this setting by considering the behavior of the Least-Squares Temporal Difference (LSTD) estimator on the classic Linear Quadratic Regulator (LQR) problem from optimal control. We give the first finite-time analysis of the number of samples needed to estimate the value function for a fixed static state-feedback policy to within epsilon-relative error. In the process of deriving our result, we give a general characterization for when the minimum eigenvalue of the empirical covariance matrix formed along the sample path of a fast-mixing stochastic process concentrates above zero, extending a result by Koltchinskii and Mendelson in the independent covariates setting. Finally, we provide experimental evidence indicating that our analysis correctly captures the qualitative behavior of LSTD on several LQR instances.

paragraphs: This paper studies the amount of experience needed for reinforcement learning in a continuous-control setting. It focuses on least-squares temporal difference learning, or LSTD, applied to the linear quadratic regulator. The specific task is to estimate the value function of a fixed static state-feedback policy, making policy evaluation the object of analysis.

The authors provide the first finite-time sample analysis for reaching a specified relative error in that estimate. A central technical issue is that observations collected along a trajectory are dependent. They characterize conditions under which the smallest eigenvalue of the empirical covariance matrix stays bounded away from zero for a fast-mixing stochastic process.

That covariance result extends an earlier result for independent observations and supports the analysis of trajectory-based learning. Experiments on several linear quadratic regulator instances indicate that the theory captures LSTD’s qualitative behavior. The contribution gives a concrete sample-complexity account for this policy-evaluation problem, together with a broader tool for analyzing dependent data.
summary.tldr: The paper gives finite-time sample guarantees for LSTD policy evaluation in linear quadratic control.

title: Least-Squares Temporal Difference Learning for the Linear Quadratic Regulator

abstract: Motivated by the rapid rise in statistical tools in Functional Data Analysis , we consider the Gaussian mechanism for achieving differential privacy (DP) with parameter estimates taking values in a, potentially infinite-dimensional, separable Banach space. Using classic results from probability theory, we show how densities over function spaces can be utilized to achieve the desired DP bounds. This extends prior results of Hall et al (2013) to a much broader class of statistical estimates and summaries, including “path level" summaries, nonlinear functionals, and full function releases. By focusing on Banach spaces, we provide a deeper picture of the challenges for privacy with complex data, especially the role regularization plays in balancing utility and privacy. Using an application to penalized smoothing, we highlight this balance in the context of mean function estimation. Simulations and an application to {diffusion tensor imaging} are briefly presented, with extensive additions included in a supplement.

This paper studies how Gaussian perturbations can provide differential privacy for estimates in separable Banach spaces, which may be infinite-dimensional. That setting allows the privacy analysis to address a broad range of functional data summaries.

The authors use classical probability results to show how densities over spaces of functions can establish the required privacy bounds. Their analysis extends earlier results to a wider collection of outputs, including path-level summaries, nonlinear functionals, and complete functions. The contribution brings these richer releases into a common mathematical treatment of Gaussian privacy mechanisms.

The paper also examines the role of regularization in balancing privacy and usefulness. An application to penalized smoothing illustrates that balance when estimating a mean function. Simulations and an application to diffusion tensor imaging provide additional demonstrations. Together, the theory and examples clarify how protecting complex statistical outputs depends on the structure of the estimates and their regularization.
summary.tldr: The paper extends Gaussian differential privacy analysis to function-valued estimates and examines how regularization balances privacy with statistical usefulness.

title: Formal Privacy for Functional Data with Gaussian Perturbations

abstract: Stochastic variational inference is an established way to carry out approximate Bayesian inference for deep models flexibly and at scale. While there have been effective proposals for good initializations for loss minimization in deep learning, far less attention has been devoted to the issue of initialization of stochastic variational inference. We address this by proposing a novel layer-wise initialization strategy based on Bayesian linear models. The proposed method is extensively validated on regression and classification tasks, including Bayesian Deep Nets and Conv Nets, showing faster and better convergence compared to alternatives inspired by the literature on initializations for loss minimization.

paragraphs: Stochastic variational inference makes approximate Bayesian inference practical for deep models, but its optimization still needs a starting point. The paper observes that initialization has received substantial attention for ordinary deep-learning loss minimization and much less attention for variational inference. It addresses that gap with an initialization strategy designed for the Bayesian setting.

The proposed method initializes the model layer by layer using Bayesian linear models. This makes the construction of the starting state part of the inference methodology, rather than simply borrowing a scheme developed for another optimization objective. The approach specifically targets how stochastic variational inference begins, which can affect its subsequent convergence.

The authors validate the strategy on regression and classification tasks, including Bayesian deep networks and convolutional networks. In those evaluations, it converges faster and better than alternatives inspired by initialization methods for loss minimization. The finding supports treating initialization as an important design choice for scalable Bayesian learning: changing the starting configuration improves the reported optimization behavior across multiple model and task types.
summary.tldr: Layer-wise initialization using Bayesian linear models improves stochastic variational inference convergence in evaluated deep and convolutional networks.

title: Good Initializations of Variational Bayes for Deep Models

abstract: The upper confidence reinforcement learning (UCRL2) algorithm introduced in \citep{jaksch2010near} is a popular method to perform regret minimization in unknown discrete Markov Decision Processes under the average-reward criterion. Despite its nice and generic theoretical regret guarantees, this algorithm and its variants have remained until now mostly theoretical as numerical experiments in simple environments exhibit long burn-in phases before the learning takes place. In pursuit of practical efficiency, we present UCRL3, following the lines of UCRL2, but with two key modifications: First, it uses state-of-the-art time-uniform concentration inequalities to compute confidence sets on the reward and (component-wise) transition distributions for each state-action pair. Furthermore, to tighten exploration, it uses an adaptive computation of the support of each transition distribution, which in turn enables us to revisit the extended value iteration procedure of UCRL2 to optimize over distributions with reduced support by disregarding low probability transitions, while still ensuring near-optimism. We demonstrate, through numerical experiments in standard environments, that reducing exploration this way yields a substantial numerical improvement compared to UCRL2 and its variants. On the theoretical side, these key modifications enable us to derive a regret bound for UCRL3 improving on UCRL2, that for the first time makes appear notions of local diameter and local effective support, thanks to variance-aware concentration bounds.

paragraphs: Upper-confidence reinforcement learning provides regret guarantees for unknown discrete environments, but existing methods can spend a long time exploring before useful learning emerges. This paper introduces UCRL3 to improve that practical behavior while retaining theoretical control under the average-reward objective.

UCRL3 makes two principal changes to UCRL2. It uses time-uniform concentration inequalities to construct tighter confidence sets for rewards and transition probabilities. It also estimates transition support adaptively, allowing planning to disregard sufficiently low-probability transitions while preserving near-optimism. This reduces the range of possibilities considered during the extended value-iteration procedure.

Experiments in standard environments show substantial improvement over UCRL2 and its variants. The authors also derive an improved regret bound involving local diameter and local effective support, enabled by variance-aware concentration. The result connects more selective exploration with finer descriptions of the environment’s structure, rather than relying solely on broad worst-case properties of the entire state space.
summary.tldr: UCRL3 tightens confidence estimates and transition support to improve exploration and regret bounds in discrete reinforcement learning.

title: Tightening Exploration in Upper Confidence Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Despite remarkable success in practice, modern machine learning models have been found to be susceptible to adversarial attacks that make human-imperceptible perturbations to the data, but result in serious and potentially dangerous prediction errors. To address this issue, practitioners often use adversarial training to learn models that are robust against such attacks at the cost of higher generalization error on unperturbed test sets. The conventional wisdom is that more training data should shrink the gap between the generalization error of adversarially-trained models and standard models. However, we study the training of robust classifiers for both Gaussian and Bernoulli models under $\ell_\infty$ attacks, and we prove that more data may actually increase this gap. Furthermore, our theoretical results identify if and when additional data will finally begin to shrink the gap. Lastly, we experimentally demonstrate that our results also hold for linear regression models, which may indicate that this phenomenon occurs more broadly.

paragraphs: Adversarial training aims to protect models against small input perturbations that can cause prediction errors. It can also increase generalization error on unperturbed test data relative to standard training. This paper examines the common expectation that collecting more training data should reduce that clean-test performance gap.

The authors analyze robust classifiers in Gaussian and Bernoulli models under attacks constrained by the infinity norm. They prove that additional training data can increase the gap between robust and standard models. This is a statement about their relative generalization errors: a larger gap does not by itself establish that both models, or either individual model, become worse with more data.

The theory also identifies whether and when further data will begin reducing the gap. Experiments demonstrate the phenomenon for linear regression as well, suggesting that it may extend beyond the classification settings analyzed theoretically. The findings make the role of sample size more nuanced: more data can change the robust-versus-standard comparison in different directions depending on the setting.
summary.tldr: More training data can widen the clean-test generalization gap between robust and standard models in the settings analyzed.

title: More Data Can Expand The Generalization Gap Between Adversarially Robust and Standard Models

abstract: We consider a new unsupervised learning task of inferring parameters of a multiobjective decision making model, based on a set of observed decisions from the human expert. This setting is important in applications (such as the task of portfolio management) where it may be difficult to obtain the human expert’s intrinsic decision making model. We formulate such a learning problem as an inverse multiobjective optimization problem (IMOP) and propose its first sophisticated model with statistical guarantees. Then, we reveal several fundamental connections between IMOP, K-means clustering, and manifold learning. Leveraging these critical insights and connections, we propose two algorithms to solve IMOP through manifold learning and clustering. Numerical results confirm the effectiveness of our model and the computational efficacy of algorithms.

paragraphs: An expert's decisions can be observable even when the model behind them is inaccessible. This paper asks how to infer the parameters of a decision model that balances multiple objectives using only a collection of observed expert choices. Portfolio management motivates the setting, where obtaining an expert's intrinsic decision-making model may be difficult.

The authors formulate this unsupervised task as inverse multiobjective optimization. The direction of inference runs from decisions back to the model parameters that could explain them. They propose a model with statistical guarantees and identify connections to K-means clustering and manifold learning, linking the decision-inference problem to methods for organizing the structure of observed data.

Those connections lead to two algorithms that solve the inverse problem through clustering and manifold learning. Numerical results support both the effectiveness of the proposed model and the computational efficiency of the algorithms. The contribution therefore combines a statistically grounded formulation with practical solution methods, making observed expert behavior a source of information about a multiobjective decision process.
summary.tldr: The paper infers multiobjective decision-model parameters from expert choices using statistically grounded inverse optimization and connections to clustering and manifold learning.

title: Expert Learning through Generalized Inverse Multiobjective Optimization: Models, Insights, and Algorithms

abstract: We introduce a new framework for the exact point-wise ℓp robustness verification problem that exploits the layer-wise geometric structure of deep feed-forward networks with rectified linear activations (ReLU networks). The activation regions of the network partition the input space, and one can verify the ℓp robustness around a point by checking all the activation regions within the desired radius. The GeoCert algorithm (Jordan et al., NeurIPS 2019) treats this partition as a generic polyhedral complex in order to detect which region to check next. In contrast, our LayerCert framework considers the nested hyperplane arrangement structure induced by the layers of the ReLU network and explores regions in a hierarchical manner. We show that, under certain conditions on the algorithm parameters, LayerCert provably reduces the number and size of the convex programs that one needs to solve compared to GeoCert. Furthermore, our LayerCert framework allows the incorporation of lower bounding routines based on convex relaxations to further improve performance. Experimental results demonstrate that LayerCert can significantly reduce both the number of convex programs solved and the running time over the state-of-the-art.

paragraphs: Exact point-wise robustness verification asks whether a network’s prediction is protected against perturbations within a chosen distance of a particular input. For feed-forward ReLU networks, activation patterns divide input space into geometric regions. Checking the relevant regions can establish robustness, but finding and processing them requires solving convex optimization problems.

LayerCert uses the nested geometric structure created by successive network layers to explore these regions hierarchically. The comparison method, GeoCert, treats the partition as a more general polyhedral complex. Exploiting the layered structure gives LayerCert additional organization for deciding which regions to examine and how to formulate the associated optimization work.

Under certain conditions on algorithm parameters, the authors prove that LayerCert reduces both the number and size of convex programs relative to GeoCert. The framework can also incorporate lower bounds from convex relaxations to improve performance further. Experiments show substantial reductions in solved programs and runtime. The theoretical improvement is conditional, while the reported runtime reductions provide empirical evidence of its practical value.
summary.tldr: LayerCert exploits ReLU networks’ layered geometry to accelerate exact robustness verification, with conditional guarantees of reduced optimization work.

title: Hierarchical Verification for Adversarial Robustness

abstract: We introduce a new budgeted framework for online influence maximization, considering the total cost of an advertising campaign instead of the common cardinality constraint on a chosen influencer set. Our approach models better the real-world setting where the cost of influencers varies and advertizers want to find the best value for their overall social advertising budget. We propose an algorithm assuming an independent cascade diffusion model and edge-level semi-bandit feedback, and provide both theoretical and experimental results. Our analysis is also valid for the cardinality-constraint setting and improves the state of the art regret bound in this case.

We propose an algorithm assuming an independent cascade diffusion model and edge-level semi-bandit feedback, and provide both theoretical and experimental results. Our analysis is also valid for the cardinality-constraint setting and improves the state of the art regret bound in this case.

paragraphs: Influence maximization concerns choosing people whose participation helps information spread through a network. Many formulations restrict how many influencers can be selected. This paper instead considers the total cost of an advertising campaign, addressing the practical fact that different influencers can charge different amounts.

The resulting online framework asks how to obtain value from an overall advertising budget while learning about influence. A spending constraint changes which choices are attractive: the number of selected influencers alone does not capture their affordability. The proposed algorithm assumes an independent cascade model of diffusion and edge-level semi-bandit feedback, so its analysis depends on a particular spreading model and access to feedback about individual network edges.

The paper provides both theoretical and experimental results for this budgeted approach. Its analysis also applies to the more familiar setting that limits the number of selected influencers, where it improves the stated best available regret bound. Thus, the contribution includes both a more cost-sensitive problem formulation and a stronger learning guarantee for an existing formulation.
summary.tldr: A budget-based influence-maximization framework accounts for differing influencer costs and improves the regret bound for the cardinality-constrained setting.

title: Budgeted Online Influence Maximization

abstract: We consider the problem of allocating a fixed budget of samples to a finite set of discrete distributions to learn them uniformly well (minimizing the maximum error) in terms of four common distance measures: $\ell_2^2$, $\ell_1$, $f$-divergence, and separation distance. To present a unified treatment of these distances, we first propose a general \emph{optimistic tracking algorithm} and analyze its sample allocation performance w.r.t. an oracle. We then instantiate this algorithm for the four distance measures and derive bounds on their regret. We also show that the allocation performance of the proposed algorithm cannot, in general, be improved, by deriving lower-bounds on the expected deviation from the oracle allocation for any adaptive scheme. We verify our theoretical findings through some experiments. Finally, we show that the techniques developed in the paper can be easily extended to learn some classes of continuous distributions as well as to the related setting of minimizing the average error (in terms of the four distances) in learning a set of distributions.

paragraphs: When several probability distributions must be learned from a fixed sampling budget, the central decision is how to divide observations among them. This paper studies allocating samples to a finite collection of discrete distributions so that the largest estimation error is as small as possible. That objective prioritizes learning every distribution reasonably well, rather than achieving a good average while leaving one poorly estimated.

The authors introduce a general optimistic tracking algorithm and compare its allocation with an oracle allocation. They then specialize the framework to four measures of discrepancy: squared L2 distance, L1 distance, f-divergence, and separation distance. The resulting regret bounds describe performance across these different ways of measuring estimation error.

Lower bounds on expected deviation from the oracle show that the algorithm’s allocation performance cannot generally be improved by an adaptive scheme. Experiments support the theoretical findings. The authors also extend their techniques to some continuous distribution classes and to minimizing average error, showing that the allocation framework reaches beyond its original worst-error objective.
summary.tldr: An adaptive sampling framework allocates a fixed budget across distributions, with regret guarantees and lower bounds on tracking an oracle allocation.

title: Adaptive Sampling for Estimating Probability Distributions

abstract: High-dimensional observations and unknown dynamics are major challenges when applying optimal control to many real-world decision making tasks. The Learning Controllable Embedding (LCE) framework addresses these challenges by embedding the observations into a lower dimensional latent space, estimating the latent dynamics, and then performing control directly in the latent space. To ensure the learned latent dynamics are predictive of next-observations, all existing LCE approaches decode back into the observation space and explicitly perform next-observation prediction—a challenging high-dimensional task that furthermore introduces a large number of nuisance parameters (i.e., the decoder) which are discarded during control. In this paper, we propose a novel information-theoretic LCE approach and show theoretically that explicit next-observation prediction can be replaced with predictive coding. We then use predictive coding to develop a decoder-free LCE model whose latent dynamics are amenable to locally-linear control. Extensive experiments on benchmark tasks show that our model reliably learns a controllable latent space that leads to superior performance when compared with state-of-the-art LCE baselines.

paragraphs: Controlling a system from high-dimensional observations is challenging when its dynamics are unknown. Learning Controllable Embedding methods address this by compressing observations, learning dynamics in the latent space, and controlling the system there. Existing approaches also reconstruct the next observation to ensure that the learned dynamics retain predictive information, requiring a decoder that is later discarded during control.

This paper develops an information-theoretic approach and shows theoretically that predictive coding can replace explicit prediction in the original observation space. The authors use that result to construct a decoder-free model. Its latent dynamics are designed to support locally linear control, connecting the learned representation directly to the requirements of the control procedure.

Experiments on benchmark tasks show that the model reliably learns a controllable latent space and outperforms state-of-the-art LCE baselines. The contribution removes the need to solve a high-dimensional reconstruction task as part of learning a useful control representation. Its theoretical replacement and empirical results support learning predictive latent dynamics without maintaining the extra decoder parameters.
summary.tldr: Predictive coding replaces explicit next-observation reconstruction in a decoder-free latent model that supports locally linear control.

title: Predictive Coding for Locally-Linear Control

abstract: Deep models, while being extremely flexible and accurate, are surprisingly vulnerable to “small, imperceptible” perturbations known as adversarial attacks. While the majority of existing attacks focus on measuring perturbations under the $\ell_p$ metric, Wasserstein distance, which takes geometry in pixel space into account, has long been known to be a suitable metric for measuring image quality and has recently risen as a compelling alternative to the $\ell_p$ metric in adversarial attacks. However, constructing an effective attack under the Wasserstein metric is computationally much more challenging and calls for better optimization algorithms. We address this gap in two ways: (a) we develop an exact yet efficient projection operator to enable a stronger projected gradient attack; (b) we show that the Frank-Wolfe method equipped with a suitable linear minimization oracle works extremely fast under Wasserstein constraints. Our algorithms not only converge faster but also generate much stronger attacks. For instance, we decrease the accuracy of a residual network on CIFAR-10 to $3.4%$ within a Wasserstein perturbation ball of radius $0.005$, in contrast to $65.6%$ using the previous Wasserstein attack based on an \emph{approximate} projection operator. Furthermore, employing our stronger attacks in adversarial training significantly improves the robustness of adversarially trained models.

paragraphs: Wasserstein distance measures image perturbations in a way that accounts for pixel-space geometry. It offers an alternative to the usual ℓp measures for adversarial attacks, but finding effective attacks under its constraints is computationally harder. This paper addresses that optimization challenge with two methods.

First, the authors develop an exact, efficient projection operator for projected gradient attacks. Second, they combine Frank–Wolfe optimization with a suitable linear minimization oracle to obtain very fast attacks under Wasserstein constraints. This shows how a weaker optimizer can substantially understate vulnerability in that setting. Using the stronger attacks for adversarial training also significantly improves robustness in the reported experiments, connecting better attack optimization to improved defense training.
summary.tldr: Improved projection and Frank–Wolfe methods produce faster, stronger Wasserstein attacks and improve robustness when used in adversarial training.

title: Stronger and Faster Wasserstein Adversarial Attacks

abstract: Machine learned models often must abide by certain requirements (e.g., fairness or legal). This has spurred interested in developing approaches that can provably verify whether a model satisfies certain properties. This paper introduces a generic algorithm called Veritas that enables tackling multiple different verification tasks for tree ensemble models like random forests (RFs) and gradient boosted decision trees (GBDTs). This generality contrasts with previous work, which has focused exclusively on either adversarial example generation or robustness checking. Veritas formulates the verification task as a generic optimization problem and introduces a novel search space representation. Veritas offers two key advantages. First, it provides anytime lower and upper bounds when the optimization problem cannot be solved exactly. In contrast, many existing methods have focused on exact solutions and are thus limited by the verification problem being NP-complete. Second, Veritas produces full (bounded suboptimal) solutions that can be used to generate concrete examples. We experimentally show that our method produces state-of-the-art robustness estimates, especially when executed with strict time constraints. This is exceedingly important when checking the robustness of large datasets. Additionally, we show that Veritas enables tackling more real-world verification scenarios.

This paper introduces Veritas, a generic algorithm for verification tasks involving random forests and gradient-boosted decision trees. It represents verification as an optimization problem and supplies a new search-space representation for solving it.

The contribution is a reusable optimization framework that supplies both quantitative bounds and example-producing solutions across multiple tree-ensemble verification tasks.
summary.tldr: Veritas verifies multiple tree-ensemble properties using anytime optimization bounds and concrete solutions, with strong robustness estimates under time limits.

title: Versatile Verification of Tree Ensembles

abstract: We show that adding differential privacy to Explainable Boosting Machines (EBMs), a recent method for training interpretable ML models, yields state-of-the-art accuracy while protecting privacy. Our experiments on multiple classification and regression datasets show that DP-EBM models suffer surprisingly little accuracy loss even with strong differential privacy guarantees. In addition to high accuracy, two other benefits of applying DP to EBMs are: a) trained models provide exact global and local interpretability, which is often important in settings where differential privacy is needed; and b) the models can be edited after training without loss of privacy to correct errors which DP noise may have introduced.

The resulting DP-EBM models aim to preserve the usefulness of that model family while protecting private information.

Experiments across multiple classification and regression datasets show surprisingly small accuracy losses even with strong differential privacy guarantees. The authors report state-of-the-art accuracy for their approach. These findings support the practical possibility of retaining predictive performance while adding privacy protection in the evaluated settings.

The approach also retains exact explanations at both the overall model level and the individual prediction level. A further benefit is that the trained model can be edited to correct errors introduced by privacy noise without losing its privacy protection. Together, these properties make the contribution broader than an accuracy result: the private model remains understandable and can be corrected after training.
summary.tldr: Private Explainable Boosting Machines retain strong accuracy, exact interpretability, and the ability to correct trained models without losing privacy protection.

title: Accuracy, Interpretability, and Differential Privacy via Explainable Boosting

abstract: In this work, we study the computational complexity of reducing the squared gradient magnitude for smooth minimax optimization problems. First, we present algorithms with accelerated $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$ last-iterate rates, faster than the existing $\mathcal{O}(1/k)$ or slower rates for extragradient, Popov, and gradient descent with anchoring. The acceleration mechanism combines extragradient steps with anchoring and is distinct from Nesterov’s acceleration. We then establish optimality of the $\mathcal{O}(1/k^2)$ rate through a matching lower bound.

paragraphs: This paper studies how quickly algorithms can reduce the squared gradient magnitude in smooth convex-concave minimax problems. These problems involve minimizing with respect to one set of variables while maximizing with respect to another. The quantity being tracked measures the remaining gradient signal, so the focus is on progress toward a stationary solution.

The proposed algorithms combine extragradient steps with anchoring. The authors identify this combination as an acceleration mechanism distinct from Nesterov’s acceleration. They establish an O(1/k²) rate after k iterations, improving on the O(1/k) or slower rates cited for extragradient, Popov, and gradient descent with anchoring.

The guarantee applies to the last iterate, meaning the algorithm’s current output receives the stated rate. The paper also supplies a matching lower bound, establishing optimality within the analyzed setting. Together, the upper and lower bounds show both how to achieve faster reduction of squared gradient magnitude and why that rate represents a theoretical limit for the problem framework studied.
summary.tldr: Combining extragradient steps with anchoring achieves an optimal O(1/k²) last-iterate rate for squared gradient magnitude in smooth convex-concave minimax optimization.

title: Accelerated Algorithms for Smooth Convex-Concave Minimax Problems with O(1/k^2) Rate on Squared Gradient Norm

abstract: The last decade saw impressive progress towards understanding the performance of algorithms in adaptive settings, where subsequent inputs may depend on the output from prior inputs. Adaptive settings arise in processes with feedback or with adversarial attacks. Existing designs of robust algorithms are generic wrappers of non-robust counterparts and leave open the possibility of better tailored designs. The lowers bounds (attacks) are similarly worst-case and their significance to practical setting is unclear. Aiming to understand these questions, we study the robustness of \texttt{CountSketch}, a popular dimensionality reduction technique that maps vectors to a lower dimension using randomized linear measurements. The sketch supports recovering $\ell_2$-heavy hitters of a vector (entries with $v[i]^2 \geq \frac{1}{k}\|\boldsymbol{v}\|^2_2$). We show that the classic estimator is not robust, and can be attacked with a number of queries of the order of the sketch size. We propose a robust estimator (for a slightly modified sketch) that allows for quadratic number of queries in the sketch size, which is an improvement factor of $\sqrt{k}$ (for $k$ heavy hitters) over prior "blackbox" approaches.

paragraphs: CountSketch compresses vectors using randomized linear measurements while supporting recovery of entries that contribute a substantial share of the vector’s squared magnitude. This paper asks what happens when later inputs depend on answers to earlier queries. Such adaptive inputs arise through feedback and adversarial interaction.

The authors show that the classic CountSketch estimator is vulnerable: an attack can succeed with a number of queries on the order of the sketch size. This exposes a difference between using a randomized sketch on inputs independent of its answers and repeatedly interacting with it in a way that responds to those answers.

They then propose a robust estimator for a slightly modified sketch that supports a number of queries quadratic in the sketch size. For recovering k heavy hitters, the stated improvement over earlier generic robustness wrappers is a factor of the square root of k. The contribution shows that a design tailored to CountSketch can improve adaptive robustness beyond what those black-box approaches provide.
summary.tldr: A tailored CountSketch estimator supports quadratically many adaptive queries in sketch size, improving on prior generic robustness approaches.

title: On the Robustness of CountSketch to Adaptive Inputs

abstract: Offline reinforcement learning (RL) enables effective learning from previously collected data without exploration, which shows great promise in real-world applications when exploration is expensive or even infeasible. The discount factor, $\gamma$, plays a vital role in improving online RL sample efficiency and estimation accuracy, but the role of the discount factor in offline RL is not well explored. This paper examines two distinct effects of $\gamma$ in offline RL with theoretical analysis, namely the regularization effect and the pessimism effect. On the one hand, $\gamma$ is a regulator to trade-off optimality with sample efficiency upon existing offline techniques. On the other hand, lower guidance $\gamma$ can also be seen as a way of pessimism where we optimize the policy’s performance in the worst possible models. We empirically verify the above theoretical observation with tabular MDPs and standard D4RL tasks. The results show that the discount factor plays an essential role in the performance of offline RL algorithms, both under small data regimes upon existing offline methods and in large data regimes without other conservative methods.

paragraphs: Offline reinforcement learning develops a policy from previously collected data, without gathering new experience through exploration. This paper examines the discount factor, which controls how future rewards enter the learning objective. Although its effects have been studied in online learning, the authors investigate what it does when learning must rely on a fixed dataset.

Their theoretical analysis identifies two roles. First, the discount factor acts as a regulator that trades optimality against sample efficiency when used with existing offline methods. Second, a lower guidance discount factor can express pessimism: the resulting policy optimization can be understood in terms of performance under the worst possible models.

Experiments with tabular decision processes and standard D4RL tasks support these theoretical observations. The reported effects appear both with small datasets alongside existing offline techniques and with larger datasets without other conservative methods. The findings make the discount factor a consequential design choice for offline learning, with distinct regularization and pessimism interpretations rather than a guarantee that lowering it always helps.
summary.tldr: The discount factor shapes offline reinforcement learning through both an optimality–sample-efficiency trade-off and a pessimistic optimization effect.

title: On the Role of Discount Factor in Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: Modern reinforcement learning (RL) commonly engages practical problems with large state spaces, where function approximation must be deployed to approximate either the value function or the policy. While recent progresses in RL theory address a rich set of RL problems with general function approximation, such successes are mostly restricted to the single-agent setting. It remains elusive how to extend these results to multi-agent RL, especially in the face of new game-theoretical challenges. This paper considers two-player zero-sum Markov Games (MGs). We propose a new algorithm that can provably find the Nash equilibrium policy using a polynomial number of samples, for any MG with low multi-agent Bellman-Eluder dimension —a new complexity measure adapted from its single-agent version (Jin et al., 2021). A key component of our new algorithm is the exploiter, which facilitates the learning of the main player by deliberately exploiting her weakness. Our theoretical framework is generic, which applies to a wide range of models including but not limited to tabular MGs, MGs with linear or kernel function approximation, and MGs with rich observations.

paragraphs: Large state spaces make function approximation central to reinforcement learning: a model must represent policies or values across many possible situations. Extending theoretical guarantees from one agent to multiple agents introduces strategic complications. This paper studies two-player zero-sum Markov games, where each player's decisions interact with an opponent pursuing the opposing payoff.

The proposed algorithm includes an exploiter that deliberately targets weaknesses in the main player's behavior. That opponent helps the main player learn through exposure to exploitable choices. To characterize which problems permit efficient learning, the authors introduce multi-agent Bellman-Eluder dimension, adapting a complexity measure previously used in single-agent reinforcement learning.

For games with low values of this complexity measure, the algorithm provably finds a Nash equilibrium policy using a polynomial number of samples. The low-complexity condition is central to that guarantee. The framework applies across a range of representations, including tabular games, linear and kernel function approximation, and rich observations. Its contribution combines a strategic training component with a general way to state sample-efficiency guarantees.
summary.tldr: An exploiter helps learn Nash equilibrium policies with polynomial sample complexity in zero-sum Markov games with low multi-agent Bellman-Eluder dimension.

title: The Power of Exploiter: Provable Multi-Agent RL in Large State Spaces

abstract: We propose discrete Langevin proposal (DLP), a simple and scalable gradient-based proposal for sampling complex high-dimensional discrete distributions. In contrast to Gibbs sampling-based methods, DLP is able to update all coordinates in parallel in a single step and the magnitude of changes is controlled by a stepsize. This allows a cheap and efficient exploration in the space of high-dimensional and strongly correlated variables. We prove the efficiency of DLP by showing that the asymptotic bias of its stationary distribution is zero for log-quadratic distributions, and is small for distributions that are close to being log-quadratic. With DLP, we develop several variants of sampling algorithms, including unadjusted, Metropolis-adjusted, stochastic and preconditioned versions. DLP outperforms many popular alternatives on a wide variety of tasks, including Ising models, restricted Boltzmann machines, deep energy-based models, binary neural networks and language generation.

paragraphs: Sampling from a discrete distribution becomes difficult when there are many variables and their values strongly depend on one another. This paper introduces the discrete Langevin proposal, or DLP, which uses gradient information to propose changes. Its central feature is the ability to update every coordinate in parallel during a single step.

A stepsize controls the magnitude of those changes, providing a way to regulate movement through the space of possible configurations. The authors use this proposal to build several sampling algorithms, including unadjusted and Metropolis-adjusted versions, along with stochastic and preconditioned variants. The proposal therefore serves as a shared component for multiple sampling approaches.

The theoretical analysis establishes zero asymptotic stationary-distribution bias for log-quadratic distributions and small bias for distributions close to that family. This qualification matters: the stated guarantee depends on the distribution's structure. Experiments report improvements over many popular alternatives across tasks involving Ising models, restricted Boltzmann machines, deep energy-based models, binary neural networks, and language generation.
summary.tldr: DLP uses gradient-guided parallel updates to sample discrete distributions, with bias guarantees for log-quadratic and nearby distributions.

title: A Langevin-like Sampler for Discrete Distributions

abstract: Automated design of analog and radio-frequency circuits using supervised or reinforcement learning from simulation data has recently been studied as an alternative to manual expert design. It is straightforward for a design agent to learn an inverse function from desired performance metrics to circuit parameters. However, it is more common for a user to have threshold performance criteria rather than an exact target vector of feasible performance measures. In this work, we propose a method for generating from simulation data a dataset on which a system can be trained via supervised learning to design circuits to meet threshold specifications. We moreover perform the to-date most extensive evaluation of automated analog circuit design, including experimenting in a significantly more diverse set of circuits than in prior work, covering linear, nonlinear, and autonomous circuit configurations, and show that our method consistently reaches success rate better than 90% at 5% error margin, while also improving data efficiency by upward of an order of magnitude.

paragraphs: Automated circuit design often learns a mapping from desired performance measurements to circuit parameters. The paper points out that users commonly express requirements as thresholds rather than exact performance values. A useful design system therefore needs to find a circuit satisfying those requirements, without requiring the user to supply a precisely achievable target vector.

The authors propose a way to construct a training dataset from circuit simulations specifically for this threshold-based task. A supervised learning system can then learn to produce circuit parameters that meet the requested specifications. The key contribution is aligning the training problem with the form of requirements users actually provide, making threshold satisfaction the design objective.

The evaluation covers linear, nonlinear, and autonomous circuits, with a more diverse collection than prior work according to the authors. Their method consistently exceeds a 90% success rate at a 5% error margin in the reported evaluation. They also report more than an order-of-magnitude improvement in data efficiency. These results support learning threshold-oriented design from simulation data across the tested range of circuit configurations.
summary.tldr: A simulation-derived training dataset teaches circuit designers to satisfy threshold specifications, with high reported success and improved data efficiency.

title: Learning to Design Analog Circuits to Meet Threshold Specifications

abstract: By incorporating regret minimization, double oracle methods have demonstrated rapid convergence to Nash Equilibrium (NE) in normal-form games and extensive-form games, through algorithms such as online double oracle (ODO) and extensive-form double oracle (XDO), respectively. In this study, we further examine the theoretical convergence rate and sample complexity of such regret minimization-based double oracle methods, utilizing a unified framework called Regret-Minimizing Double Oracle. Based on this framework, we extend ODO to extensive-form games and determine its sample complexity. Moreover, we demonstrate that the sample complexity of XDO can be exponential in the number of information sets $|S|$, owing to the exponentially decaying stopping threshold of restricted games. To solve this problem, we propose the Periodic Double Oracle (PDO) method, which has the lowest sample complexity among regret minimization-based double oracle methods, being only polynomial in $|S|$. Empirical evaluations on multiple poker and board games show that PDO achieves significantly faster convergence than previous double oracle algorithms and reaches a competitive level with state-of-the-art regret minimization methods.

paragraphs: Double-oracle methods combined with regret minimization have shown fast convergence toward Nash equilibrium in games. This paper develops a unified framework for analyzing their convergence rates and sample requirements. It covers both normal-form methods and extensive-form methods, which represent games with sequential decisions and information sets.

Within this framework, the authors extend online double oracle to extensive-form games and determine its sample complexity. They also identify a potential problem with extensive-form double oracle: its sample complexity can grow exponentially with the number of information sets because its stopping threshold for restricted games decreases exponentially.

The proposed Periodic Double Oracle addresses that issue with sample complexity polynomial in the number of information sets. The authors report the lowest sample complexity among regret-minimizing double-oracle methods. Experiments on poker and board games show substantially faster convergence than previous double-oracle algorithms and performance competitive with state-of-the-art regret-minimization methods. The theoretical and empirical results together motivate changing how the restricted-game solving process is organized.
summary.tldr: Periodic Double Oracle achieves polynomial sample complexity and faster empirical convergence after analysis exposes a possible exponential cost in XDO.

title: Regret-Minimizing Double Oracle for Extensive-Form Games

abstract: Machine learning (ML) holds great potential for accurately forecasting treatment outcomes over time, which could ultimately enable the adoption of more individualized treatment strategies in many practical applications. However, a significant challenge that has been largely overlooked by the ML literature on this topic is the presence of informative sampling in observational data. When instances are observed irregularly over time, sampling times are typically not random, but rather informative–depending on the instance’s characteristics, past outcomes, and administered treatments. In this work, we formalize informative sampling as a covariate shift problem and show that it can prohibit accurate estimation of treatment outcomes if not properly accounted for. To overcome this challenge, we present a general framework for learning treatment outcomes in the presence of informative sampling using inverse intensity-weighting, and propose a novel method, TESAR-CDE, that instantiates this framework using Neural CDEs. Using a simulation environment based on a clinical use case, we demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach in learning under informative sampling.

paragraphs: Forecasting treatment outcomes from observational records requires dealing with when measurements are taken. Observation times can depend on an individual's characteristics, earlier outcomes, and treatments. Consequently, irregular observations can carry information about the underlying process, and the recorded examples may provide a distorted view of the outcomes a model needs to predict.

The paper formalizes this informative sampling as a covariate shift problem: the distribution represented by observations differs from the relevant prediction distribution. It shows that failing to account for this shift can prevent accurate treatment-outcome estimation. Its general framework uses inverse intensity weighting to adjust learning for the process governing observation times.

The authors instantiate the framework in TESAR-CDE, a method built with neural controlled differential equations. In a simulation environment based on a clinical use case, the approach demonstrates effective learning under informative sampling. The contribution connects a specific source of observational bias to a corrective learning framework, with the reported effectiveness established in simulation.
summary.tldr: TESAR-CDE accounts for informative observation times through inverse intensity weighting to improve treatment-outcome learning in a clinical-use-case simulation.

title: Accounting For Informative Sampling When Learning to Forecast Treatment Outcomes Over Time

abstract: Accurately reconstructing the global ocean deoxygenation over a century is crucial for assessing and protecting marine ecosystem. Existing expert-dominated numerical simulations fail to catch up with the dynamic variation caused by global warming and human activities. Besides, due to the high-cost data collection, the historical observations are severely sparse, leading to big challenge for precise reconstruction. In this work, we propose OxyGenerator, the first deep learning based model, to reconstruct the global ocean deoxygenation from 1920 to 2023. Specifically, to address the heterogeneity across large temporal and spatial scales, we propose zoning-varying graph message-passing to capture the complex oceanographic correlations between missing values and sparse observations. Additionally, to further calibrate the uncertainty, we incorporate inductive bias from dissolved oxygen (DO) variations and chemical effects. Compared with in-situ DO observations, OxyGenerator significantly outperforms CMIP6 numerical simulations, reducing MAPE by 38.77%, demonstrating a promising potential to understand the “breathless ocean” in data-driven manner.

paragraphs: OxyGenerator reconstructs global ocean deoxygenation from 1920 to 2023 using deep learning. The challenge is that historical oxygen measurements are extremely sparse because collecting them is expensive. The paper also argues that existing expert-driven numerical simulations struggle to capture dynamic changes associated with global warming and human activity, motivating a data-driven reconstruction approach.

summary.tldr: OxyGenerator combines graph learning and oceanographic knowledge to reconstruct historical oxygen loss more accurately than CMIP6 in the reported comparison.

title: OxyGenerator: Reconstructing Global Ocean Deoxygenation Over a Century with Deep Learning

abstract: We study the behavior of optimal ridge regularization and optimal ridge risk for out-of-distribution prediction, where the test distribution deviates arbitrarily from the train distribution. We establish general conditions that determine the sign of the optimal regularization level under covariate and regression shifts. These conditions capture the alignment between the covariance and signal structures in the train and test data and reveal stark differences compared to the in-distribution setting. For example, a negative regularization level can be optimal under covariate shift or regression shift, even when the training features are isotropic or the design is underparameterized. Furthermore, we prove that the optimally tuned risk is monotonic in the data aspect ratio, even in the out-of-distribution setting and when optimizing over negative regularization levels. In general, our results do not make any modeling assumptions for the train or the test distributions, except for moment bounds, and allow for arbitrary shifts and the widest possible range of (negative) regularization levels.

paragraphs: This paper studies how ridge regularization should be tuned when the test distribution differs from the training distribution. It considers both covariate shifts and changes in the regression relationship. The central question is how these shifts alter the best regularization level and the prediction risk achieved after optimal tuning.

The authors establish conditions determining whether the optimal regularization level is positive or negative. These conditions depend on how covariance and signal structures align across training and test data. Negative regularization can be optimal even with isotropic training features or an underparameterized design, revealing behavior that differs sharply from familiar in-distribution settings.

They also prove that optimally tuned risk is monotonic in the data aspect ratio, including when tuning permits negative regularization. The results generally require moment bounds but impose no other modeling assumptions on the training or test distributions. By allowing arbitrary distribution shifts and a broad range of regularization levels, the analysis clarifies why conclusions about optimal ridge tuning can change when prediction moves beyond the training distribution.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes optimal ridge regularization under distribution shifts, including conditions where negative regularization is best.

title: Optimal Ridge Regularization for Out-of-Distribution Prediction

abstract: We present X-MDPT ($\underline{Cross}$-view $\underline{M}$asked $\underline{D}$iffusion $\underline{P}$rediction $\underline{T}$ransformers), a novel diffusion model designed for pose-guided human image generation. X-MDPT distinguishes itself by employing masked diffusion transformers that operate on latent patches, a departure from the commonly-used Unet structures in existing works. The model comprises three key modules: 1) a denoising diffusion Transformer, 2) an aggregation network that consolidates conditions into a single vector for the diffusion process, and 3) a mask cross-prediction module that enhances representation learning with semantic information from the reference image. X-MDPT demonstrates scalability, improving FID, SSIM, and LPIPS with larger models. Despite its simple design, our model outperforms state-of-the-art approaches on the DeepFashion dataset while exhibiting efficiency in terms of training parameters, training time, and inference speed. Our compact 33MB model achieves an FID of 7.42, surpassing a prior Unet latent diffusion approach (FID 8.07) using only $11\times$ fewer parameters. Our best model surpasses the pixel-based diffusion with $\frac{2}{3}$ of the parameters and achieves $5.43 \times$ faster inference. The code is available at https://github.com/trungpx/xmdpt.
