Our compact 33MB model achieves an FID of 7.42, surpassing a prior Unet latent diffusion approach (FID 8.07) using only $11\times$ fewer parameters. Our best model surpasses the pixel-based diffusion with $\frac{2}{3}$ of the parameters and achieves $5.43 \times$ faster inference. The code is available at https://github.com/trungpx/xmdpt.

paragraphs: X-MDPT generates person images guided by a target pose and information from a reference image. It uses a masked diffusion transformer operating on latent patches, replacing the commonly used U-Net architecture. Working with these patches provides the foundation for a model whose image quality improves as its size increases in the reported evaluations.

The design combines three components. A diffusion transformer performs denoising, an aggregation network combines conditioning information into one vector, and a masked cross-prediction module strengthens representations using semantic information from the reference image. Together, these components connect the generation process with the conditions specifying the desired person image.

On DeepFashion, the authors report state-of-the-art performance and efficiency gains. Their compact 33 MB model achieves FID 7.42 versus 8.07 for a prior latent U-Net diffusion approach, using one-eleventh as many parameters. Their best model also surpasses a pixel-based diffusion approach with two-thirds as many parameters and 5.43 times faster inference. Larger variants improve FID, SSIM, and LPIPS.
summary.tldr: X-MDPT uses masked diffusion transformers to improve pose-guided person generation, with reported gains in image quality and efficiency on DeepFashion.

title: Cross-view Masked Diffusion Transformers for Person Image Synthesis

abstract: Cross-domain offline reinforcement learning leverages source domain data with diverse transition dynamics to alleviate the data requirement for the target domain. However, simply merging the data of two domains leads to performance degradation due to the dynamics mismatch. Existing methods address this problem by measuring the dynamics gap via domain classifiers while relying on the assumptions of the transferability of paired domains. In this paper, we propose a novel representation-based approach to measure the domain gap, where the representation is learned through a contrastive objective by sampling transitions from different domains. We show that such an objective recovers the mutual-information gap of transition functions in two domains without suffering from the unbounded issue of the dynamics gap in handling significantly different domains. Based on the representations, we introduce a data filtering algorithm that selectively shares transitions from the source domain according to the contrastive score functions. Empirical results on various tasks demonstrate that our method achieves superior performance, using only 10% of the target data to achieve 89.2% of the performance on 100% target dataset with state-of-the-art methods.

paragraphs: Cross-domain offline reinforcement learning tries to reduce the target domain’s data needs by reusing previously collected source data. The difficulty is that the same actions can produce different transitions in different domains. Simply combining the datasets can therefore hurt performance, making the choice of which source transitions to share important.

The paper learns representations through a contrastive objective built from transitions sampled across domains. The authors show that this objective recovers a mutual-information gap between the domains’ transition functions. Their formulation avoids an unbounded-gap issue that arises when handling substantially different domains. The learned contrastive scores then guide a filtering algorithm that selectively transfers source transitions.

Experiments across several tasks support the value of selecting data through these representations. With only 10% of the target data, the method reaches 89.2% of the performance obtained by state-of-the-art methods using the full target dataset. This result indicates that carefully filtered source experience can substantially reduce target-data requirements in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: Contrastively learned transition representations help filter source data, reducing target-data needs in cross-domain offline reinforcement learning.

title: Contrastive Representation for Data Filtering in Cross-Domain Offline Reinforcement Learning

abstract: We address the convergence problem in learning the Optimal Transport (OT) map, where the OT Map refers to a map from one distribution to another while minimizing the transport cost. Semi-dual Neural OT, a widely used approach for learning OT Maps with neural networks, often generates spurious solutions that fail to transfer one distribution to another accurately. We identify a sufficient condition under which the max-min solution of Semi-dual Neural OT recovers the true OT Map. Moreover, to address cases when this sufficient condition is not satisfied, we propose a novel method, OTP, which learns both the OT Map and the Optimal Transport Plan, representing the optimal coupling between two distributions. Under sharp assumptions on the distributions, we prove that our model eliminates the spurious solution issue and correctly solves the OT problem. Our experiments show that the OTP model recovers the optimal transport map where existing methods fail and outperforms current OT-based models in image-to-image translation tasks. Notably, the OTP model can learn stochastic transport maps when deterministic OT Maps do not exist, such as one-to-many tasks like colorization.

paragraphs: Optimal transport seeks to move one distribution to another while minimizing transport cost. Neural methods based on a semi-dual formulation can produce spurious solutions: their learned maps fail to transfer the source distribution accurately. The paper investigates when this formulation recovers the intended transport map.

The authors establish a sufficient condition for its max-min solution to recover the true map. They also propose OTP for cases where that condition is not satisfied. OTP learns both a transport map and a transport plan, which describes the coupling between the distributions. Under stated sharp assumptions on the distributions, they prove that it avoids spurious solutions and solves the transport problem correctly.

OTP can also learn stochastic transport maps when deterministic optimal maps do not exist, including one-to-many tasks such as colorization. This extends the method’s relevance to problems where a single fixed output for each input cannot express the required transport.
summary.tldr: OTP learns transport maps and plans to address spurious neural optimal-transport solutions, with guarantees under distributional assumptions.

title: Overcoming Spurious Solutions in Semi-Dual Neural Optimal Transport: A Smoothing Approach for Learning the Optimal Transport Plan

abstract: Stability is a central property in learning and statistics promising the output of an algorithm $\mathcal{A}$ does not change substantially when applied to similar datasets $S$ and $S’$. It is an elementary fact that any sufficiently stable algorithm (e.g. one returning the same result with high probability, satisfying privacy guarantees, etc.) must be randomized. This raises a natural question: can we quantify how much randomness is needed for algorithmic stability? We study the randomness complexity of two influential notions of stability in learning: replicability (which promises $\mathcal{A}$ usually outputs the same result when run over samples from the same distribution), and differential privacy (which promises the output distribution of $\mathcal{A}$ remains similar under neighboring datasets). In particular, building on the ideas of (Dixon, Pavan, Vander Woude, and Vinodchandran ICML 2024) and (Cannone, Su, and Vadhan ITCS 2024), we prove a "weak-to-strong" boosting theorem for stability in these settings: the randomness complexity of a task $\mathcal{M}$ is tightly controlled by the best replication probability of any deterministic algorithm solving $\mathcal{M}$, a parameter known as $\mathcal{M}$’s "global stability" (Chase, Moran, Yehudayoff FOCS 2023). Finally, we use this connection to characterize the randomness complexity of PAC Learning: a class has bounded randomness complexity iff it has finite Littlestone dimension, and moreover scales at worst logarithmically in the excess error of the learner. As a corollary, we resolve a question of (Chase, Chornomaz, Moran, and Yehudayoff STOC 2024) about the error-dependent list-replicability of agnostic learning.

paragraphs: This paper asks how much randomness a learning algorithm needs to behave stably across related datasets. It examines replicability, where repeated sampling from the same distribution usually yields the same answer, and differential privacy, where changing a neighboring dataset only modestly changes the output distribution. The focus is the randomness needed to achieve these properties.

The authors prove a weak-to-strong boosting theorem connecting randomness complexity to global stability. Here, global stability measures the best replication probability attainable by a deterministic algorithm solving the task. This gives a bridge between the repeatability already achievable without randomization and the randomness needed for stronger stability guarantees.

Applying the connection to PAC learning, the paper characterizes bounded randomness complexity exactly through finite Littlestone dimension. It also establishes at-worst logarithmic scaling with the learner's excess-error requirement and resolves a question about error-dependent list-replicability in agnostic learning. Together, these results turn randomness from a general ingredient of stable learning into a resource whose required amount can be characterized through properties of the learning task.
summary.tldr: The paper characterizes the randomness needed for stable learning through deterministic global stability and Littlestone dimension.

title: The Role of Randomness in Stability

abstract: Estimating optimal transport maps between two distributions from respective samples is an important element for many machine learning methods. To do so, rather than extending discrete transport maps, it has been shown that estimating the Brenier potential of the transport problem and obtaining a transport map through its gradient is near minimax optimal for smooth problems. In this paper, we investigate the private estimation of such potentials and transport maps with respect to the distribution samples. We propose a differentially private transport map estimator with $L^2$ error at most $n^{-1} \vee n^{-\frac{2 \alpha}{2 \alpha - 2 + d}} \vee (n\epsilon)^{-\frac{2 \alpha}{2 \alpha + d}} $ up do polylog terms where $n$ is the sample size, $\epsilon$ is the desired level of privacy, $\alpha$ is the smoothness of the true transport map, and $d$ is the dimension of the feature space. We also provide a lower bound for the problem.

paragraphs: An optimal transport map describes how to move one distribution into another. Estimating such a map from samples is useful in machine learning, but the samples may require privacy protection. This paper studies private estimation for smooth transport problems through the Brenier potential, a function whose gradient supplies the transport map.

The authors propose a differentially private estimator and bound its L² error. Up to polylogarithmic factors, the bound is the largest of n^(-1), n^(-2α/(2α−2+d)), and (nε)^(-2α/(2α+d)). The parameters describe sample size n, privacy level ε, true-map smoothness α, and feature dimension d. Writing the bound as a maximum makes explicit that different terms can dominate in different settings.

The privacy-dependent term quantifies how the privacy requirement enters the estimation guarantee alongside sample size, smoothness, and dimension. The paper also provides a lower bound for the problem. Together, these results give an achievable error guarantee and a constraint on what private estimation can accomplish, extending the potential-based approach to a setting where distribution samples must be protected.
summary.tldr: A differentially private estimator for smooth transport maps comes with an error bound linking privacy, sample size, smoothness, and dimension.

title: On the Private Estimation of Smooth Transport Maps

abstract: Solving various types of vehicle routing problems (VRPs) using a unified neural solver has garnered significant attentions in recent years. Despite their effectiveness, existing neural multi-task solvers often fail to account for the geometric structures inherent in different tasks, which may result in suboptimal performance. To address this limitation, we propose a curvature-aware pre-training framework. Specifically, we leverage mixed-curvature spaces during the feature fusion stage, encouraging the model to capture the underlying geometric properties of each instance. Through extensive experiments, we evaluate the proposed pre-training strategy on existing neural multi-task solvers across a variety of testing scenarios. The results demonstrate that the curvature-aware pre-training approach not only enhances the generalization capabilities of existing neural VRP solvers on synthetic datasets but also improves solution quality on real-world benchmarks.

paragraphs: A unified neural vehicle-routing solver must handle several kinds of routing problems using one model. The paper identifies a possible weakness in existing approaches: different tasks can have different underlying geometric structures, yet their representations may not account for those differences. Ignoring that structure can lead to poorer solutions even when the solver works across multiple tasks.

The authors propose curvature-aware pre-training, introducing mixed-curvature spaces at the stage where features are combined. Rather than treating all instances as having the same geometry, this representation encourages the model to capture geometric properties associated with each instance. The contribution is a pre-training strategy evaluated with existing multi-task solvers.

Experiments cover multiple testing scenarios and report better generalization on synthetic datasets, alongside improved solution quality on real-world benchmarks. These findings suggest that geometry-aware representations can benefit both transfer across generated routing instances and performance on practical routing data. The stated result concerns improvements to existing solvers through pre-training, with the feature-fusion stage providing the central mechanism.
summary.tldr: Curvature-aware pre-training improves multi-task vehicle-routing solvers by incorporating instance geometry when combining features.

title: A Mixed-Curvature based Pre-training Paradigm for Multi-Task Vehicle Routing Solver

abstract: Unsupervised Graph Domain Adaptation (UGDA) leverages labeled source domain graphs to achieve effective performance in unlabeled target domains despite distribution shifts. However, existing methods often yield suboptimal results due to the entanglement of causal-spurious features and the failure of global alignment strategies. We propose SLOGAN (Sparse Causal Discovery with Generative Intervention), a novel approach that achieves stable graph representation transfer through sparse causal modeling and dynamic intervention mechanisms. Specifically, SLOGAN first constructs a sparse causal graph structure, leveraging mutual information bottleneck constraints to disentangle sparse, stable causal features while compressing domain-dependent spurious correlations through variational inference. To address residual spurious correlations, we innovatively design a generative intervention mechanism that breaks local spurious couplings through cross-domain feature recombination while maintaining causal feature semantic consistency via covariance constraints. Furthermore, to mitigate error accumulation in target domain pseudo-labels, we introduce a category-adaptive dynamic calibration strategy, ensuring stable discriminative learning. Extensive experiments on multiple real-world datasets demonstrate that SLOGAN significantly outperforms existing baselines.

paragraphs: Unsupervised graph domain adaptation uses labeled graphs from one domain to make predictions in another domain without target labels. SLOGAN addresses the difficulty of separating useful, stable features from correlations that depend on the source domain. The paper also identifies shortcomings in global alignment strategies when transferring graph representations across distribution shifts.

The method first builds a sparse causal graph. Mutual-information bottleneck constraints and variational inference aim to isolate stable causal features while compressing domain-dependent correlations. It then recombines features across domains through a generative intervention mechanism to break remaining local spurious couplings. Covariance constraints preserve the semantic consistency of causal features during this process.

SLOGAN also introduces category-adaptive dynamic calibration to reduce the accumulation of errors in target-domain pseudo-labels. This addresses the supervision used during adaptation alongside the representation being transferred. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets report significant improvements over existing baselines. The findings support combining sparse causal modeling, feature interventions, and calibrated pseudo-labels for more stable graph transfer in the evaluated settings.
summary.tldr: SLOGAN combines sparse causal modeling, cross-domain feature interventions, and pseudo-label calibration to improve unsupervised graph transfer.

title: Sparse Causal Discovery with Generative Intervention for Unsupervised Graph Domain Adaptation

abstract: Pseudo-labeling is a widely used strategy in semi-supervised learning. Existing methods typically select predicted labels with high confidence scores and high training stationarity, as pseudo-labels to augment training sets. In contrast, this paper explores the pseudo-labeling potential of predicted labels that do not exhibit these characteristics. We discover a new type of predicted labels suitable for pseudo-labeling, termed two-phase labels, which exhibit a two-phase pattern during training: they are initially predicted as one category in early training stages and switch to another category in subsequent epochs. Case studies show the two-phase labels are informative for decision boundaries. To effectively identify the two-phase labels, we design a 2-phasic metric that mathematically characterizes their spatial and temporal patterns. Furthermore, we propose a loss function tailored for two-phase pseudo-labeling learning, allowing models not only to learn correct correlations but also to eliminate false ones. Extensive experiments on eight datasets show that our proposed 2-phasic metric acts as a powerful booster for existing pseudo-labeling methods by additionally incorporating the two-phase labels, achieving an average classification accuracy gain of 1.73% on image datasets and 1.92% on graph datasets.

paragraphs: Pseudo-labeling expands training data using a model’s own predictions. Common approaches favor predictions that are confident and stable during training. This paper studies a different pattern: examples initially assigned to one category that switch to another in later epochs. The authors call these two-phase labels and investigate their value as additional supervision.

Case studies indicate that these changing predictions contain information about decision boundaries. To identify them, the authors develop a 2-phasic metric that characterizes their spatial and temporal patterns. They also introduce a loss tailored to learning from these labels, allowing the model to reinforce correct correlations and eliminate false ones.

The reported average classification accuracy gains are 1.73% on image datasets and 1.92% on graph datasets. It does not require assuming that every unstable prediction is informative; the contribution centers on identifying and learning from this particular two-phase pattern.
summary.tldr: Predictions that switch categories in a two-phase training pattern can supply useful pseudo-labels and improve existing methods.

title: Non-Stationary Predictions May Be More Informative: Exploring Pseudo-Labels with a Two-Phase Pattern of Training Dynamics

abstract: Language model pretraining involves training on extensive corpora, where data quality plays a pivotal role. In this work, we aim to directly estimate the contribution of data during pretraining and select pretraining data in an efficient manner. Specifically, we draw inspiration from recent findings showing that compression efficiency (i.e., normalized loss) of diverse models on certain text correlates strongly with their downstream performance, when the text domain aligns with the downstream benchmarks (Huang et al., 2024). Building on this observation, we hypothesize that data on which model losses are predictive of downstream abilities also contribute effectively to learning, which shares similar intuition with Thrush et al. (2024). To leverage this insight, we introduce predictive data selection (PreSelect), a lightweight and efficient data selection method that requires training and deploying only a fastText-based scorer. Through comprehensive experiments with 1B and 3B parameter models, we demonstrate that models trained on 30B tokens selected with PreSelect surpass the performance of the vanilla baseline trained on 300B tokens, achieving a 10x reduction in compute requirements. Furthermore, PreSelect significantly outperforms other competitive data selection baselines, such as DCLM and FineWeb-Edu on a scale of 3B models trained on 100B tokens. We open-source our trained data selection scorer along with the curated datasets at https://github.com/hkust-nlp/PreSelect.

The authors hypothesize that text whose losses predict downstream abilities will also make effective training material.

This connects data evaluation to data selection: evidence that a text sample distinguishes stronger models becomes a signal for whether to include it in training. The approach aims to estimate useful contributions without making selection itself an expensive modeling task.

summary.tldr: PreSelect uses a lightweight scorer to select training text, outperforming a baseline using ten times as many tokens in reported experiments.

title: Predictive Data Selection: The Data That Predicts Is the Data That Teaches

abstract: Inspired by the impressive capabilities of GPT-4o, there is growing interest in enabling speech language models (SLMs) to engage in natural, fluid spoken interactions with humans. Recent advancements have led to the development of several SLMs that demonstrate promising results in this area. However, current approaches have yet to fully exploit dual-channel speech data, which inherently captures the structure and dynamics of human conversation. In this work, we systematically explore the use of dual-channel speech data in the context of modern large language models, and introduce a novel generative modeling paradigm—Next-Token-Pair Prediction (NTPP)—to enable speaker-independent dual-channel spoken dialogue learning using decoder-only architectures for the first time. We evaluate our approach on standard benchmarks, and empirical results show that our proposed method, NTPP, significantly improves the conversational abilities of SLMs in terms of turn-taking prediction, response coherence, and naturalness. Moreover, compared to existing methods, NTPP achieves substantially lower inference latency, highlighting its practical efficiency for real-time applications. Demo and code can be found at https://audio-3059.pages.dev.

paragraphs: Natural spoken dialogue depends on more than generating a suitable verbal response. A model must also capture conversational dynamics, including when speakers take turns. This paper studies dual-channel speech data, which preserves the structure of a conversation across two channels, as a resource for learning more fluid spoken interactions.

The authors introduce Next-Token-Pair Prediction, or NTPP, as a generative modeling approach for speaker-independent dual-channel dialogue. It uses a decoder-only architecture and makes paired-token prediction central to learning from the two channels. The approach is intended to make fuller use of the conversational structure already present in dual-channel recordings.

On standard benchmarks, NTPP improves turn-taking prediction, response coherence, and naturalness relative to existing approaches. It also achieves substantially lower inference latency in the reported comparisons. These findings connect the modeling choice to both conversational behavior and practical response speed: exploiting the two-channel structure helps the model learn how dialogue unfolds while supporting the low delays needed for real-time spoken interaction.
summary.tldr: NTPP learns dual-channel spoken dialogue through paired-token prediction, improving conversational behavior and reducing inference latency in reported evaluations.

title: NTPP: Generative Speech Language Modeling for Dual-Channel Spoken Dialogue via Next-Token-Pair Prediction

abstract: In recent years there have been remarkable breakthroughs in image-to-video generation. However, the 3D consistency and camera controllability of generated frames have remained unsolved. Recent studies have attempted to incorporate camera control into the generation process, but their results are often limited to simple trajectories or lack the ability to generate consistent videos from multiple distinct camera paths for the same scene. To address these limitations, we introduce Cavia, a novel framework for camera-controllable, multi-view video generation, capable of converting an input image into multiple spatiotemporally consistent videos. Our framework extends the spatial and temporal attention modules into view-integrated attention modules, improving both viewpoint and temporal consistency. This flexible design allows for joint training with diverse curated data sources, including scene-level static videos, object-level synthetic multi-view dynamic videos, and real-world monocular dynamic videos. To the best of our knowledge, Cavia is the first framework that enables users to generate multiple videos of the same scene with precise control over camera motion, while simultaneously preserving object motion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Cavia surpasses state-of-the-art methods in terms of geometric consistency and perceptual quality.

To the best of our knowledge, Cavia is the first framework that enables users to generate multiple videos of the same scene with precise control over camera motion, while simultaneously preserving object motion. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Cavia surpasses state-of-the-art methods in terms of geometric consistency and perceptual quality.

paragraphs: Cavia addresses a demanding version of image-to-video generation: producing several videos of the same scene, each following a different camera path. The outputs need to agree about both scene geometry and motion over time. Previous camera-control approaches described in the abstract often support only simple trajectories or struggle to maintain agreement across separate views.

The framework extends spatial and temporal attention so that these mechanisms also integrate information across views. This allows generation to account for relationships between camera viewpoints alongside relationships between successive frames. Its design supports joint training on several complementary sources: static scene videos, synthetic dynamic objects shown from multiple views, and real dynamic videos recorded from a single viewpoint.

The authors report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in geometric consistency and perceptual quality. Cavia also enables control over camera movement while preserving object motion. The practical significance is coordinated generation: the multiple outputs are intended to depict the same evolving scene under different camera movements.
summary.tldr: Cavia uses attention across views and time to generate consistent videos from one image under multiple controlled camera paths.

title: Cavia: Camera-controllable Multi-view Video Diffusion with View-Integrated Attention

abstract: Ensemble clustering has demonstrated great success in practice; however, its theoretical foundations remain underexplored. This paper examines the generalization performance of ensemble clustering, focusing on generalization error, excess risk and consistency. We derive a convergence rate of generalization error bound and excess risk bound both of $\mathcal{O}(\sqrt{\frac{\log n}{m}}+\frac{1}{\sqrt{n}})$, with $n$ and $m$ being the numbers of samples and base clusterings. Based on this, we prove that when $m$ and $n$ approach infinity and $m$ is significantly larger than log $n$, i.e., $m,n\to \infty, m\gg \log n$, ensemble clustering is consistent. Furthermore, recognizing that $n$ and $m$ are finite in practice, the generalization error cannot be reduced to zero. Thus, by assigning varying weights to finite clusterings, we minimize the error between the empirical average clusterings and their expectation. From this, we theoretically demonstrate that to achieve better clustering performance, we should minimize the deviation (bias) of base clustering from its expectation and maximize the differences (diversity) among various base clusterings. Additionally, we derive that maximizing diversity is nearly equivalent to a robust (min-max) optimization model. Finally, we instantiate our theory to develop a new ensemble clustering algorithm. Compared with SOTA methods, our approach achieves average improvements of 6.0%, 7.3%, and 6.0% on 10 datasets w.r.t. NMI, ARI, and Purity. The code is available at https://github.com/xuz2019/GPEC.

title: Generalization Performance of Ensemble Clustering: From Theory to Algorithm

abstract: In generative modeling, tokenization simplifies complex data into compact, structured representations, creating a more efficient, learnable space. For high-dimensional visual data, it reduces redundancy and emphasizes key features for high-quality generation. Current visual tokenization methods rely on a traditional autoencoder framework, where the encoder compresses data into latent representations, and the decoder reconstructs the original input. In this work, we offer a new perspective by proposing denoising as decoding, shifting from single-step reconstruction to iterative refinement. Specifically, we replace the decoder with a diffusion process that iteratively refines noise to recover the original image, guided by the latents provided by the encoder. We evaluate our approach by assessing both reconstruction (rFID) and generation quality (FID), comparing it to state-of-the-art autoencoding approaches. By adopting iterative reconstruction through diffusion, our autoencoder, namely Epsilon-VAE, achieves high reconstruction quality, which in turn enhances downstream generation quality by 22% at the same compression rates or provides 2.3x inference speedup through increasing compression rates. We hope this work offers new insights into integrating iterative generation and autoencoding for improved compression and generation.

A conventional autoencoder learns an encoder for compression and a decoder that reconstructs an image in one step. Epsilon-VAE changes the reconstruction stage by treating decoding as an iterative denoising problem.

Its encoder still supplies a compressed latent representation, but a diffusion process replaces the conventional decoder. Starting from noise, this process repeatedly refines an image under guidance from the encoded information. This connects the compressed representation to a sequence of reconstruction steps, giving the decoder an iterative route to recover the original visual content.

It reports a 22% improvement in downstream generation quality at the same compression rates, or a 2.3-fold inference speedup when increasing compression. These are two reported ways of using the approach's improved reconstruction capability. The findings show that changing how compressed information is decoded can affect both the quality and efficiency of the wider generation pipeline.
summary.tldr: Epsilon-VAE uses diffusion-based iterative decoding to improve visual reconstruction and downstream generation or enable faster inference through greater compression.

title: Epsilon-VAE: Denoising as Visual Decoding

abstract: We study a class of iterated empirical risk minimization (ERM) procedures in which two successive ERMs are performed on the same dataset, and the predictions of the first estimator enter as an argument in the loss function of the second. This setting, which arises naturally in active learning and reweighting schemes, introduces intricate statistical dependencies across samples and fundamentally distinguishes the problem from classical single-stage ERM analyses. For linear models trained with a broad class of convex losses on Gaussian mixture data, we derive a sharp asymptotic characterization of the test error in the high-dimensional regime where the sample size and ambient dimension scale proportionally. Our results provide explicit, fully asymptotic predictions for the performance of the second-stage estimator despite the reuse of data and the presence of prediction-dependent losses. We apply this theory to revisit a well-studied pool-based active learning problem, removing oracle and sample-splitting assumptions made in prior work. We uncover a fundamental tradeoff in how the labeling budget should be allocated across stages, and demonstrate a double-descent behavior of the test error driven purely by data selection, rather than model size or sample count.

paragraphs: Some learning procedures fit a model and then use its predictions to guide a second fit on the same dataset. This happens in active learning and data reweighting. Reusing examples creates statistical dependencies: the second training objective already reflects information learned from those examples, so ordinary analyses of a single training stage do not directly apply.

The paper develops a precise asymptotic description of the second model’s test error for linear models with a broad family of convex losses on Gaussian mixture data. Its setting lets the number of examples and the number of features grow proportionally. Within that regime, the theory explicitly accounts for both data reuse and losses that depend on the first model’s predictions.

Applied to pool-based active learning, the analysis removes earlier assumptions requiring oracle information or separate data splits. It reveals a tradeoff in distributing a labeling budget between stages. It also identifies double descent caused solely by which data are selected, showing that this error pattern can arise without changing model size or sample count.
summary.tldr: A high-dimensional theory explains two-stage learning with reused data and reveals how active data selection alone can produce double descent.

title: Asymptotic Theory of Iterated Empirical Risk Minimization, with Applications to Active Learning

abstract: Slice sampling is a standard Monte Carlo technique for Dirichlet process (DP)-based models, widely used in posterior simulation. However, formal assessments of the scalability of posterior slice samplers have remained largely unexplored, primarily because the computational cost of a slice-sampling iteration is random and potentially unbounded. In this work, we obtain high-probability bounds on the computational complexity of DP slice samplers. Our main results show that, uniformly across posterior cluster-growth regimes, the overhead induced by slice variables, relatively to the number of clusters supported by the posterior, is $O_{\mathbb P}(\log n)$. As a consequence, even in worst-case configurations, superlinear blow-ups in per-iteration computational cost occur with vanishing probability. Our analysis applies broadly to DP–based models without any likelihood-specific assumptions, still providing complexity guarantees for posterior sampling on arbitrary datasets. These results establish a theoretical foundation for assessing the practical scalability of slice sampling in DP-based models.

paragraphs: Slice sampling is widely used to draw posterior samples from Dirichlet process models, but its computational demands are difficult to characterize. The amount of work in an iteration is random and can, in principle, be unbounded. This paper develops probability-based complexity guarantees to explain how that cost scales.

The central result concerns extra work introduced by slice variables relative to the number of clusters supported by the posterior. Across different posterior cluster-growth regimes, this overhead is logarithmic in the dataset size in a probabilistic sense. The result controls the likelihood of large costs; it does not impose a fixed deterministic ceiling on every iteration.

The analysis implies that superlinear per-iteration cost blow-ups become vanishingly unlikely, even in worst-case configurations. It applies broadly to Dirichlet process models without assumptions tailored to a particular likelihood, and provides guarantees for arbitrary datasets. This supplies a theoretical basis for judging practical scalability despite the sampler’s potentially unbounded iteration cost.
summary.tldr: The paper gives probabilistic complexity bounds showing that excessive per-iteration costs become unlikely for Dirichlet process slice samplers.

title: Complexity Bounds for Dirichlet Process Slice Samplers

abstract: Video action models are a promising foundation for Vision–Language–Action (VLA) because they can learn rich visual dynamics directly from video. However, likelihood-oriented training of diffusion predictors emphasizes globally plausible futures and does not guarantee precision-critical visual dynamics needed for manipulation, so small prediction errors can be amplified by downstream policies. We propose Dyn-VPP, a post-training framework that casts multi-step denoising as policy optimization and aligns predicted future latents with expert visual dynamics via verifiable terminal reward, without modifying any architecture. This enables explicit optimization of dynamics signals that are not captured by likelihood-only training. As a result, Dyn-VPP yields more accurate visual dynamics and improves downstream task execution. Experiments across diverse simulated and real-world manipulation settings show improved dynamics consistency and consistently higher task success.

paragraphs: Video predictors can provide useful dynamics knowledge for systems that connect vision, language, and action. Yet predicting a broadly plausible future does not necessarily capture the precise changes needed for manipulation. Small visual prediction errors can be amplified when a downstream policy uses those predictions to choose actions.

Dyn-VPP addresses this through post-training of diffusion predictors. It treats the sequence of denoising steps as a policy to optimize and uses a verifiable terminal reward to align predicted future latent representations with expert visual dynamics. The method leaves the architecture unchanged while explicitly training for dynamics signals that likelihood-oriented learning may miss.

Experiments in varied simulated and real-world manipulation settings show improved consistency of visual dynamics and consistently higher task success. These results connect better future prediction with better execution by the downstream system. The paper's contribution is therefore a way to refine an existing predictor around the particular aspects of motion that matter for action, rather than relying on overall future plausibility alone.
summary.tldr: Dyn-VPP post-trains diffusion video predictors with policy optimization to improve manipulation-relevant dynamics and downstream task success.

title: Dyn-VPP: Video Prediction Policy Optimization for Improved Visual Dynamics

abstract: Protein mutation effect prediction is fundamental to protein engineering and disease variant interpretation, yet experimentally measured mutation data remain accurate but extremely sparse. To provide scalable supplementary mutation signals, we construct a PDB-wide mutation augmentation dataset that exhaustively enumerates single-site substitutions on experimentally resolved protein structures and aligns mutation signals from physics-based energy models, protein language models, and inverse folding models. Large-scale analysis under a unified mutation preference representation reveals substantial differences in the consistency, concentration, and substitution patterns of mutation distributions across models, indicating that disagreement is pervasive and reflects conflicting inductive biases rather than random noise. Motivated by these observations, we propose an unsupervised multi-source mutation preference distillation framework that learns from relative mutation preferences while explicitly modeling cross-source disagreement. Without using any experimental mutation labels during training, our approach achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated zero-shot baselines and naive multi-source fusion strategies on ProteinGym. We release the dataset and evaluation pipeline to support reproducible studies of protein mutation effects.

paragraphs: MutAtlas addresses the scarcity of experimentally measured protein mutation effects by building a large supplementary dataset. It enumerates single-site substitutions on experimentally resolved protein structures across the PDB and aligns signals from physics-based energy models, protein language models, and inverse folding models. These sources provide different perspectives on which mutations are preferred.

A unified representation lets the authors compare those preferences directly. They find substantial differences in agreement, concentration, and substitution patterns across models. Their analysis interprets this disagreement as pervasive and connected to conflicting modeling biases, rather than simply random noise. That finding motivates a learning method that explicitly represents disagreement between sources.

The resulting unsupervised distillation framework learns relative mutation preferences without experimental mutation labels during training. On ProteinGym, it achieves the best overall performance among the evaluated zero-shot baselines and naive multi-source fusion strategies. The result supports combining sources while accounting for their conflicts. The released dataset and evaluation pipeline also provide a basis for reproducible mutation-effect research.
summary.tldr: MutAtlas combines large-scale mutation signals through unsupervised distillation that explicitly models disagreement among protein prediction methods.

title: MutAtlas: A PDB-Wide Energy-Guided Atlas of Protein Mutation Effects

abstract: Multimodal systems encounter partial observability from sensor dropout and degradation, yet adverse tails can remain unreliable even when average performance is preserved. Under a locked same-support contract, matched-average runs can exhibit same-support tail failure, diverging on worst-case and shift-reweighted metrics over the same observable support. The failure arises because conditional interaction separates environment coverage from parameter exposure. Gated routing sends information through different groups, so high-leverage groups may receive few updates despite complete coverage, and tail aggregation amplifies their errors. We audit this mismatch with TailPressure, an exposure-normalized statistic of tail-leveraged interaction from gating logs. We propose Heterogeneity-aware Closed-loop Exposure Stabilizer (H-CES), a lightweight controller that stabilizes per-group pressure via deterministic increment-branch gating and group-wise decoupled weight decay, without changing loss or inference. Across multimodal settings and backbones, H-CES improves same-support tail reliability while preserving clean performance.

paragraphs: This paper examines why multimodal systems can preserve average performance yet remain unreliable on adverse cases when sensors drop out or degrade. Its comparison holds observable support fixed: the failures occur over the same observable possibilities, even between runs with matched averages. The explanation separates seeing relevant environments from adequately updating the parameters responsible for handling them.

Gated routing directs information through different parameter groups. Some groups can strongly influence tail outcomes while receiving relatively few updates, despite complete environment coverage. Tail-focused evaluation then magnifies their errors. The authors introduce TailPressure, a statistic derived from gating logs that measures tail-relevant interaction relative to parameter exposure, making this mismatch auditable.

Their H-CES controller stabilizes pressure across groups using deterministic increment-branch gating and independently managed group-wise weight decay. It leaves the loss and inference procedure unchanged. Across the reported multimodal settings and backbones, it improves reliability on same-support tails while preserving clean performance. The findings identify training exposure as a practical control point when average accuracy and environment coverage alone conceal uneven reliability.
summary.tldr: H-CES improves multimodal tail reliability by auditing and stabilizing parameter-group exposure that average performance and environment coverage can conceal.

title: Coverage $\not =$ Exposure: Auditable Control of Same-Support Tail Failures under Multimodal Missingness

abstract: Structured State-Space Duality (SSD) [Dao & Gu, ICML 2024] is an equivalence between a simple Structured State-Space Model (SSM) and a masked attention mechanism. In particular, a state-space model with a scalar-times-identity state matrix is equivalent to a masked self-attention with a $1$-semiseparable causal mask. Consequently, the same sequence transformation (model) has two algorithmic realizations: as a linear-time $O(T)$ recurrence or as a quadratic-time $O(T^2)$ attention. In this note, we formalize and generalize this duality: (i) we extend SSD from the scalar-identity case to general diagonal SSMs (diagonal state matrices); (ii) we show that these diagonal SSMs match the scalar case’s training complexity lower bounds while supporting richer dynamics; (iii) we establish a necessary and sufficient condition under which an SSM is equivalent to $1$-semiseparable masked attention; and (iv) we show that such duality fails to extend to standard softmax attention due to rank explosion. Together, these results tighten the bridge between recurrent SSMs and Transformers, and widen the design space for expressive yet efficient sequence models. Code is available at https://github.com/MAGICS-LAB/state_space_daulity.

paragraphs: Structured state-space duality describes how the same sequence transformation can be implemented as either a recurrent state-space model or a particular masked attention mechanism. The established scalar-identity case offers a linear-time recurrence and a quadratic-time attention realization. This paper formalizes that relationship and investigates how far it extends.

The authors generalize the duality to state-space models with diagonal state matrices. These models support richer dynamics while matching the scalar case’s training-complexity lower bounds. The paper also establishes a necessary and sufficient condition for a state-space model to be equivalent to attention with the specified 1-semiseparable causal mask, making the boundary of that equivalence explicit.

The analysis additionally shows that the duality does not extend to standard softmax attention because of rank explosion. This is a concrete boundary on the connection between these model families. Together, the results broaden the class of state-space dynamics covered by the theory while clarifying which attention structures permit an equivalent recurrent realization.
summary.tldr: The paper extends state-space–attention duality to diagonal dynamics and precisely characterizes its applicability and failure for standard softmax attention.

title: On Structured State-Space Duality

abstract: Bayesian Optimization is widely used for expensive black-box optimization, yet its success often depends on choosing a kernel that matches the objective’s unknown structure. In this work, we propose ALAS, a flexible Gaussian Process kernel family built from symmetric $\alpha$-stable spectral components. By learning the stability parameter $\alpha$, ALAS adapts its effective smoothness from data, capturing both smooth trends and sharp irregularities. We present two parameterizations: ALAS, a single stationary component with joint spectral modulation, and ALAS-Sep, a separable variant that learns dimension-wise tail behavior to improve robustness on approximately decomposable objectives. Experiments on standard benchmarks and real-world surrogates demonstrate strong and robust performance across diverse settings.

By learning the stability parameter $\alpha$, ALAS adapts its effective smoothness from data, capturing both smooth trends and sharp irregularities. We present two parameterizations: ALAS, a single stationary component with joint spectral modulation, and ALAS-Sep, a separable variant that learns dimension-wise tail behavior to improve robustness on approximately decomposable objectives. Experiments on standard benchmarks and real-world surrogates demonstrate strong and robust performance across diverse settings.

paragraphs: Bayesian optimization searches for good settings when evaluating each candidate is expensive. Its success often depends on the kernel, which determines how a Gaussian process relates observations at different inputs. Choosing that kernel is difficult when the objective’s shape is unknown: a useful model may need to represent both gradual changes and sharp irregularities.

ALAS introduces a kernel family built from symmetric alpha-stable spectral components. Its central adjustment is to learn the stability parameter alpha from data, allowing the kernel’s effective smoothness to adapt. The paper presents two versions. ALAS uses one stationary component with joint spectral modulation, while ALAS-Sep learns separate tail behavior for individual dimensions.

The separable version is intended to improve robustness when the objective is approximately decomposable into contributions associated with different dimensions. Experiments on standard benchmarks and real-world surrogates report strong, robust performance across varied settings. The contribution is a way to make the kernel’s structural assumptions more adaptable during optimization, reducing dependence on a fixed smoothness choice made before observing the objective.
summary.tldr: ALAS learns the smoothness behavior of Gaussian process kernels to support Bayesian optimization across objectives with different structures.

title: ALAS: Additive Learnable Alpha-Stable Kernels for Flexible Bayesian Optimization

abstract: Diffusion (Large) Language Models (dLLMs) now match the downstream performance of their autoregressive counterparts on many tasks, while holding the promise of being more efficient during inference. One critical design aspect of dLLMs is the sampling procedure that selects which tokens to unmask at each diffusion step. Indeed, recent work has found that heuristic strategies such as confidence thresholding improve both sample quality and token throughput compared to random unmasking. However, such heuristics have downsides: they require manual tuning, and we observe that their performance degrades with larger block sizes. In this work, we instead propose to train sampling procedures using reinforcement learning. Specifically, we formalize masked diffusion sampling as a Markov decision process in which the dLLM serves as the environment, and propose a lightweight policy based on a single-layer transformer that maps dLLM token confidences to unmasking decisions. Our experiments show that these trained policies match the performance of state-of-the-art heuristics when combined with semi-autoregressive (block) generation, while outperforming them in the full-diffusion setting. Our code is available at https://github.com/apple/ml-rl-dllm.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models generate text by repeatedly deciding which masked tokens to reveal. This sampling procedure affects both output quality and token throughput. Confidence-based heuristics can improve on random unmasking, but they require manual tuning, and the authors observe that their performance worsens as generation blocks become larger.

The paper learns the unmasking procedure with reinforcement learning. It describes sampling as a Markov decision process, treating the diffusion language model as the environment. A lightweight controller consisting of a single transformer layer receives token confidence scores and decides which tokens to unmask. This makes the generation schedule itself a learned policy instead of a manually specified rule.

In experiments using semi-autoregressive block generation, the learned policies match state-of-the-art heuristics. In full-diffusion generation, they outperform those heuristics. The distinction matters: the reported advantage depends on the generation setting. The results show that a compact learned controller can successfully manage unmasking decisions, with particular benefits when generation uses the full-diffusion setting.
summary.tldr: Reinforcement learning trains compact unmasking controllers that match leading block-generation heuristics and outperform them in full-diffusion generation.

title: Learning Unmasking Policies for Diffusion Language Models

abstract: Higher-order structures are powerful relational modeling tools, yet existing spectral operators decompose topology into separate ranks, leaving practitioners to fuse information back to vertices through ad-hoc choices. We introduce Collapsed Effective Operators, which condense higher-order degrees of freedom into a single vertex-level operator via Schur complementation of a graded Laplacian. This yields a (generally dense) operator that encodes long-range interactions mediated by topology and is applicable to arbitrary higher-order constructs. title: Collapsed Effective Operators for Higher-order Structures

abstract: scRNA-seq clustering is a critical task for analyzing single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data, as it groups cells with similar gene expression profiles. Transformers, as powerful foundational models, have been applied to scRNA-seq clustering. Their self-attention mechanism automatically assigns higher attention weights to cells within the same cluster, enhancing the distinction between clusters. Existing methods for scRNA-seq clustering, such as graph transformer-based models, treat each cell as a token in a sequence. Their computational and space complexities are $\mathcal{O}(n^2)$ with respect to the number of cells, limiting their applicability to large-scale scRNA-seq datasets. To address this challenge, we propose a Bipartite Graph Transformer-based clustering model (BGFormer) for scRNA-seq data. We introduce a set of learnable anchor tokens as shared reference points to represent the entire dataset. A bipartite graph attention mechanism is introduced to learn the similarity between cells and anchor tokens, bringing cells of the same class closer together in the embedding space. BGFormer achieves linear computational complexity with respect to the number of cells, making it scalable to large datasets. Experimental results on multiple large-scale scRNA-seq datasets demonstrate the effectiveness and scalability of BGFormer.

paragraphs: Clustering single-cell RNA sequencing data groups cells with similar gene expression patterns. Transformer attention can help separate these groups by emphasizing relationships among similar cells. However, treating every cell as a token makes existing approaches expensive: their computation and memory requirements grow quadratically with the number of cells.

BGFormer introduces learnable anchor tokens that act as shared reference points for the dataset. Its bipartite attention mechanism learns relationships between cells and these anchors. This changes the structure of the comparison problem: cells relate to a common set of references, and the learned representation brings cells of the same class closer together.

Experiments on multiple large single-cell datasets support both its clustering effectiveness and scalability. The contribution combines a representation-learning mechanism with a computational redesign, allowing attention to help organize cell populations without retaining the quadratic computational growth of the described cell-token approaches.
summary.tldr: BGFormer uses shared learnable anchors to cluster single-cell data with computation that scales linearly with cell count.

title: Bipartite Graph Attention-based Clustering for Large-scale scRNA-seq Data

abstract: Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) achieve high-fidelity synthesis but suffer from latent space brittleness, causing discontinuous semantic jumps during editing. We introduce a Riemannian framework to diagnose this instability by analyzing the generative Jacobian, decomposing geometry into Local Scaling (capacity) and Local Complexity (curvature). Our study uncovers a "Geometric Decoupling": while curvature in normal generation functionally encodes image detail, Out-of-Distribution (OOD) generation exhibits a functional decoupling where extreme curvature is wasted on unstable semantic boundaries rather than perceptible details. This geometric misallocation identifies "Geometric Hotspots" as the structural root of instability, providing a robust intrinsic metric for diagnosing generative reliability. Our code is at https://github.com/Byronliang8/Diffusion-Geometry.

paragraphs: Editing a latent diffusion model's internal representation can produce abrupt changes in image meaning, even when the intended edit is small. This paper examines that brittleness through the geometry of the generative mapping. It asks how the local structure of latent space relates to useful image detail and unstable semantic changes.

The authors use a Riemannian framework based on the generative Jacobian, which describes local sensitivity of generated output to latent changes. They separate local scaling, interpreted as capacity, from local complexity, interpreted as curvature. In normal generation, curvature functionally represents image detail. In out-of-distribution generation, the study finds that extreme curvature can instead concentrate around unstable semantic boundaries.

The authors call this mismatch geometric decoupling: geometric complexity becomes disconnected from perceptible detail. They identify the resulting geometric hotspots as the structural source of instability and use them to motivate an intrinsic diagnostic metric for generative reliability. The contribution explains why high local complexity can correspond to useful detail in one setting and brittle editing behavior in another.
summary.tldr: A geometric analysis links latent diffusion instability to extreme curvature concentrated at semantic boundaries rather than visible image detail.

title: Geometric Decoupling: Diagnosing the Structural Instability of Latent

abstract: Tree-search decoding is an effective form of test-time scaling for large language models (LLMs), but real-world deployment often imposes a fixed per-query token budget that varies across settings. Existing tree-search policies are largely budget-agnostic, treating the budget merely as a termination condition, thereby risking late-stage over-branching or premature termination. We propose Budget-Guided MCTS (BG-MCTS), a tree-search decoding algorithm that aligns its search policy with the remaining token budget: it starts with broad exploration, then prioritizes refinement and answer completion as the remaining budget decreases while reducing late-stage branching from shallow nodes. BG-MCTS consistently outperforms budget-agnostic tree-search baselines across inference budgets on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and an additional physics reasoning benchmark with open-weight LLMs.

paragraphs: Tree-search decoding gives a language model additional opportunities to explore reasoning paths before producing an answer. In deployment, however, each query may have a fixed allowance of generated tokens. A search policy that ignores the remaining allowance can spend its final tokens opening new branches or stop before developing a useful answer.

Budget-Guided MCTS makes the remaining token budget part of the search policy itself. It initially explores broadly, then shifts toward refining existing paths and completing answers as the available tokens decrease. It also reduces late branching from shallow nodes, where starting another path can consume resources that could otherwise finish ongoing reasoning.

The authors evaluate this approach with open-weight language models on mathematical reasoning benchmarks and an additional physics benchmark. They report consistent improvements over budget-agnostic tree-search baselines across inference budgets. The result supports adapting how search spends computation throughout a query, rather than relying only on a stopping rule when the token allowance runs out.
summary.tldr: BG-MCTS improves reasoning search by shifting from exploration toward answer completion as its token budget runs down.

title: Aligning Tree-Search Policies with Fixed Token Budgets in Test-Time Scaling of LLMs

abstract: AI agents are increasingly deployed to execute important tasks. While rising accuracy scores on standard benchmarks suggest rapid progress, many agents still continue to fail in practice. This discrepancy highlights a major limitation of current evaluations: focusing on a single metric is not enough to understand agent behavior. Notably, it ignores whether agents behave consistently across runs, withstand perturbations, fail predictably, or have bounded error severity. Grounded in safety-critical engineering, we provide a holistic performance profile consisting of twelve metrics that decompose agent reliability along four key dimensions: consistency, robustness, predictability, and safety. Evaluating 15 models across two complementary benchmarks, we find that recent capability gains have only yielded small improvements in reliability. By exposing these persistent limitations, our metrics complement traditional evaluations while offering tools for reasoning about how agents perform, degrade, and fail.

paragraphs: An agent's average task score gives an incomplete picture of how dependably it behaves. An agent may vary across repeated runs, react poorly to small changes, or make errors with very different consequences. This paper develops an evaluation framework intended to expose those distinctions alongside conventional measures of task success.

Drawing on safety-critical engineering, the authors propose twelve metrics organized into consistency, robustness, predictability, and safety. Together, these dimensions examine repeatability, resistance to perturbations, the predictability of failures, and error severity. The result is a performance profile that makes several aspects of reliability visible instead of compressing them into one aggregate score.

The authors evaluate 15 models across two complementary benchmarks and find that recent capability gains correspond to only small reliability improvements. This finding helps explain why stronger benchmark performance can coexist with persistent practical failures. The proposed metrics provide tools for comparing how agents succeed, degrade, and fail, complementing accuracy with evidence about the behavior surrounding those outcomes.
summary.tldr: Twelve reliability metrics reveal that recent agent capability gains have brought only small reliability improvements across the evaluated models and benchmarks.

title: Towards a Science of AI Agent Reliability

abstract: Controlling spreading processes on networks, such as epidemics, information cascades, and product adoption, requires policies that perform on realistic stochastic dynamics, not just tractable approximations. Yet policies trained on standard simplifications (mean-field ODEs, Markovian dynamics) suffer severe performance degradation at deployment. We trace this sim-to-real gap to three theoretical pathologies: Optimism Bias, where deterministic approximations systematically underestimate variance via Jensen’s inequality; Hub Blindness, where global state aggregation obscures the super-spreaders driving scale-free networks; and the Valley of Death, where mean-value critics fail to navigate the bimodal nature (extinction vs. viral) of cascade outcomes. We resolve these challenges through two synergistic contributions. First, the Stratified Mean-Field Observer partitions nodes by influence tier, preserving hub dynamics at $O(N)$ cost while producing fixed-dimensional observations that enable zero-shot transfer across network scales and topologies. Second, we show that distributional RL via Truncated Quantile Critics improves risk-aware control of bimodal cascades. Trained on a GPU-accelerated simulator supporting non-Markovian renewal dynamics, our approach achieves $59\times$ improvement over Markovian baselines and robust zero-shot transfer to real-world social networks (Facebook, Twitter, YouTube), significantly mitigating the simulation-to-reality gap.

paragraphs: Policies for controlling network spread can perform poorly when realistic randomness replaces simplified training dynamics. The paper identifies three causes: deterministic approximations underrepresent variability, aggregated observations hide highly influential nodes, and critics that predict only average outcomes struggle with cascades that tend either to die out or become widespread.

The proposed observer groups nodes by influence level, retaining information about hubs while keeping computation linear in the number of nodes. Its observations have a fixed dimension, allowing the policy to transfer across network sizes and topologies. A second component uses distributional reinforcement learning with Truncated Quantile Critics to represent outcome variability and improve risk-aware decisions.

The authors report a 59-fold improvement over Markovian baselines and robust zero-shot transfer to Facebook, Twitter, and YouTube networks. Together, the findings support preserving influential-node structure and outcome distributions when learning policies for stochastic spreading processes.
summary.tldr: Influence-aware observations and distributional reinforcement learning improve control of stochastic network cascades and transfer across network settings.

title: Closing the Sim-to-Real Gap in Network Spreading Processes via GPU-Accelerated Distributional RL

abstract: Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models are bottlenecked by the scarcity of expert demonstrations—expensive triplets of observations, language instructions, and actions. We propose that learning ”how to move” can be decoupled from learning ”what to do,” and that the former requires no task labels at all. Our two-stage framework, Task-Agnostic Pretraining (TAP) first pre-trains on abundant, cheap task-agnostic data (discarded off-task trajectories or autonomous robot play) using an Inverse Dynamics objective that predicts actions from consecutive observations. This self-supervised phase instills physical affordances—grasping, contact dynamics, end-effector control—without human annotation. A lightweight second stage then aligns these physical priors with language instructions using minimal expert data. On the SIMPLER benchmark, our approach matches models trained on 1M+ expert trajectories while using orders of magnitude less labeled data, achieving a 10% absolute gain over standard behavior cloning. In real-world WidowX experiments, it surpasses internet-scale baselines under visual distribution shifts (e.g., 25% vs. 0% under camera perturbations), demonstrating that task-agnostic pretraining yields robust, transferable physical representations for Embodied AI.

title: Learning to Move Before Learning to Do: Task-Agnostic pretraining for VLAs

abstract: Diffusion-based generative image steganography converts the input single secret image into noise, and generates the stego image with it serves as the initial noise. Nevertheless, existing methods exhibit three severe limitations: (1) the fixed hiding space constrains their capacity to one secret image; (2) severe inter-secret interference arising from substantial information divergence among multiple secret images while concealing them within a shared hiding space; (3) security risks owing to the absence of the receiver-side verification mechanism. To systematically address these issues, this paper proposes a novel Receiver Authenticable Generative Image Steganography framework based on diffusion models. We introduce a Dynamic Cover Selection and Optimization Engine to adaptively allocate suitable hiding spaces for different secret images. This design permits the concealment of disparate secret images (or fragments of a single image) into separate spaces, enabling dynamic multi-image concealment while effectively preventing inter-secret interference and expanding capacity through the enlarged hiding spaces. Furthermore, a Signature Authentication Controller cryptographically signs the secret container after concealing and verifies it before extraction, ensuring secure receiver isolation and precise localization of the secret data container. Experiments demonstrate that the proposed framework achieves superior secure multi-receiver isolation and high-performance generative image steganography with large capacity.

paragraphs: Generative image steganography hides secret images within images produced by a diffusion model. The paper identifies three problems with existing approaches: a fixed hiding space limits capacity, multiple secrets interfere when placed in the same space, and receivers lack a verification mechanism. Its framework addresses capacity allocation and receiver authentication together.

It can distribute either separate images or fragments of one image across distinct spaces. This separation is designed to prevent interference between secrets while increasing total capacity. A signature controller then cryptographically signs the secret container after concealment and checks it before extraction, supporting receiver isolation and identification of the relevant container.

summary.tldr: The framework combines adaptive hiding-space allocation with signed secret containers to support higher-capacity image steganography and receiver verification.

title: Large-capacity and Receiver Authenticable Generative Image Steganography

abstract: Achieving a complete and explorable 360-degree visual world is a cornerstone of immersive content creation. While recent advances in video generation have achieved impressive results, they follow a 2D paradigm that treats content generation as transitions of 2D pixels, lacking an intrinsic understanding of the physical 3D world, resulting in frequent geometric inconsistencies. To achieve an explorable and physical-consistent visual world, the generation process should shift to a 3D paradigm: the visual content is governed by the physical relationships of the entire 3D environment together with 3D motion signals. However, under this setting, the conventional modeling methods and control signals, such as spatial attention computation in a 2D space, become unsuitable and ineffective. To address this, we propose PanoWorld-X for explorable immersive scene video generation. Our framework is built on the panoramic representation, which naturally maps a 3D scene into a standard format and provides an ideal basis for consistency. Specifically, we first develop a data curation pipeline to produce high-quality and large-motion 3D scene evolution with movement trajectories. To achieve precise control, we design the Exploration Panoramic Plücker Embedding (PPE), a guidance signal tailored for 3D motion. Furthermore, leveraging the spherical geometric properties of panoramic data, we propose a sphere-aware attention mechanism, which can capture true geometric adjacency by reprojecting features onto a spherical surface. Extensive experiments demonstrate that PanoWorld-X achieves superior performance in motion range, control precision, and visual quality, underscoring its potential for real-world applications.

Its approach uses panoramic representations and three-dimensional motion signals to better connect generation with the geometry of the surrounding environment.

These components address complementary requirements: examples of scene evolution, precise movement control, and spatial relationships suited to panoramic content. The authors report superior motion range, control precision, and visual quality in extensive experiments. The findings support the potential of spherical geometry and motion-aware guidance for immersive scene generation, while the stated results concern generated visual worlds rather than a guarantee of complete physical simulation.
summary.tldr: PanoWorld-X combines panoramic geometry, sphere-aware attention, and 3D motion guidance to generate more controllable explorable visual scenes.

title: PanoWorld-X: Generating Explorable Panoramic Worlds via Sphere-Aware Video Diffusion

abstract: Gesture interaction and touchless sensing is a natural and intuitive control method that allows users to control devices through natural hand or body movements, reducing reliance on physical input and enhancing convenience and functional efficiency. The biggest challenge is balancing accuracy and model parameter count for custom gesture tasks, while minimizing the number of data samples required for training. This paper proposes a novel IMU-based BiCrossNet model and two novel data augmentation models (delta-generator and embedding-generator) to address this challenge. Compared with existing methods, the model proposed in this article boosts accuracy by 11.7% and 12.7% in UMAHand (public datasets); and 8.85% and 5.25% in GRHand (self-developed datasets), with decreasing 27.8% pretrained feature-extractor model parameters. This research lays a solid foundation for deploying and implementing custome gesture recognition engineering on intelligent terminal devices.

paragraphs: Custom gesture recognition must accommodate movements chosen for a particular interaction while keeping training data requirements manageable. For intelligent devices, model size also matters. This paper targets the combined challenge of recognizing gestures accurately, learning from few examples, and limiting the number of parameters needed by the recognition system.

The proposed framework combines an IMU-based recognition model called BiCrossNet with two data augmentation models, named the delta-generator and embedding-generator. The recognition model and augmentation components address the learning problem together: the system seeks better recognition under limited examples while reducing the size of its pretrained feature extractor. Its intended application is touchless control through hand or body movements.

Compared with existing methods, the abstract reports accuracy improvements of 11.7% and 12.7% on the public UMAHand dataset, and 8.85% and 5.25% on the authors’ GRHand dataset. It also reports 27.8% fewer pretrained feature-extractor parameters. These results indicate a favorable experimental balance between recognition performance and model size, supporting the framework’s intended use on intelligent terminal devices.
summary.tldr: BiCrossNet combines IMU-based gesture recognition with two augmentation models, reporting higher accuracy with fewer feature-extractor parameters.

title: BiCrossNet with Decoupled Dual Generators: A Parameter-Efficient and Generalizable Few-Shot Custom Gesture Recognition Framework

abstract: Traditional evaluations measure a learning algorithm’s final performance on an i.i.d. test set, reducing learning to a single aggregate score. This approach obscures a fundamental question: to what extent does learning from a specific example generalize to others? Such per-sample generalization—akin to learning by analogy in human cognition—captures how far the knowledge extracted from one example can transfer, yet remains invisible to standard benchmarks. We introduce the Generalization Spectrum, an evaluation framework designed to expose this hidden dimension. For each training example, we construct a controlled suite of test variants arranged by increasing transfer distance—from exact recall to implementation transfer across languages, context transfer under complete narrative re-framing, category-matched in-domain problems, and an unpaired baseline. By tracking performance across these distances, we reveal not just whether an algorithm learns, but how far that learning extends. We instantiate this framework on competitive programming, using a synthetic generation pipeline seeded with recent problems to mitigate contamination. We first compare three canonical learning paradigms under matched memorization. RL converts memorization into near-transfer more efficiently than SFT-family baselines, while ICL exhibits strong but correspondence-dependent transfer. We then use the Spectrum to diagnose within-family variants. The resulting profiles show that local gains need not expand the generalization radius: abstractions and hints mainly lift local transfer, RFT preserves a stronger far-transfer tail than reference SFT, and self-distillation or hint-assisted RL can reduce far transfer even when local transfer or optimization improves.
