The resulting profiles show that local gains need not expand the generalization radius: abstractions and hints mainly lift local transfer, RFT preserves a stronger far-transfer tail than reference SFT, and self-distillation or hint-assisted RL can reduce far transfer even when local transfer or optimization improves.

paragraphs: An aggregate test score does not reveal how far learning from a particular example transfers. The Generalization Spectrum measures this by constructing related test variants at increasing transfer distances. These range from exact recall through implementations in other languages, complete narrative reframing, category-matched problems, and an unpaired baseline.

The authors instantiate the framework in competitive programming using synthetic generation seeded by recent problems to mitigate contamination. Comparing learning paradigms at matched memorization, they find that reinforcement learning converts memorization into nearby transfer more efficiently than supervised fine-tuning methods. In-context learning shows strong transfer that depends on correspondence between examples and test problems.

The framework also reveals differences within learning families. Abstractions and hints mainly improve nearby transfer, while RFT retains stronger distant transfer than reference SFT. Self-distillation and hint-assisted reinforcement learning can reduce distant transfer even as local transfer or optimization improves. These profiles show why an improvement close to training examples need not mean that an algorithm’s learning extends farther.
summary.tldr: The Generalization Spectrum measures how far learning transfers from individual examples, revealing gains and tradeoffs hidden by aggregate scores.

title: The Generalization Spectrum: A Chromatographic Approach to Evaluating Learning Algorithms

abstract: Despite rapid progress in Grounded Visual Reasoning (GVR) with MLLMs and RL-style fine-tuning, existing approaches often lack effective learning signals for intermediate grounding decisions and are prone to shortcut solutions. In this work, we explicitly decompose GVR into Evidence Generation followed by Counterfactual Answer Reasoning, and formalize this structure as a Causal Grounding Graph (CGG) in which the generated evidence acts as a causal mediator. Building on this formulation, we propose CofactGVR, which estimates the mediator’s utility via a matched counterfactual intervention that perturbs the predicted region while keeping the original image–question context fixed. The factual–counterfactual reward gap yields a principled intermediate bonus, selectively assigned to high-quality factual rollouts to promote evidence-faithful reasoning. To further stabilize and efficiently exploit this causal training signal, we incorporate a Quantile-filtered Prioritized Advantage Sampling (Q-PAS) strategy that preferentially updates on trajectories with high-magnitude advantages while filtering low-signal samples. Extensive experiments across GVR benchmarks show consistent improvements, indicating that CofactGVR strengthens reliance on informative visual evidence under controlled interventions. Our source code will be released at https://github.com/zhangy0822/CofactGVR.

paragraphs: Visual reasoning systems need to choose useful image evidence as well as produce correct answers. A training signal focused on the final answer can leave those intermediate choices weakly supervised and permit shortcuts. CofactGVR separates evidence generation from answer reasoning and represents their connection with a causal graph in which the selected evidence mediates the answer.

The method tests the value of that evidence through a matched counterfactual intervention. It perturbs the predicted region while holding the original image and question context fixed, then compares factual and counterfactual rewards. This helps stabilize and use the intervention-based feedback efficiently. Experiments across grounded visual reasoning benchmarks show consistent improvements. The findings indicate stronger reliance on useful visual evidence under the controlled interventions, connecting better intermediate grounding decisions with improved overall reasoning.
summary.tldr: CofactGVR rewards useful visual evidence by measuring how controlled changes to a selected image region affect answer rewards.

title: CofactGVR: Counterfactual Intervention for Grounded Visual Reasoning

abstract: Modern Latent Diffusion Models (LDMs) typically operate in low-level Variational Autoencoder (VAE) latent spaces that are primarily optimized for pixel-level reconstruction. To unify vision generation and understanding, a burgeoning trend is to adopt high-dimensional features from representation encoders as generative latents. However, we empirically identify two fundamental obstacles in this paradigm: (1) the discriminative feature space lacks compact regularization, making diffusion models prone to off-manifold latents that lead to inaccurate object structures; and (2) the encoder’s inherently weak pixel-level reconstruction hinders the generator from learning accurate fine-grained geometry and texture. In this paper, we propose a systematic framework to adapt understanding-oriented encoder features for generative tasks. We introduce a semantic–pixel reconstruction objective to regularize the latent space, enabling the compression of both semantic information and fine-grained details into a highly compact representation (96 channels with $16\times$ spatial downsampling). This design allows the latent space to remain semantically rich while achieving state-of-the-art image reconstruction, and keeps it compact enough for accurate generation. Leveraging this representation, we design a unified text-to-image (T2I) and image editing model. Across diverse generation spaces, our approach achieves state-of-the-art reconstruction, faster convergence, and substantial gains in both T2I and editing tasks, demonstrating that representation encoders can be effectively adapted into robust generative components.

paragraphs: Features learned for visual understanding are attractive building blocks for image generation because they contain semantic information. However, the authors identify two obstacles: these feature spaces lack compact regularization, and their encoders reconstruct pixels poorly. In their experiments, the first problem permits generated representations that produce inaccurate object structures, while the second interferes with learning fine geometry and texture.

The paper adapts these features using a training objective that combines semantic and pixel reconstruction. It compresses meaning and visual detail into a representation with 96 channels and 16-fold spatial downsampling. The goal is to retain useful semantic structure while making the representation compact and detailed enough for accurate reconstruction and generation.

Using this representation, the authors build a unified model for text-to-image generation and image editing. Across the evaluated generation spaces, they report state-of-the-art reconstruction, faster convergence, and substantial improvements in both tasks. The findings indicate that understanding-oriented encoders can become effective generative components when their training addresses both semantic organization and faithful visual reconstruction.
summary.tldr: Joint semantic and pixel reconstruction makes visual-understanding features more compact and effective for image generation and editing.

title: Both Semantics and Reconstruction Matter: Making Representation Encoders Ready for Text-to-Image Generation and Editing

abstract: Native 4K (2176$\times$3840) video generation remains a critical challenge due to the quadratic computational explosion of full-attention as spatiotemporal resolution increases, making it difficult for models to strike a balance between efficiency and quality. This paper proposes a novel Transformer retrofit strategy termed T3 (Transform Trained Transformer) that, without altering the core architecture of full-attention pretrained models, significantly reduces compute requirements by optimizing their forward logic. Specifically, T3-Video introduces a multi-scale weight-sharing window attention mechanism and, via hierarchical blocking together with an axis-preserving full-attention design, can effect an “attention pattern” transformation of a pretrained model using only modest compute and data. Results on 4K-VBench show that T3-Video substantially outperforms existing approaches: while delivering performance improvements (+4.29$\uparrow$ VQA and +0.08$\uparrow$ VTC), it accelerates native 4K video generation by more than 10$\times$. Demo and source code are available in #Supp.

paragraphs: Native 4K video generation puts heavy pressure on full attention because its computational cost grows quadratically as spatiotemporal resolution increases. T3, short for Transform Trained Transformer, addresses this cost by changing the forward computation of an already trained model. The strategy preserves the core architecture while transforming the attention patterns used during generation.

T3-Video combines multi-scale window attention with shared weights, hierarchical blocking, and an axis-preserving full-attention design. These mechanisms reorganize how the pretrained model performs attention. The paper reports that this transformation requires only modest computation and data, making adaptation of an existing full-attention model central to the approach.

On 4K-VBench, T3-Video accelerates native video generation at 2176 by 3840 resolution by more than tenfold. It also reports improvements of 4.29 in VQA and 0.08 in VTC. The findings show an efficiency gain accompanied by improvements on the reported quality measures, supporting attention-pattern transformation as a way to make pretrained models more practical for native high-resolution video generation.
summary.tldr: T3-Video transforms pretrained attention patterns to accelerate native 4K generation by over tenfold while improving reported quality measures.

title: Transform Trained Transformer for Accelerating Native 4K Video Generation

abstract: Parallel thinking has emerged as a promising paradigm for reasoning, yet it imposes significant computational burdens. Existing efficiency methods primarily rely on local, per-trajectory signals and lack principled mechanisms to exploit global dynamics across parallel branches. We introduce 2D probing, an interface that exposes the width–depth dynamics of parallel thinking by periodically eliciting intermediate answers from all branches. Our analysis reveals three key insights: non-monotonic scaling across width–depth allocations, heterogeneous reasoning branch lengths, and early stabilization of global consensus. Guided by these insights, we introduce $\textbf{{Parallel-Probe}}$, a training-free controller designed to optimize online parallel thinking. Parallel-Probe employs consensus-based early stopping to regulate reasoning depth and deviation-based branch pruning to dynamically adjust width. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks and multiple models demonstrate that Parallel-Probe establishes a superior Pareto frontier for test-time scaling. Compared to standard majority voting, it reduces sequential tokens by up to $\textbf{35.8}$% and total token cost by over $\textbf{25.8}$% while maintaining competitive accuracy.

Our analysis reveals three key insights: non-monotonic scaling across width–depth allocations, heterogeneous reasoning branch lengths, and early stabilization of global consensus. Guided by these insights, we introduce $\textbf{{Parallel-Probe}}$, a training-free controller designed to optimize online parallel thinking. Extensive experiments across three benchmarks and multiple models demonstrate that Parallel-Probe establishes a superior Pareto frontier for test-time scaling. paragraphs: Parallel reasoning explores multiple solution branches, increasing computational cost through both the number of branches and their length. Parallel-Probe studies these two dimensions together by periodically asking every branch for an intermediate answer. This exposes the collective behavior of the reasoning process, beyond the local signals available from individual trajectories.

The analysis finds that allocating more width or depth does not improve results monotonically, that branches require different reasoning lengths, and that global consensus can stabilize early. These observations motivate a training-free controller. It uses consensus to decide when to stop reasoning and deviation-based pruning to adjust how many branches remain active.

Across three benchmarks and multiple models, the authors report an improved tradeoff between accuracy and computational cost. Compared with standard majority voting, sequential token use falls by up to 35.8% and total token cost by over 25.8%, while accuracy remains competitive. The results support coordinating reasoning resources using intermediate agreement across branches, allowing computation to respond to how the parallel search is developing.
summary.tldr: Parallel-Probe uses intermediate answers across reasoning branches to reduce token costs while maintaining competitive accuracy.

title: Parallel-Probe: Towards Efficient Parallel Thinking via 2D Probing

abstract: AI safety research has mainly focused on two areas: technical alignment (ensuring AI systems produce human-aligned outputs) and the regulation of generative AI’s societal impacts (including unemployment risk and labor market disruption). However, an equally important dimension remains underexplored: the risk inherent in dependence on AI systems themselves. In this position paper, we argue that AI safety research should address $\textbf{\textit{AI Lock-In}}$, the phenomenon whereby excessive reliance on AI systems leads to human deskilling, diminishes human capacity for independent functioning, and creates systemic vulnerabilities when AI systems become unavailable or compromised. We highlight that AI Lock-In is a systemic threat that is already emerging at individual, societal, and national levels, one that could be dramatically amplified by AI service disruptions or geopolitical conflicts. Drawing on detailed scenarios, we investigate how AI Lock-In emerges and escalates across multiple levels, ranging from individual skill atrophy to national-scale infrastructure failures. To address this, we provide guidance on how such risks can be mitigated and prepared for at each level. We contend that proactively addressing AI Lock-In before such dependencies become entrenched and irreversible is essential for preserving individual autonomy and national security.

paragraphs: This paper identifies dependence on AI as a safety concern in its own right. The authors use AI Lock-In to describe excessive reliance that erodes human skills and the capacity to function independently. Such dependence creates vulnerabilities when systems become unavailable or compromised, even apart from questions about their usual outputs.

Using detailed scenarios, the paper examines how this process can develop at individual, societal, and national levels. Its scope extends from people losing practiced abilities to failures involving national infrastructure. The authors argue that the threat is already emerging and could become much more severe during service disruptions or geopolitical conflicts.

The paper provides guidance for mitigation and preparation at each level and calls for dependence to receive more attention within AI safety research. Its central concern is the persistence of these dependencies: once skills and independent capacity have been lost, reliance may become difficult to reverse. The authors therefore advocate acting before lock-in becomes entrenched, linking preparation to personal autonomy and national security.
summary.tldr: The paper argues that growing dependence on AI can erode independent human capacity and create systemic vulnerabilities requiring preparation.

abstract: We describe a probabilistic approach for supervised learning when we have multiple experts/annotators providing (possibly noisy) labels but no absolute gold standard. The proposed algorithm evaluates the different experts and also gives an estimate of the actual hidden labels. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method clearly beats the commonly used majority voting baseline.
originalAbstract: We describe a probabilistic approach for supervised learning when we have multiple experts/annotators providing (possibly noisy) labels but no absolute gold standard. The proposed algorithm evaluates the different experts and also gives an estimate of the actual hidden labels. Experimental results indicate that the proposed method clearly beats the commonly used majority voting baseline.

paragraphs: Supervised learning becomes more complicated when several annotators provide labels and those labels may be noisy. This paper considers the setting where there is also no absolute gold standard to resolve disagreements. The available expert judgments must therefore support learning even though the actual labels are hidden and cannot simply be read from a trusted reference.

The proposed probabilistic approach addresses two linked questions: how to evaluate the different experts and how to estimate the underlying labels. Its algorithm produces both kinds of estimates. This makes the quality of the annotation sources part of the learning problem, alongside the task of deciding what labels the examples should receive.

Experiments indicate that the method clearly outperforms majority voting, a commonly used way to combine annotations. The result supports modeling the experts and hidden labels when learning from uncertain judgments. Its practical significance is that disagreement need not be resolved solely by counting votes; the proposed probabilistic treatment offers a tested alternative in the stated setting without a gold standard.
summary.tldr: A probabilistic method jointly evaluates annotators and estimates hidden labels, outperforming majority voting in reported experiments without a gold standard.

title: Supervised learning from multiple experts: whom to trust when everyone lies a bit

abstract: This short paper summarizes challenges and opportunities of applying machine learning methods to Web design problems, and describes how structured prediction, deep learning, and probabilistic program induction can enable useful interactions for designers. We intend for these techniques to foster new work in data-driven Web design.
originalAbstract: This short paper summarizes challenges and opportunities of applying machine learning methods to Web design problems, and describes how structured prediction, deep learning, and probabilistic program induction can enable useful interactions for designers. We intend for these techniques to foster new work in data-driven Web design.

paragraphs: This short paper examines how machine learning could contribute to web design. Its focus is on the challenges and opportunities involved in applying learning methods to design problems, with particular attention to useful interactions for designers. It presents a research direction centered on bringing data-driven methods into the design process.

The discussion identifies structured prediction, deep learning, and probabilistic program induction as relevant approaches. By bringing these methods into the same discussion, the paper frames data-driven web design as a problem that can draw on several kinds of machine learning. The emphasis is on how these techniques can support designer interactions and motivate further work in the area.

The intended contribution is an agenda for research and application. The abstract describes possibilities for useful interactions and invites new work, so its claims concern opportunities rather than established performance improvements. Its significance lies in connecting machine learning methods with the needs of web designers and treating that connection as a topic worthy of focused investigation.
summary.tldr: The paper outlines how structured prediction, deep learning, and probabilistic program induction could support useful interactions in web design.
